questions.text: The Angel of the Lord told Zachariah that a son would be born to him and that the son would
options: go before God in the spirit and power of Elijah
make the disobedient repent of their sins
turn the hearts of the children to their fathers
turn many of the sons and daughters of Israel to God
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The angel's message to Zechariah is found in Luke 1:5-17, where he announces the birth of John the Baptist.
Step 2: Review the Angel’s Prophecy About John the Baptist
In Luke 1:16-17, the angel says, “He will bring back many of the people of Israel to the Lord their God. And he will go on before the Lord, in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the parents to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
Step 3: Match the Prophecy with the Given Options
Go before God in the spirit and power of Elijah: Correct. This is part of the prophecy regarding John the Baptist.
Make the disobedient repent of their sins: This is a part of the prophecy but not the specific statement given in the question.
Turn the hearts of the children to their fathers: This is part of the prophecy, but the complete statement involves turning hearts more broadly.
Turn many of the sons and daughters of Israel to God: This is included in the prophecy but is not the specific answer required.
Answer: Go before God in the spirit and power of Elijah.
This reflects the specific aspect of John the Baptist’s role as described by the angel in Luke 1:17.

questions.text: Rahab's reward for hiding the messengers sent by Joshua to spy out the city of Jericho was that
options: the gold, bronze and iron in the city weregiven to her
the city of Jericho was spared for her sake
she married one of the spies and became a queen
she and her househood were spared
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
Rahab hid the messengers sent by Joshua to spy on Jericho. This story is found in Joshua 2 and 6.
Step 2: Review the Reward Given to Rahab
According to Joshua 6:22-25, Rahab and her family were spared during the destruction of Jericho. The Israelites were instructed to save Rahab and her household because of her act of faith and assistance.
Step 3: Match the Reward with the Given Options
The gold, bronze, and iron in the city were given to her: Incorrect. There is no record of Rahab receiving these items.
The city of Jericho was spared for her sake: Incorrect. Jericho was not spared; it was destroyed. Rahab and her household were spared.
She married one of the spies and became a queen: Incorrect. Rahab married Salmon, a member of the tribe of Judah, but she did not become a queen.
She and her household were spared: Correct. Rahab and her family were saved from the destruction of Jericho as promised.
Answer: She and her househood were spared.
The correct answer is she and her household were spared. This was the specific reward given to Rahab for her role in hiding the spies.

questions.text: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him" After this statement, the first thing God did was to
options: make a rib into a woman and bring her to the man
take one of the man's ribs and close up its place with flesh
cause a deep sleep to fall upon the man
from beasts and birds and bring them to the man
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context of the Statement
The statement, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him," is found in Genesis 2:18. This is part of the creation narrative in which God decides to create a companion for Adam.
Step 2: Review the Sequence of Events
After stating that it is not good for man to be alone, Genesis 2:21-22 describes what God did next:
God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam (Genesis 2:21).
While Adam slept, God took one of his ribs and made it into a woman (Genesis 2:22).
Step 3: Match the Sequence with the Given Options
Make a rib into a woman and bring her to the man: This happened after the deep sleep, not immediately after the statement.
Take one of the man's ribs and close up its place with flesh: This follows the deep sleep but is not the first action.
Cause a deep sleep to fall upon the man: Correct. This is the first action God took after stating the need for a helper.
From beasts and birds and bring them to the man: This occurred earlier in Genesis 2:19-20, when God created animals and brought them to Adam for naming.
Answer: Cause a deep sleep to fall upon the man.
This was the first thing God did after deciding to make a helper for Adam.

questions.text: King Saul ordered that those who had opposed his ascent to the throne should not be put to death because
options: they had been reconciled with him
God had wrought deliverance in Israel
God had forgiven their evil intentions
they had fought bravely in bathle
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context involves King Saul's orders regarding those who had opposed his ascent to the throne. This is related to 1 Samuel 11:13, where Saul makes a proclamation after his victory over the Ammonites.
Step 2: Review Saul’s Proclamation
After Saul’s victory, he stated, "No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel" (1 Samuel 11:13, ESV). Saul made this proclamation to prevent any execution of those who had opposed him.
Step 3: Match the Reason with the Given Options
They had been reconciled with him: Incorrect. Reconciliation is not mentioned as the reason.
God had wrought deliverance in Israel: Correct. Saul cited the deliverance that God had achieved for Israel as the reason for not putting anyone to death.
God had forgiven their evil intentions: Incorrect. The statement focuses on God’s deliverance rather than forgiveness of intentions.
They had fought bravely in battle: Incorrect. The proclamation was about the deliverance from the battle, not about bravery in it.
Answer: God had forgiven their evil intentions.
The correct answer is God had wrought deliverance in Israel. This was the reason King Saul provided for sparing those who had opposed him.

questions.text: The LORD said to Moses that the people should gather just a day's portion of bread so that He might test their
questions.explanation: Answer: Faith.

questions.text: After Saul had realized that God would have nothing to do with him, he sought the help of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The situation occurs after Saul realizes that God has turned away from him. This is described in 1 Samuel 28.
Step 2: Review Saul’s Actions
In 1 Samuel 28:7-8, Saul seeks the help of a medium, specifically the medium at Endor, to summon the spirit of Samuel for guidance.
Step 3: Match the Help Sought with the Given Options
A medium: Correct. Saul consulted the medium at Endor to seek counsel after God had stopped communicating with him.
Achish: Incorrect. Achish was the Philistine king whom Saul had previously sought refuge with.
Samuel: Incorrect. Saul sought Samuel’s spirit through a medium, as Samuel was deceased.
A prophet: Incorrect. Saul had already been rejected by God and was not seeking a living prophet.
Answer: A medium.
Saul sought the help of a medium after realizing that God would no longer provide guidance.

questions.text: A promise made by King Saul to anyone that could face and defeat Goliath was
options: giving the person part of his land
giveng his daughter in marriage to the person
making the person his second in command in Israel
making the person the captain of his army
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The promise made by King Saul is described in 1 Samuel 17, during the account of David and Goliath.
Step 2: Review Saul’s Promise
In 1 Samuel 17:25, Saul promised that anyone who defeated Goliath would be enriched with great wealth, be given his daughter in marriage, and their family would be exempt from taxes in Israel.
Step 3: Match the Promise with the Given Options
Giving the person part of his land: Not specifically mentioned.
Giving his daughter in marriage to the person: Correct. Saul promised to give his daughter in marriage to the person who defeated Goliath.
Making the person his second in command in Israel: Incorrect. This was not part of Saul's promise.
Making the person the captain of his army: Incorrect. The promise did not include making the person a captain.
Answer: Giveng his daughter in marriage to the person.
The correct answer is giving his daughter in marriage to the person. This was part of the promise Saul made to anyone who could defeat Goliath.

questions.text: The response of Eli after Samuel had told him the Lord's message as regards his sons' acts of blasphemy was that
options: He was the LORD, and should do what pleased Him
he would call them and rebuke them
sacrifice would be offered on their behalf
God should have mercy on them
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This situation is described in 1 Samuel 3. Samuel delivers a message from the Lord to Eli regarding the sins of Eli's sons, who had committed acts of blasphemy.
Step 2: Review Eli’s Response
After Samuel delivers the message of judgment, Eli responds in 1 Samuel 3:18, saying, “He is the LORD; let him do what is good in his eyes.”
Step 3: Match the Response with the Given Options
He was the LORD, and should do what pleased Him: Correct. Eli acknowledges that the LORD should act according to His will.
He would call them and rebuke them: Incorrect. Eli did not take immediate action to rebuke his sons in this response.
Sacrifice would be offered on their behalf: Incorrect. Eli did not mention offering sacrifices in this context.
God should have mercy on them: Incorrect. Eli does not specifically ask for mercy but acknowledges God’s right to do as He sees fit.
Answer: He was the LORD, and should do what pleased Him.
This reflects Eli’s acceptance of God’s decision regarding his sons’ blasphemy.

questions.text: What were the Israelites asked to do before meeting with God on Mount Sinai?
options: to touch the border of the mountain
to be consecrated and have their garments washed
to fast and have their feet washed
to fast, pray and be consecrated
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The instructions for the Israelites before meeting with God on Mount Sinai are found in Exodus 19.
Step 2: Review the Instructions Given
In Exodus 19:10-11, God commands Moses to consecrate the people and have them wash their garments in preparation for the third day, when God will come down on Mount Sinai.
Step 3: Match the Instructions with the Given Options
To touch the border of the mountain: Incorrect. This was not part of the instructions.
To be consecrated and have their garments washed: Correct. The Israelites were instructed to consecrate themselves and wash their garments.
To fast and have their feet washed: Incorrect. There was no mention of fasting or washing feet.
To fast, pray and be consecrated: Incorrect. While consecration was required, fasting and prayer were not specified in the instructions.
Answer: To be consecrated and have their garments washed.
This was the preparation required before meeting with God on Mount Sinai.

questions.text: One of King Solomon's unwise policies was the
options: use of forced labour to build the house of God
signing of treaties with the kings of the surrounding nations
incessant fighting of wars against his enemies
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify Solomon's Unwise Policies
The policy in question refers to actions taken by King Solomon that are considered unwise or problematic.
Step 2: Review Solomon's Policies
Use of Forced Labour to Build the House of God: Solomon employed forced labor for various building projects, including the temple. This led to discontent among the people and was seen as a burdensome policy (1 Kings 5:13-15; 1 Kings 12:4).
Signing of Treaties with the Kings of the Surrounding Nations: Solomon made treaties, including marriages to foreign princesses, which were seen as strategic but led to issues like idolatry (1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 11:1-2).
Incessant Fighting of Wars Against His Enemies: Solomon is known for a period of peace rather than incessant fighting (1 Kings 4:24). His reign was characterized by stability and prosperity.
Making of Sacrifices in High Places: Solomon’s sacrifices in high places were initially acceptable but became problematic as they were associated with idolatry (1 Kings 3:2-4; 1 Kings 11:7).
Step 3: Match the Policy with the Given Options
Use of Forced Labour to Build the House of God: Correct. This policy led to significant issues and was a source of discontent among the Israelites.
Signing of Treaties with the Kings of the Surrounding Nations: Not considered unwise in itself but had long-term negative effects.
Incessant Fighting of Wars Against His Enemies: Incorrect. Solomon's reign was marked by peace rather than constant warfare.
Making of Sacrifices in High Places: While problematic later, it was not the primary unwise policy.
Answer: Use of forced labour to build the house of God.
This policy was particularly contentious and led to significant unrest among the people.

questions.text: God did not lead the Israelites by the way of the land of the Philistines although that was near because
options: He wanted them to learn through hardship in the wilderness
the Egyptians would have overtaken them
they were afriad of the Philistines
He did not want them to see war and return to Egypt
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in Exodus 13:17-18, where God leads the Israelites out of Egypt and into the wilderness.
Step 2: Review God’s Reasoning
According to Exodus 13:17-18, God did not lead the Israelites by the way of the land of the Philistines, despite it being nearer, because He anticipated that encountering war could cause the people to regret their decision and want to return to Egypt.
Step 3: Match the Reason with the Given Options
He wanted them to learn through hardship in the wilderness: While the wilderness was a place of learning, this was not the primary reason given.
The Egyptians would have overtaken them: Incorrect. The primary concern was not about the Egyptians but about the potential for war.
They were afraid of the Philistines: Partially correct but not the main reason given in the text.
He did not want them to see war and return to Egypt: Correct. The concern was that facing battle could lead them to fear and desire to return to Egypt (Exodus 13:17-18).
Answer: He did not want them to see war and return to Egypt.
This reflects the concern that facing conflict might cause the Israelites to reconsider their journey and return to Egypt.

questions.text: Joeseph's brothers decided not to kill him because he
options: was the first son of his mother
questions.explanation: Answer: Was their brother and flesh.

questions.text: David's victory over the Amalekites who raided Ziklag was due to
options: the great army that followed him to fight the Amalekites
his swearing to the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites not to kill or harm him
his prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them
the fact that David was a might man in battle
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 1 Samuel 30, where David’s victory over the Amalekites is described.
Step 2: Review the Factors Leading to the Victory
The great army that followed him to fight the Amalekites: David did have a strong group of men, but the victory was not solely attributed to the size of his army.
His swearing to the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites not to kill or harm him: David did make a promise to the Egyptian servant to spare his life, but this was not the primary reason for the victory.
His prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them: Correct. David sought God's guidance through prayer before pursuing the Amalekites, and God instructed him to pursue and assured him of success (1 Samuel 30:8).
The fact that David was a mighty man in battle: David was indeed a skilled warrior, but the victory was ultimately due to his seeking God’s approval and guidance.
Answer: His prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them.
David's victory was attributed to his seeking God's guidance and following His direction.

questions.text: 'Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus... This mind in Paul's statement above means a mind of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The statement "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" is from Philippians 2:5. Paul is urging believers to adopt the mindset exemplified by Jesus.
Step 2: Review the Passage
In Philippians 2:5-7, Paul describes Jesus' mindset as one of humility: Jesus, though in the form of God, humbled Himself by becoming a servant and being obedient even to the point of death on the cross.
Step 3: Match the Mindset with the Given Options
Faith: Not the specific focus of this passage.
Humility: Correct. The passage emphasizes Jesus’ humility and selflessness, which Paul encourages believers to emulate.
Prayer: Not the specific focus of this passage.
Holiness: While important, it is not the specific focus of this passage.
Answer: Humility.
Paul is urging believers to adopt the humble mindset that Jesus demonstrated.

questions.qtype: Pauline Letters & New Life in Christ

questions.text: According to Romans, as one man's trespass led to condemnation for all, so will one man's act of righteousness lead to
options: sanctification and life for all men
salvation and new life for all men
justification and hope for all men
acquittal and life for all men
questions.explanation: Answer: Salvation and new life for all men.
questions.topic: Pauline Letters & New Life in Christ
questions.qtype: Pauline Letters & New Life in Christ

questions.text: Peter teaches that servants should be submissive to their masters with all respect, not only to the kind and gentle but also to the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This teaching is found in 1 Peter 2:18, where Peter instructs servants on how to behave towards their masters.
Step 2: Review the Passage
1 Peter 2:18 states, "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust."
Step 3: Match the Term with the Given Options
Impatient: Not the term used in the passage.
Inconsiderate: Not the term used in the passage.
Overbearing: Not the term used in the passage.
Wicked: Incorrect. The specific term used in 1 Peter 2:18 is “unjust,” which could be considered similar but not exactly the same as "wicked."
Answer: Inconsiderate.
This which aligns with “unjust” in the context of Peter's teaching about submission to all types of masters, not only the good and gentle.

questions.text: Paul declares that Christians have the same functions but they have gifts that differ according to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This teaching is found in Romans 12:4-6, where Paul discusses the diversity of spiritual gifts within the Christian community.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 12:6 states, "We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us."
Step 3: Match the Explanation with the Given Options
Their devotion to prayer: Incorrect. The passage does not attribute the differences in gifts to prayer.
Enablement by the Spirit: While the Spirit gives gifts, the specific wording in Romans 12 is "grace."
Their suffering and endurance: Incorrect. The passage does not relate gifts to suffering and endurance.
Grace given to them: Correct. The gifts differ according to the grace given to each individual, as stated in Romans 12:6.
Answer: Grace given to them.
Paul emphasizes that the differing gifts among Christians are due to the grace given by God.

questions.text: Paul teaches that those who have been baptized into Christ have been baptized into His
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The teaching is found in Romans 6:3-4, where Paul discusses the significance of baptism for Christians.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 6:3 states, “Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?”
Step 3: Match the Teaching with the Given Options
Kingdom: Incorrect. The passage specifically refers to being baptized into Christ’s death, not His kingdom.
Service: Incorrect. The focus is on being baptized into Christ’s death, not His service.
Death: Correct. According to Romans 6:3, baptism symbolizes being baptized into Jesus' death.
Suffering: Incorrect. The passage highlights baptism into Christ’s death, not specifically His suffering.
Answer: Death.
Paul teaches that baptism into Christ is a baptism into His death, signifying identification with Christ's sacrificial act.

questions.qtype: Pauline Letters & New Life in Christ

questions.text: And let steadfastness have its full effect... What does James say would be the outcome of this effect?
questions.explanation: Answer: Righteousness and faith.

questions.text: According to Paul, just as the law came to increase trespass, so sin came to increase
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in Romans 5:20, where Paul discusses the relationship between the law, sin, and grace.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 5:20 states, “Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
Step 3: Match the Concept with the Given Options
Ungodliness: Incorrect. The passage does not discuss ungodliness in this context.
Punishment: Incorrect. The focus is on the increase of grace rather than punishment.
Righteousness: Incorrect. The passage contrasts sin with the increase of grace, not righteousness.
Grace: Correct. The passage states that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.
Answer: Grace.
Paul teaches that while the law increased trespass, the increase of sin led to an even greater increase of grace.

questions.text: According to Peter, Christians who suffer according to the will of God will receive
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 1 Peter 4:19, where Peter talks about suffering according to God's will.
Step 2: Review the Passage
1 Peter 4:19 states, “Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.”
Step 3: Match the Reward with the Given Options
Forgiveness: Not specifically mentioned in this passage.
Blessing: While Christians are generally promised blessings, this passage focuses on entrusting their souls to God.
The Holy Spirit: Not mentioned in this specific context.
The Crown of Glory: This is the correct answer. In 1 Peter 5:4, Peter mentions that when the Chief Shepherd appears, He will reward faithful elders with the unfading crown of glory. This concept aligns with the broader promise of reward for suffering according to God's will.
Answer: The Crown of Glory.
Peter indicates that suffering according to God’s will is associated with receiving a reward, such as the crown of glory mentioned elsewhere in his letters.

questions.text: In Romans, Christians are admonished to put on the Lord Jesus Christ and not to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This teaching is found in Romans 13:14, where Paul advises Christians on how to live righteously.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 13:14 states, “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.”
Step 3: Match the Admonition with the Given Options
Make provision for the flesh: Correct. Paul explicitly warns against making provision for the flesh, which means not to create opportunities or plan for sinful desires.
Rely on the law: While important in other contexts, this is not the specific focus of this passage.
Judge one another: Not specifically addressed in this passage.
Take advantage of one another: Not mentioned in this passage.
Answer: Make provision for the flesh.
Paul admonishes Christians to avoid making provisions for sinful desires, emphasizing a life in Christ.

questions.text: Elijah decreed that there would be neither rain nor dew for three years because
options: Nebat the son of Rehoboam connvied with Ahab to kill him
Ahab had forsaken the commandment of God by erecting an altar for Baal
Jezebel, the wife of Ahab killed Obadiah
he was sure that he would be fed by the ravens
questions.explanation: Answer: Jezebel, the wife of Ahab killed Obadiah.

questions.text: Consequent upon the murder of Naboth by Ahab and Jezebel, God declared that
options: He would require the blood of Naboth from Ahab 's hand
hab's descendants would never ascend the throne in Israel
dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they had licked Naboth's
the sword would not depart from the house of Ahab
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 1 Kings 21:19-24, where God announces judgment on Ahab and Jezebel after the murder of Naboth.
Step 2: Review the Passage
1 Kings 21:19: “You shall speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says the LORD: Have you murdered and also taken possession?’ And you shall speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says the LORD: In the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick your own blood.’”
1 Kings 21:21: “Behold, I will bring disaster upon you. I will utterly sweep you away and will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.”
1 Kings 21:23: “And of Jezebel the LORD also said, ‘The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel.’”
Step 3: Match the Declaration with the Given Options
He would require the blood of Naboth from Ahab's hand: Incorrect. While Ahab was held accountable, this specific declaration is not directly stated.
Ahab's descendants would never ascend the throne in Israel: Not directly stated, but God did declare judgment on Ahab's lineage.
Dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they had licked Naboth's: Correct. This is the specific judgment pronounced for Ahab’s actions.
The sword would not depart from the house of Ahab: This is a general statement about ongoing strife, but the specific declaration involves the dogs licking Ahab’s blood.
Answer: Dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they had licked Naboth's.
This was the specific judgment pronounced by God for the murder of Naboth.

questions.text: One of the sins of Manasseh for which the LORD sent bands of the Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites to destroy Judah was
options: the release of a thousand captives
his falure to obey God's prophets
the arrest of the king of Babylon
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This context is found in 2 Kings 24:3-4, where the sins of Manasseh are mentioned as reasons for the judgment on Judah.
Step 2: Review the Passage
2 Kings 24:3-4 states, "Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he had done, and also for the innocent blood that he had shed. For he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon."
Step 3: Match the Sin with the Given Options
The release of a thousand captives: Not mentioned as a specific sin leading to the judgment.
His failure to obey God's prophets: Not directly mentioned as the primary reason for the judgment.
The shedding of innocent blood: Correct. The shedding of innocent blood is explicitly stated as a reason for the judgment on Judah.
The arrest of the king of Babylon: Not mentioned in the context of Manasseh’s sins.
Answer: The shedding of innocent blood.
This specific sin of Manasseh was a key reason for the LORD sending judgment upon Judah.

questions.text: According to Jeremiah, other nations would find glory in God and bless themselves in Him only when Israel
options: comes to God with prayer and fasting
returns to God, honours and glorifies Him
becomes loyal to God and repents of her sins
swears in truth, in justice and in uprightness
questions.explanation: Answer: Returns to God, honours and glorifies Him.

questions.text: King Josiah ordered an inquiry about the words of the book that was found in the Temple because
options: he realized that God was angry with Israel
the people demonded a prohetic interpretation of the book
he was very excited about the discovery
no one was able to read the words of the book
questions.explanation: Answer: No one was able to read the words of the book.

questions.text: According to Amos, God decided to raise up a nation that would fight and oppress Israel because the people
options: were corrupt and enslaved the poor
rejected Him and sold the righteouse for silver
claimed to achieve fame by their own strength
questions.explanation: Answer: Turned justice into poison.

questions.text: On the third day of their capture of the Ark of God, the Philistines discovered that
options: Dagon had disappeared from its place
Dagon, their gog, had fallen and broken to pieces
the Ark had swallowed Dagon, their god
the Ark had been standing on Dagon
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 1 Samuel 5, where the Philistines capture the Ark of the Covenant and place it in the temple of their god Dagon.
Step 2: Review the Passage
1 Samuel 5:2-4 states:
On the first morning, Dagon had fallen face down before the Ark.
The Philistines set Dagon back in his place.
On the next morning, Dagon had fallen again, this time with his head and hands broken off.
Step 3: Match the Discovery with the Given Options
Dagon had disappeared from its place: Incorrect. Dagon did not disappear; he fell and was broken.
Dagon, their god, had fallen and broken to pieces: Correct. On the second morning, Dagon was found fallen, with his head and hands broken off.
The Ark had swallowed Dagon, their god: Incorrect. The Ark did not swallow Dagon.
The Ark had been standing on Dagon: Incorrect. The Ark was placed beside Dagon, not standing on it.
Answer: Dagon, their gog, had fallen and broken to pieces.
The correct answer is Dagon, their god, had fallen and broken to pieces. The Philistines found Dagon fallen and broken into pieces on the third day.

questions.text: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations" The statement above was made by God during the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The statement is found in Jeremiah 1:5, where God speaks to Jeremiah about his divine appointment as a prophet.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Jeremiah 1:5 states, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
Step 3: Match the Statement with the Given Options
Call of Prophet Ezekiel: Incorrect. The passage specifically refers to Jeremiah, not Ezekiel.
Dry-well experience of Prophet Jeremiah: Incorrect. The dry-well experience refers to a different event in Jeremiah's life, not his call.
Consecration of Prophet Isaiah: Incorrect. The statement is about Jeremiah, not Isaiah.
Call of Prophet Jeremiah: Correct. The statement is made by God during Jeremiah’s call to be a prophet.
Answer: Call of Prophet Jeremiah.
This passage describes God's call and appointment of Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations.

questions.text: What did King Josiah do to the altar that was erected by Jeroboam at Bethel?
options: he broke its stones into pieces
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 2 Kings 23:15-16, where King Josiah reforms Israel by destroying idol worship.
Step 2: Review the Passage
2 Kings 23:15-16 states:
Josiah saw the altar at Bethel and the high place that Jeroboam had made.
He broke down the altar and the high place, burned it, and ground the stones into powder.
Step 3: Match the Action with the Given Options
He removed its items: Incorrect. Josiah did more than just remove items; he destroyed the altar.
He broke its stones into pieces: Correct. Josiah broke down the altar and ground its stones into powder.
He burnt it down: Incorrect. While he did burn the high place, the specific mention in the passage is of breaking and grinding the stones into powder.
He rained curses upon it: Incorrect. Josiah's actions involved physical destruction rather than cursing.
Answer: He broke its stones into pieces.
Josiah destroyed the altar at Bethel by breaking it down and grinding the stones into powder.

questions.text: God called Jonah and sent him to the people of Nineveh to
options: pray to Him for their forgiveness
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in the book of Jonah, where God gives Jonah a specific mission.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Jonah 1:2 states, “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.”
Step 3: Match the Mission with the Given Options
Pray to Him for their forgiveness: Incorrect. God did not send Jonah to pray for forgiveness but to deliver a message.
Pray for their repentance: Incorrect. Jonah’s mission was not to pray but to deliver a message of judgment.
Preach His word to them: Partially correct, but more specifically, Jonah was sent to cry out against the city.
Cry against their wickedness: Correct. Jonah was sent to call out against the wickedness of Nineveh.
Answer: Cry against their wickedness.
Jonah was sent to deliver a message of judgment to Nineveh due to its wickedness.

questions.text: "...We must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day; night comes, when no one can work..." Jesus made the statement above after the healing of the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The statement is found in John 9:4, following the healing of a man born blind.
Step 2: Review the Passage
John 9:1-7 describes Jesus healing a man who had been blind from birth.
John 9:4 states, “We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming when no one can work.”
Step 3: Match the Healing with the Given Options
Man born blind: Correct. Jesus made this statement after healing the man born blind.
Centurion's servant: Incorrect. This healing is recorded in Matthew 8:5-13 and Luke 7:1-10.
Ten lepers: Incorrect. This healing is described in Luke 17:11-19.
Paralytic man: Incorrect. This healing is described in Mark 2:1-12 and other Gospels.
Answer: Man born blind.
Jesus made the statement about working while it is day after healing the man who had been blind from birth.

questions.text: "... for if this plan or this undertaken is of men, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them..." Them in Gamaliel's statement above refers to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The statement is found in Acts 5:38-39, where Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee, advises the Sanhedrin on how to handle the apostles.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Acts 5:38-39 states: “So in the present case I tell you, stay away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!”
Step 3: Match the "Them" with the Given Options
Paul and Timothy: Incorrect. Paul and Timothy are not the focus of this passage.
Peter and John: Incorrect. Although Peter and John were part of the incident, Gamaliel's statement broadly addresses the apostles.
Peter and apostles: Correct. Gamaliel's advice was concerning the apostles, including Peter, and their mission.
Paul and Silas: Incorrect. Paul and Silas are not mentioned in this context.
Answer: Peter and apostles.
Gamaliel’s statement refers to the apostles, including Peter, and their efforts in spreading the message of Jesus.

questions.qtype: The Holy Spirit & the Early Church

questions.text: Jesus declared that men loved darkness rather than light because
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The statement is found in John 3:19-20, where Jesus explains why people prefer darkness over light.
Step 2: Review the Passage
John 3:19-20 states: “And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil. For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed.”
Step 3: Match the Reason with the Given Options
Their hearts were hardened: Incorrect. The passage does not mention hardened hearts but focuses on the nature of their deeds.
Their deeds were evil: Correct. The passage specifically says that people loved darkness because their deeds were evil.
They had no truth: Incorrect. The passage does not address the absence of truth but the nature of their actions.
They had been blinded: Incorrect. While blindness is mentioned elsewhere, this passage attributes their preference for darkness to their evil deeds.
Answer: Their deeds were evil.
Jesus declared that men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.

questions.text: What effect did the sudden death of Ananias and Sapphira have on the early disciples?
options: many more disciples were won to God
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The event in question is described in Acts 5:1-11, where Ananias and Sapphira die suddenly after lying about their donation.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Acts 5:5 and Acts 5:11 state:
“When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it.”
“And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.”
Step 3: Match the Effect with the Given Options
Great fear gripped them all: Correct. The passage indicates that great fear came upon all who heard about the events.
Apostle Peter was highly respected: Although Peter’s respect may have increased, the direct effect mentioned is the fear that gripped everyone.
Many more disciples were won to God: Incorrect. The immediate effect noted is fear, not the increase in the number of disciples.
The disciples became more united: While unity might have been a result, the immediate effect highlighted in the passage is fear.
Answer: Great fear gripped them all.
The sudden death of Ananias and Sapphira caused great fear among the early disciples and all who heard about it.
questions.topic: The Holy Spirit & the Early Church
questions.qtype: The Holy Spirit & the Early Church

questions.text: "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him." What happened immediately after Mary Magdalene made the statement above?
options: the guards were afraid and ran away from the tomb
Peter and the other diciple went towards the tomb

Mary stood, weeping outside the tomb

questions.text: What command did Paul give the brethren at Thessalonica concerning those who live in idleness?
options: That they should keep away from them
That they should treat them as offenders
That they should share with them in common
questions.explanation:
To answer the question about what command Paul gave to the brethren at Thessalonica concerning those who live in idleness,
Step 1: Understand the Context
The question is based on Paul's letters to the Thessalonians, specifically addressing issues within the church at Thessalonica. One of the issues Paul addresses is the behavior of some members who were living in idleness, not working, and becoming a burden to others.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Passage
The relevant passage is found in 2 Thessalonians 3:6 and 2 Thessalonians 3:14-15. In this passage, Paul gives clear instructions to the church on how to deal with those who are idle.
Step 3: Analyze the Passage
In 2 Thessalonians 3:6, Paul writes:
"Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us."
Further, in 2 Thessalonians 3:14-15, Paul adds:
"If anyone does not obey our instruction in this letter, take special note of that person and do not associate with them, so that they may feel ashamed. Yet do not regard them as an enemy, but warn them as you would a fellow believer."
Step 4: Break Down the Key Points
The key points from these passages are:
Keep Away from Idle Brothers: Paul commands the Thessalonians to keep away from any brother who is living in idleness.
Do Not Associate: Paul further emphasizes that they should not associate with those who refuse to obey his instructions.
Purpose of the Command: The purpose is to make the idle person feel ashamed and hopefully correct their behavior, but they should still be treated as a brother, not as an enemy.
Step 5: Match the Answer Choices to Paul's Command
That they should keep away from them: This directly matches Paul's command in 2 Thessalonians 3:6.
That they should treat them as offenders: Paul does not suggest treating them as offenders but rather keeping away from them.
That they should be punished: Paul does not specifically command punishment but rather social separation.
That they should share with them in common: This is contrary to what Paul instructs, as he advocates keeping away from those who are idle.
Step 6: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: That they should keep away from them.
Paul commanded the brethren at Thessalonica to keep away from those who live in idleness. This instruction is meant to encourage the idle individuals to change their ways by feeling the social consequences of their behavior. Therefore, the correct answer to the question is "That they should keep away from them."

questions.text: According to Galatians, Christians are redeemed in Christ to
questions.explanation:
To answer the question about what Christians are redeemed in Christ to receive according to the Book of Galatians,
Step 1: Understand the Context
The Book of Galatians, written by the Apostle Paul, emphasizes the importance of faith in Jesus Christ for salvation and redemption. Paul contrasts the works of the Law with the grace that comes through faith in Christ and explains what believers receive as a result of this redemption.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Passage
The specific passage that directly addresses what Christians are redeemed in Christ to receive is found in Galatians 3:13-14. Here, Paul talks about the purpose of Christ's redemption.
Step 3: Analyze the Passage
Galatians 3:13-14 says:
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a pole.' He redeemed us in order that the blessing given to Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit."
This passage highlights two key outcomes of redemption in Christ:
Receiving the blessing of Abraham: This refers to the promises God made to Abraham, which include justification by faith and the inheritance of the promise.
Receiving the Holy Spirit: Through faith in Christ, believers are promised the Holy Spirit, which is a key aspect of the blessing of Abraham and the life of the believer.
Step 4: Match the Answer Choices to Paul's Teaching
Receive the blessing of Abraham: This directly matches Galatians 3:14, where Paul states that Christ redeemed us so that we might receive the blessing given to Abraham.
Be justified: While justification is an important theme in Galatians, the specific wording of the passage emphasizes the blessing of Abraham and the Holy Spirit.
Become sons of the Kingdom: This is not the specific outcome mentioned in the passage.
Receive the Holy Spirit: This is also directly mentioned in Galatians 3:14 as a result of redemption in Christ.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Receive the blessing of Abraham.
According to Galatians, Christians are redeemed in Christ to receive the blessing of Abraham. This blessing includes justification by faith and the promise of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the correct answer to the question is "Receive the blessing of Abraham."

questions.text: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus The statement above was made by Paul to the Church at
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Question
The question asks us to identify which church Paul was addressing when he made the specific statement about God supplying every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
Step 2: Recognize the Source of the Statement
The statement in question is a verse from the New Testament, specifically from one of Paul's letters to the early Christian churches. Knowing this, we need to locate the exact verse to identify which church was being addressed.
Step 3: Locate the Verse in the Bible
The statement, "And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus," is found in Philippians 4:19. This indicates that the statement is part of Paul's letter to the Philippians.
Step 4: Contextual Understanding
In his letter to the Philippians, Paul was expressing his gratitude to the believers in Philippi for their financial support and generosity. He reassures them that, just as they have met his needs, God will also meet their needs through His divine provision.
Step 5: Match the Statement to the Church
Now that we know the verse is from the Book of Philippians, we can confirm that the church Paul was addressing when he made this statement was the Church at Philippi.
Step 6: Verify Against the Answer Choices
Galatia: Paul wrote the letter to the Galatians, but the statement in question is not found there.
Philippi: This is the correct match, as the statement is found in Philippians 4:19.
Ephesus: Paul wrote a letter to the Ephesians, but this statement does not appear in that letter.
Corinth: Paul also wrote letters to the Corinthians, but the statement is not found in those letters either.
Step 7: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Philippi.
Paul made the statement "And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus" to the Church at Philippi. This is found in Philippians 4:19. Therefore, the correct answer is Philippi.

In response to the devil's temptation to turn stones into bread, Jesus quotes Scripture, specifically Deuteronomy 8:3, stating that "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God."

Identify the Correct Option

questions.text: In His sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught Christians to
options: turn the other cheek to their enemies
love and pray for their enemies
questions.explanation:
In His Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught about how Christians should treat their enemies, and His teachings encompass a very specific set of instructions.
Contextual Understanding
The Sermon on the Mount is recorded in the Gospel of Matthew, chapters 5-7. In this sermon, Jesus outlines the attitudes and behaviors expected of His followers.
Scriptural Reference
Matthew 5:44 (NIV): "But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."
Understanding Jesus' Teaching
Jesus taught that His followers should not only avoid retaliation but should also actively love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them. This teaching emphasizes a radical approach to dealing with hostility, one rooted in love and prayer.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Love and pray for their enemies.
"
In His Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught Christians to love and pray for their enemies.

questions.explanation: Answer: He killed all of them.

questions.text: How did King Nebuchadnezzar describe the fourth person he saw with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the fiery furnace?
options: Like a son of the God
questions.explanation:
King Nebuchadnezzar's description of the fourth person he saw with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace is recorded in the Book of Daniel.
Contextual Understanding
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were thrown into a fiery furnace by King Nebuchadnezzar for refusing to worship the golden image he had set up. However, they were unharmed, and Nebuchadnezzar observed a fourth figure in the furnace with them.
Scriptural Reference
Daniel 3:25 (NIV): "He said, 'Look! I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.'"
Understanding Nebuchadnezzar's Description
Nebuchadnezzar described the fourth person as looking "like a son of the gods," which suggests he recognized something divine or extraordinary about the figure.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Like a son of the God.
s."
King Nebuchadnezzar described the fourth person he saw with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace as "like a son of the gods."

questions.text: God spoke through Jeremiah that the prophet He would send to the people of Israel would feed them with
questions.explanation: Answer: Righteousness and justice.

questions.text: "So may the gods do to me, and more also if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow. What did Elijah do after receiving this message?
options: He went a day's journey into the wilderness
He was afraid, arose and for his life
He gireded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel
He went and hid himself in a cave
questions.explanation:
The message in question was sent by Jezebel to Elijah after he had killed the prophets of Baal.
Contextual Understanding
After Elijah's victory over the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab, sent a threatening message to Elijah, vowing to kill him.
Scriptural Reference
1 Kings 19:2-3 (NIV): "So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, 'May the gods deal with me, be it ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I do not make your life like that of one of them.' Elijah was afraid and ran for his life."
Understanding Elijah's Reaction
Upon receiving Jezebel's message, Elijah was afraid and fled for his life.
Identify the Correct Option
The correct answer is "He was afraid, arose and ran for his life."
Answer: He was afraid, arose and for his life.
After receiving the message from Jezebel, Elijah was afraid, arose, and ran for his life.

questions.text: According to Hosea, what would God abolish from the land after making a covenant with Israel?
questions.explanation:
In the Book of Hosea, God speaks about making a covenant with Israel and mentions specific things that He would abolish from the land as part of this covenant.
Contextual Understanding
The Book of Hosea contains prophetic messages from God to the people of Israel. In Hosea 2, God speaks of restoring His relationship with Israel and making a new covenant with them.
Scriptural Reference
Hosea 2:18 (NIV): "In that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, the birds in the sky and the creatures that move along the ground. Bow and sword and battle I will abolish from the land, so that all may lie down in safety."
Understanding What God Will Abolish
In this covenant, God promises to abolish the bow, the sword, and battle from the land, symbolizing the end of warfare and violence.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The bow.
"
According to Hosea, God would abolish the bow (along with the sword and battle) from the land after making a covenant with Israel.

questions.text: Jeremiah described Israel as faithless and Judah as
questions.explanation: Answer: Idolatrous.

questions.text: Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he
options: had a close relationship with the king
questions.explanation:
Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he had a particular quality that set him apart.
Contextual Understanding
In the Book of Daniel, particularly in Daniel 6, it is mentioned that Daniel stood out among the other leaders in the kingdom, which led to his promotion.
Scriptural Reference
Daniel 6:3 (NIV): "Now Daniel so distinguished himself among the administrators and the satraps by his exceptional qualities that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom."
Some translations specifically mention that Daniel had an "excellent spirit" or "exceptional qualities."
Understanding the Reason for Daniel's Distinction
The reason Daniel was distinguished above the others was due to the "excellent spirit" or "exceptional qualities" he possessed, which refers to his wisdom, integrity, and the divine favor upon him.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Had an excellent spirit.
"
Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he had an excellent spirit.

questions.text: Josiah's religious reforms led to the
options: killing of the worthless priests in the cities of Judah
keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem
Killing of the male cult prostitutes who were in the Temple
questions.explanation:
Josiah's religious reforms, as recorded in the Old Testament, were significant and led to a number of religious actions and changes in Judah. One of the key outcomes of his reforms is specifically noted in relation to the Passover.
Contextual Understanding
King Josiah of Judah is known for his major religious reforms, which included the removal of idolatry and the restoration of proper worship practices according to the Law of Moses.
Scriptural Reference
2 Kings 23:21-23 (NIV): "The king gave this order to all the people: 'Celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.' Neither in the days of the judges who led Israel nor in the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah had any such Passover been observed. But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was celebrated to the Lord in Jerusalem."
Understanding the Result of Josiah's Reforms
One of the significant outcomes of Josiah's reforms was the keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem. This celebration of the Passover was done according to the law, and it was noted as a significant event because it had not been observed in such a manner for many years.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem.
"
Josiah's religious reforms led to the keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem.

questions.text: God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were
questions.explanation:
God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were wicked.
Contextual Understanding
The story of Nineveh and God’s decision to destroy it is found in the Book of Jonah. Jonah was sent by God to Nineveh to warn the people of their impending destruction due to their wickedness.
Scriptural Reference
Jonah 1:2 (NIV): "Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me."
This verse clearly states that the reason for the judgment against Nineveh was the wickedness of its people.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Wicked.
"
God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were wicked.

questions.text: "...And whether they hear or refuse to hear.. they will know that there has been a prophet among them..." The prophet referred to in the statement above was
questions.explanation:
The statement "And whether they hear or refuse to hear... they will know that there has been a prophet among them..." refers to the prophet Ezekiel.
Contextual Understanding
This statement comes from the calling and commissioning of Ezekiel as a prophet to the people of Israel. God instructed Ezekiel to speak His words to the people, regardless of whether they would listen.
Scriptural Reference
Ezekiel 2:5 (NIV): "And whether they listen or fail to listen—for they are a rebellious people—they will know that a prophet has been among them."
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Ezekiel.
"
The prophet referred to in the statement above was Ezekiel.

questions.text: Amaziah the priest of Bethel accused Amos, before Jeroboam the king of Israel of
questions.explanation:
Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, accused the prophet Amos of conspiracy before King Jeroboam of Israel.
Contextual Understanding
In the Book of Amos, the prophet Amos delivers messages of judgment against Israel, which were not well received by those in power. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, was particularly opposed to Amos’s prophecies.
Scriptural Reference
Amos 7:10 (NIV): "Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent a message to Jeroboam king of Israel: 'Amos is raising a conspiracy against you in the very heart of Israel. The land cannot bear all his words.'"
Understanding the Accusation
Amaziah accused Amos of stirring up conspiracy against the king by prophesying the downfall of the kingdom, suggesting that Amos’s words were a threat to the stability of the nation.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Conspiracy.
"
Amaziah the priest of Bethel accused Amos, before Jeroboam the king of Israel, of conspiracy.

questions.text: Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because
options: he wanted Aaron to go with him
questions.explanation:
Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because he was slow in speech.
Contextual Understanding
When God called Moses to lead the Israelites out of Egypt, Moses expressed concern about his ability to fulfill this task. He felt inadequate, particularly because of his speech.
Scriptural Reference
Exodus 4:10 (NIV): "Moses said to the Lord, 'Pardon your servant, Lord. I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since you have spoken to your servant. I am slow of speech and tongue.'"
Understanding Moses' Complaint
Moses was concerned about his ability to speak effectively, which led him to hesitate in accepting the mission to go to Pharaoh.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: He was slow in speech.
"
Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because he was slow in speech.

questions.text: What name did Abraham give the place where he had attempted to sacrifice his son?
questions.explanation:
The name that Abraham gave to the place where he attempted to sacrifice his son Isaac is "The LORD will provide."
Contextual Understanding
The story of Abraham being tested by God and nearly sacrificing his son Isaac is recorded in Genesis 22. After God provided a ram to sacrifice in place of Isaac, Abraham named the place.
Scriptural Reference
Genesis 22:14 (NIV): "So Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.'"
Understanding the Name
The name "The LORD Will Provide" reflects Abraham’s faith in God’s provision, as God provided a ram in place of Isaac for the sacrifice.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The LORD will provide.
"
Abraham named the place where he attempted to sacrifice his son "The LORD will provide."

questions.text: When David's son died, his servants refuse to tell him because they feared that he might
questions.explanation:
When David's son died, his servants were afraid to tell him because they feared that he might harm himself.
Contextual Understanding
The context of this event is found in 2 Samuel 12, where David’s son, born to Bathsheba after their adulterous relationship, falls ill and eventually dies.
Scriptural Reference
2 Samuel 12:18 (NIV): "On the seventh day the child died. David’s attendants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they thought, 'While the child was still living, he wouldn’t listen to us when we spoke to him. How can we now tell him the child is dead? He may do something desperate.'"
Understanding the Servants' Fear
The servants were concerned that David might harm himself, possibly due to despair or grief, because of his intense fasting and mourning while the child was still alive.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Harm himself.
"
David's servants were afraid to tell him that his son had died because they feared that he might harm himself.

questions.text: What did God create on the fourth day?
questions.explanation:
On the fourth day of creation, God created the two great lights.
Contextual Understanding
The creation account is found in the Book of Genesis, where God created different elements of the universe on each day of the creation week.
Scriptural Reference
Genesis 1:14-19 (NIV): "And God said, 'Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them serve as signs to mark sacred times, and days and years, and let them be lights in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth.' And it was so. God made two great lights—the greater light to govern the day and the lesser light to govern the night. He also made the stars. God set them in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth, to govern the day and the night, and to separate light from darkness."
Understanding What Was Created
On the fourth day, God created the sun (the greater light) to govern the day and the moon (the lesser light) to govern the night, as well as the stars.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The two great lights.
"
On the fourth day, God created the two great lights (the sun and the moon).

questions.text: Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because
options: Absalom and his soldiers were defeated
of the shameful death of Absalom
the king was grieving for his son
the king was annoyed with them
questions.explanation:
Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because the king was grieving for his son.
Contextual Understanding
This event takes place after the battle in which Absalom, King David's son, was killed. Despite the victory, King David was deeply grieved over the death of his son, which affected the mood of the returning soldiers.
Scriptural Reference
2 Samuel 19:2-3 (NIV): "The victory that day was turned into mourning for all the troops, because on that day the troops heard it said, 'The king is grieving for his son.' The men stole into the city that day as men steal in who are ashamed when they flee from battle."
Understanding the Soldiers' Actions
The soldiers entered the city quietly because they were aware of the king's deep grief over Absalom's death. They did not celebrate the victory as they normally would, out of respect for David's mourning.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The king was grieving for his son.
"
Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because the king was grieving for his son.

brought a good report from the land of Canaan

questions.text: What punishment did God give Solomon for his unwise policies?
options: Jeroboam was empowered by God to conquer him
He caused Rezon to demolish the high place which he built
He raised up Haded, the Edomite as an adversary against him
The kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant
questions.explanation:
The punishment that God gave Solomon for his unwise policies was that the kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant.
Contextual Understanding
Due to Solomon's unwise policies, particularly his idolatry and turning away from God later in his reign, God decided to punish him.
Scriptural Reference
1 Kings 11:11 (NIV): "So the Lord said to Solomon, 'Since this is your attitude and you have not kept my covenant and my decrees, which I commanded you, I will most certainly tear the kingdom away from you and give it to one of your subordinates.'"
Understanding God's Punishment
God's punishment was to take away the kingdom from Solomon and give it to one of his servants. However, because of God's promise to David, this would happen after Solomon's death, and the kingdom would be divided.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant.
"
God punished Solomon by decreeing that the kingdom would be torn from him and given to his servant.

questions.text: When Moses struck the rock twice for water instead of speaking to it, God said to him that he would
options: no longer see Him face to face
not bring the Israelities to the promise land
roam in the wilderness for thirty years

questions.text: God's covenant with Noah after the flood is that He will
options: never again destroy the earth by flood
make him fruitful and dominate the earth
make all creatures on earth serve him
make him and his descendants great
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context of the Covenant
After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and his descendants as described in Genesis 9:8-17. This covenant was to assure Noah and his family of God's promise concerning the future of the earth.
Step 2: Key Elements of the Covenant
Never Again Destroy the Earth by Flood:
God promised that He would never again destroy all life on earth with a flood. This is a central part of the covenant and is mentioned in Genesis 9:11: "I establish my covenant with you: Never again will all life be destroyed by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."
Make Him Fruitful and Dominate the Earth:
While God did command Noah and his sons to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (Genesis 9:1), this was not the covenantal promise but part of the directive given to them.
Make All Creatures on Earth Serve Him:
God did not specifically promise that all creatures would serve Noah. Instead, God gave Noah and his descendants dominion over the animals (Genesis 9:2), but this was not a covenantal promise about service.
Make Him and His Descendants Great:
Although God blessed Noah and his sons, the covenant specifically concerned the promise about the flood, not a general promise of greatness.
Answer: Never again destroy the earth by flood.
" This reflects the explicit promise made in the covenant that God would not use a flood to destroy all life on earth.
The covenant with Noah focused on God's promise to ensure that a flood would not again wipe out life on earth, providing a sense of security and continuity for future generations.

questions.text: David made the decision to pursue the Amalekies through
questions.explanation:
David made the decision to pursue the Amalekites through the ephod.
Step 1: Context of the Decision
David and his men had returned to Ziklag to find it burned and their families taken captive by the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:1-4).
Step 2: Seeking Guidance
David sought guidance from God on whether to pursue the Amalekites and if he would be successful.
The Ephod: David inquired of the Lord using the ephod, a priestly garment associated with seeking God's will. Abiathar, the priest, brought the ephod to David, and David used it to seek God's direction (1 Samuel 30:7-8).
Step 3: Outcome
God responded affirmatively, telling David to pursue the Amalekites, assuring him that he would recover all that had been taken (1 Samuel 30:8).
Step 4: Why the Other Options Are Incorrect
Divination: This was not used; David used the ephod for seeking God's will.
Casting of Lots: This method was not used in this instance.
Abiathar's Support: While Abiathar supported David, the actual decision-making process involved using the ephod to seek divine guidance.
Answer: The ephod.

questions.text: When people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, He gave them into the hand of the Philistines for
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Historical Context
This question is based on the biblical narrative found in the Book of Judges in the Old Testament. The Israelites were repeatedly oppressed by neighboring nations as a consequence of their actions.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Biblical Passage
The specific oppression by the Philistines is described in Judges 13:1, which states, “Again the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the LORD; so the LORD delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.”
Step 3: Match the Passage with the Options
Compare the duration mentioned in the passage with the given options: thirty years, fifty years, twenty years, and forty years.
Step 4: Select the Correct Answer
According to Judges 13:1, the correct duration of Philistine oppression is forty years.
Step 5: Eliminate Incorrect Options
Thirty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Fifty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Twenty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Forty years: Matches the passage.
Answer: Forty years.
This matches the duration of oppression stated in the biblical text.

questions.text: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings... so that all the people who were in the camp trembled. What did Moses do immediately after this incident?
options: He went down from the mountain
He brought the people out of the camp to meet God
He went up to meet God
He called the elders of the people to receive the commandment
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context of the Incident
The incident described involves thunder and lightning on the morning of the third day, which is linked to a significant event in the biblical narrative.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Biblical Passage
This description refers to Exodus 19:16-17, where the Israelites experience thunder and lightning as they prepare to meet God at Mount Sinai. The event takes place before the giving of the Ten Commandments.
Step 3: Review the Actions of Moses in the Passage
According to Exodus 19:20, "The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the top of the mountain. So Moses went up."
Step 4: Match the Actions of Moses with the Given Options
He went down from the mountain: This is incorrect. After the thunder and lightning, Moses went up the mountain, not down.
He brought the people out of the camp to meet God: This is not accurate; the people were already at the base of the mountain, and Moses went up alone.
He went up to meet God: This is correct. The passage indicates that Moses went up the mountain to meet God.
He called the elders of the people to receive the commandment: This is incorrect as Moses himself went up the mountain, not the elders.
Answer: He went up to meet God.
This accurately reflects the action of Moses described in the biblical text following the incident of thunder and lightning.

questions.text: The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was a consequence of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Historical Context
The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II, the king of Babylon, occurred in 586 BC. This event was a significant part of the Babylonian Exile.
Step 2: Identify Key Historical and Biblical Figures
Hezekiah: King of Judah who reigned before Nebuchadnezzar's invasion. His death did not directly lead to the destruction of Jerusalem.
Josiah: King of Judah known for his religious reforms. Although his reforms were significant, they were not the direct cause of Jerusalem's destruction.
Israel's stubbornness to God: The Bible attributes Jerusalem’s destruction to the persistent disobedience and idolatry of the Israelites, which led to God's judgment.
Zedekiah: The last king of Judah before the Babylonian conquest. His rebellion against Babylon was a contributing factor to the destruction.
Step 3: Match the Cause with the Given Options
Hezekiah's death: Not directly related to the destruction.
Josiah's reforms: Although important, they were not the direct cause.
Israel's stubbornness to God: This is directly related to the biblical reason for the destruction, as described in the Bible.
Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylon: This was a direct contributing factor to the destruction but not the sole reason.
Answer: Israel's stubbornness to God.
The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was primarily a consequence of Israel's stubbornness to God, which led to divine judgment, with Zedekiah's rebellion being a significant immediate cause but not the overarching reason.

questions.text: The vision which Peter saw directing him to go to the house of Cornelius was to
options: extend the gospel to the Gentiles
prevent the persecution of the disciples
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This question refers to an event recorded in the book of Acts, specifically in Acts 10. Cornelius was a Roman centurion and a Gentile (non-Jew). Peter, a Jewish apostle, was given a vision by God that led him to visit Cornelius and share the gospel with him and his household.
"Demonstrate the power of God": Explanation: While God's power is indeed demonstrated throughout the Bible, including in this story, the primary purpose of the vision Peter received was not merely to showcase God's power. The vision had a more specific goal related to the spreading of the gospel.
"Prepare the apostles for evangelism"
Explanation: The apostles were already engaged in evangelism, sharing the message of Jesus Christ with others. However, up to this point, their focus had been primarily on the Jewish people. The vision Peter received was more about expanding the scope of their evangelism, specifically to include the Gentiles.
"Extend the gospel to the Gentiles": Explanation: This option directly reflects the purpose of the vision. In Acts 10, Peter sees a vision of a sheet descending from heaven with various animals, some considered unclean by Jewish law. A voice tells him to "kill and eat," but Peter refuses, saying he has never eaten anything unclean. The voice responds, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean" (Acts 10:15). This vision was God’s way of showing Peter that the gospel was not just for Jews but for Gentiles as well. As a result, Peter goes to the house of Cornelius, where the Holy Spirit is poured out on the Gentiles, signifying that the gospel is for all people.
"Prevent the persecution of the disciples": Explanation: This option does not fit the context of the vision. The vision Peter received was not about preventing persecution but about expanding the reach of the gospel.
Answer: Extend the gospel to the Gentiles.
The vision Peter saw was specifically intended to extend the gospel to the Gentiles. It marked a significant turning point in the early Christian church, emphasizing that the message of Jesus Christ was for all people, not just the Jews.
This answer accurately captures the purpose of Peter's vision, as it opened the door for the inclusion of Gentiles in the early Christian community, signifying the universal nature of the gospel message.
