questions.explanation: Answer: Righteousness and justice.

questions.text: "So may the gods do to me, and more also if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow. What did Elijah do after receiving this message?
options: He went a day's journey into the wilderness
He was afraid, arose and for his life
He gireded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel
He went and hid himself in a cave
questions.explanation:
The message in question was sent by Jezebel to Elijah after he had killed the prophets of Baal.
Contextual Understanding
After Elijah's victory over the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab, sent a threatening message to Elijah, vowing to kill him.
Scriptural Reference
1 Kings 19:2-3 (NIV): "So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, 'May the gods deal with me, be it ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I do not make your life like that of one of them.' Elijah was afraid and ran for his life."
Understanding Elijah's Reaction
Upon receiving Jezebel's message, Elijah was afraid and fled for his life.
Identify the Correct Option
The correct answer is "He was afraid, arose and ran for his life."
Answer: He was afraid, arose and for his life.
After receiving the message from Jezebel, Elijah was afraid, arose, and ran for his life.

questions.text: According to Hosea, what would God abolish from the land after making a covenant with Israel?
questions.explanation:
In the Book of Hosea, God speaks about making a covenant with Israel and mentions specific things that He would abolish from the land as part of this covenant.
Contextual Understanding
The Book of Hosea contains prophetic messages from God to the people of Israel. In Hosea 2, God speaks of restoring His relationship with Israel and making a new covenant with them.
Scriptural Reference
Hosea 2:18 (NIV): "In that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, the birds in the sky and the creatures that move along the ground. Bow and sword and battle I will abolish from the land, so that all may lie down in safety."
Understanding What God Will Abolish
In this covenant, God promises to abolish the bow, the sword, and battle from the land, symbolizing the end of warfare and violence.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The bow.
"
According to Hosea, God would abolish the bow (along with the sword and battle) from the land after making a covenant with Israel.

questions.text: Jeremiah described Israel as faithless and Judah as
questions.explanation: Answer: Idolatrous.

questions.text: Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he
options: had a close relationship with the king
questions.explanation:
Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he had a particular quality that set him apart.
Contextual Understanding
In the Book of Daniel, particularly in Daniel 6, it is mentioned that Daniel stood out among the other leaders in the kingdom, which led to his promotion.
Scriptural Reference
Daniel 6:3 (NIV): "Now Daniel so distinguished himself among the administrators and the satraps by his exceptional qualities that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom."
Some translations specifically mention that Daniel had an "excellent spirit" or "exceptional qualities."
Understanding the Reason for Daniel's Distinction
The reason Daniel was distinguished above the others was due to the "excellent spirit" or "exceptional qualities" he possessed, which refers to his wisdom, integrity, and the divine favor upon him.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Had an excellent spirit.
"
Daniel became distinguished above all the other presidents and satraps because he had an excellent spirit.

questions.text: Josiah's religious reforms led to the
options: killing of the worthless priests in the cities of Judah
keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem
Killing of the male cult prostitutes who were in the Temple
questions.explanation:
Josiah's religious reforms, as recorded in the Old Testament, were significant and led to a number of religious actions and changes in Judah. One of the key outcomes of his reforms is specifically noted in relation to the Passover.
Contextual Understanding
King Josiah of Judah is known for his major religious reforms, which included the removal of idolatry and the restoration of proper worship practices according to the Law of Moses.
Scriptural Reference
2 Kings 23:21-23 (NIV): "The king gave this order to all the people: 'Celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.' Neither in the days of the judges who led Israel nor in the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah had any such Passover been observed. But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was celebrated to the Lord in Jerusalem."
Understanding the Result of Josiah's Reforms
One of the significant outcomes of Josiah's reforms was the keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem. This celebration of the Passover was done according to the law, and it was noted as a significant event because it had not been observed in such a manner for many years.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem.
"
Josiah's religious reforms led to the keeping of the Passover in Jerusalem.

questions.text: God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were
questions.explanation:
God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were wicked.
Contextual Understanding
The story of Nineveh and God’s decision to destroy it is found in the Book of Jonah. Jonah was sent by God to Nineveh to warn the people of their impending destruction due to their wickedness.
Scriptural Reference
Jonah 1:2 (NIV): "Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me."
This verse clearly states that the reason for the judgment against Nineveh was the wickedness of its people.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Wicked.
"
God decided to destroy the great city of Nineveh because the people were wicked.

questions.text: "...And whether they hear or refuse to hear.. they will know that there has been a prophet among them..." The prophet referred to in the statement above was
questions.explanation:
The statement "And whether they hear or refuse to hear... they will know that there has been a prophet among them..." refers to the prophet Ezekiel.
Contextual Understanding
This statement comes from the calling and commissioning of Ezekiel as a prophet to the people of Israel. God instructed Ezekiel to speak His words to the people, regardless of whether they would listen.
Scriptural Reference
Ezekiel 2:5 (NIV): "And whether they listen or fail to listen—for they are a rebellious people—they will know that a prophet has been among them."
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Ezekiel.
"
The prophet referred to in the statement above was Ezekiel.

questions.text: Amaziah the priest of Bethel accused Amos, before Jeroboam the king of Israel of
questions.explanation:
Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, accused the prophet Amos of conspiracy before King Jeroboam of Israel.
Contextual Understanding
In the Book of Amos, the prophet Amos delivers messages of judgment against Israel, which were not well received by those in power. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, was particularly opposed to Amos’s prophecies.
Scriptural Reference
Amos 7:10 (NIV): "Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent a message to Jeroboam king of Israel: 'Amos is raising a conspiracy against you in the very heart of Israel. The land cannot bear all his words.'"
Understanding the Accusation
Amaziah accused Amos of stirring up conspiracy against the king by prophesying the downfall of the kingdom, suggesting that Amos’s words were a threat to the stability of the nation.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Conspiracy.
"
Amaziah the priest of Bethel accused Amos, before Jeroboam the king of Israel, of conspiracy.

questions.text: Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because
options: he wanted Aaron to go with him
questions.explanation:
Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because he was slow in speech.
Contextual Understanding
When God called Moses to lead the Israelites out of Egypt, Moses expressed concern about his ability to fulfill this task. He felt inadequate, particularly because of his speech.
Scriptural Reference
Exodus 4:10 (NIV): "Moses said to the Lord, 'Pardon your servant, Lord. I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since you have spoken to your servant. I am slow of speech and tongue.'"
Understanding Moses' Complaint
Moses was concerned about his ability to speak effectively, which led him to hesitate in accepting the mission to go to Pharaoh.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: He was slow in speech.
"
Moses complained to God that he could not go to Pharaoh alone because he was slow in speech.

questions.text: What name did Abraham give the place where he had attempted to sacrifice his son?
questions.explanation:
The name that Abraham gave to the place where he attempted to sacrifice his son Isaac is "The LORD will provide."
Contextual Understanding
The story of Abraham being tested by God and nearly sacrificing his son Isaac is recorded in Genesis 22. After God provided a ram to sacrifice in place of Isaac, Abraham named the place.
Scriptural Reference
Genesis 22:14 (NIV): "So Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.'"
Understanding the Name
The name "The LORD Will Provide" reflects Abraham’s faith in God’s provision, as God provided a ram in place of Isaac for the sacrifice.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The LORD will provide.
"
Abraham named the place where he attempted to sacrifice his son "The LORD will provide."

questions.text: When David's son died, his servants refuse to tell him because they feared that he might
questions.explanation:
When David's son died, his servants were afraid to tell him because they feared that he might harm himself.
Contextual Understanding
The context of this event is found in 2 Samuel 12, where David’s son, born to Bathsheba after their adulterous relationship, falls ill and eventually dies.
Scriptural Reference
2 Samuel 12:18 (NIV): "On the seventh day the child died. David’s attendants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they thought, 'While the child was still living, he wouldn’t listen to us when we spoke to him. How can we now tell him the child is dead? He may do something desperate.'"
Understanding the Servants' Fear
The servants were concerned that David might harm himself, possibly due to despair or grief, because of his intense fasting and mourning while the child was still alive.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Harm himself.
"
David's servants were afraid to tell him that his son had died because they feared that he might harm himself.

questions.text: What did God create on the fourth day?
questions.explanation:
On the fourth day of creation, God created the two great lights.
Contextual Understanding
The creation account is found in the Book of Genesis, where God created different elements of the universe on each day of the creation week.
Scriptural Reference
Genesis 1:14-19 (NIV): "And God said, 'Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them serve as signs to mark sacred times, and days and years, and let them be lights in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth.' And it was so. God made two great lights—the greater light to govern the day and the lesser light to govern the night. He also made the stars. God set them in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth, to govern the day and the night, and to separate light from darkness."
Understanding What Was Created
On the fourth day, God created the sun (the greater light) to govern the day and the moon (the lesser light) to govern the night, as well as the stars.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The two great lights.
"
On the fourth day, God created the two great lights (the sun and the moon).

questions.text: Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because
options: Absalom and his soldiers were defeated
of the shameful death of Absalom
the king was grieving for his son
the king was annoyed with them
questions.explanation:
Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because the king was grieving for his son.
Contextual Understanding
This event takes place after the battle in which Absalom, King David's son, was killed. Despite the victory, King David was deeply grieved over the death of his son, which affected the mood of the returning soldiers.
Scriptural Reference
2 Samuel 19:2-3 (NIV): "The victory that day was turned into mourning for all the troops, because on that day the troops heard it said, 'The king is grieving for his son.' The men stole into the city that day as men steal in who are ashamed when they flee from battle."
Understanding the Soldiers' Actions
The soldiers entered the city quietly because they were aware of the king's deep grief over Absalom's death. They did not celebrate the victory as they normally would, out of respect for David's mourning.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The king was grieving for his son.
"
Joab and his soldiers entered the city quietly after defeating their enemy because the king was grieving for his son.

questions.text: God appointed Joshua to succeed Moses because he
options: was loyal and dedicated to Moses
brought a good report from the land of Canaan
stood by Moses when the Israelites murmured against God
was a man in whom was the spirit
questions.explanation: Answer: Brought a good report from the land of Canaan.

questions.text: What punishment did God give Solomon for his unwise policies?
options: Jeroboam was empowered by God to conquer him
He caused Rezon to demolish the high place which he built
He raised up Haded, the Edomite as an adversary against him
The kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant
questions.explanation:
The punishment that God gave Solomon for his unwise policies was that the kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant.
Contextual Understanding
Due to Solomon's unwise policies, particularly his idolatry and turning away from God later in his reign, God decided to punish him.
Scriptural Reference
1 Kings 11:11 (NIV): "So the Lord said to Solomon, 'Since this is your attitude and you have not kept my covenant and my decrees, which I commanded you, I will most certainly tear the kingdom away from you and give it to one of your subordinates.'"
Understanding God's Punishment
God's punishment was to take away the kingdom from Solomon and give it to one of his servants. However, because of God's promise to David, this would happen after Solomon's death, and the kingdom would be divided.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: The kingdom was torn from him and given to his servant.
"
God punished Solomon by decreeing that the kingdom would be torn from him and given to his servant.

questions.text: When Moses struck the rock twice for water instead of speaking to it, God said to him that he would
options: no longer see Him face to face
not bring the Israelities to the promise land
roam in the wilderness for thirty years
questions.explanation: Answer: Not bring the Israelities to the promise land.

questions.text: God's covenant with Noah after the flood is that He will
options: never again destroy the earth by flood
make him fruitful and dominate the earth
make all creatures on earth serve him
make him and his descendants great
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context of the Covenant
After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and his descendants as described in Genesis 9:8-17. This covenant was to assure Noah and his family of God's promise concerning the future of the earth.
Step 2: Key Elements of the Covenant
Never Again Destroy the Earth by Flood:
God promised that He would never again destroy all life on earth with a flood. This is a central part of the covenant and is mentioned in Genesis 9:11: "I establish my covenant with you: Never again will all life be destroyed by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."
Make Him Fruitful and Dominate the Earth:
While God did command Noah and his sons to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (Genesis 9:1), this was not the covenantal promise but part of the directive given to them.
Make All Creatures on Earth Serve Him:
God did not specifically promise that all creatures would serve Noah. Instead, God gave Noah and his descendants dominion over the animals (Genesis 9:2), but this was not a covenantal promise about service.
Make Him and His Descendants Great:
Although God blessed Noah and his sons, the covenant specifically concerned the promise about the flood, not a general promise of greatness.
Answer: Never again destroy the earth by flood.
" This reflects the explicit promise made in the covenant that God would not use a flood to destroy all life on earth.
The covenant with Noah focused on God's promise to ensure that a flood would not again wipe out life on earth, providing a sense of security and continuity for future generations.

questions.text: David made the decision to pursue the Amalekies through
questions.explanation:
David made the decision to pursue the Amalekites through the ephod.
Step 1: Context of the Decision
David and his men had returned to Ziklag to find it burned and their families taken captive by the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:1-4).
Step 2: Seeking Guidance
David sought guidance from God on whether to pursue the Amalekites and if he would be successful.
The Ephod: David inquired of the Lord using the ephod, a priestly garment associated with seeking God's will. Abiathar, the priest, brought the ephod to David, and David used it to seek God's direction (1 Samuel 30:7-8).
Step 3: Outcome
God responded affirmatively, telling David to pursue the Amalekites, assuring him that he would recover all that had been taken (1 Samuel 30:8).
Step 4: Why the Other Options Are Incorrect
Divination: This was not used; David used the ephod for seeking God's will.
Casting of Lots: This method was not used in this instance.
Abiathar's Support: While Abiathar supported David, the actual decision-making process involved using the ephod to seek divine guidance.
Answer: The ephod.

questions.text: When people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, He gave them into the hand of the Philistines for
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Historical Context
This question is based on the biblical narrative found in the Book of Judges in the Old Testament. The Israelites were repeatedly oppressed by neighboring nations as a consequence of their actions.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Biblical Passage
The specific oppression by the Philistines is described in Judges 13:1, which states, “Again the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the LORD; so the LORD delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.”
Step 3: Match the Passage with the Options
Compare the duration mentioned in the passage with the given options: thirty years, fifty years, twenty years, and forty years.
Step 4: Select the Correct Answer
According to Judges 13:1, the correct duration of Philistine oppression is forty years.
Step 5: Eliminate Incorrect Options
Thirty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Fifty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Twenty years: Not mentioned in the passage.
Forty years: Matches the passage.
Answer: Forty years.
This matches the duration of oppression stated in the biblical text.

questions.text: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings... so that all the people who were in the camp trembled. What did Moses do immediately after this incident?
options: He went down from the mountain
He brought the people out of the camp to meet God
He went up to meet God
He called the elders of the people to receive the commandment
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context of the Incident
The incident described involves thunder and lightning on the morning of the third day, which is linked to a significant event in the biblical narrative.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Biblical Passage
This description refers to Exodus 19:16-17, where the Israelites experience thunder and lightning as they prepare to meet God at Mount Sinai. The event takes place before the giving of the Ten Commandments.
Step 3: Review the Actions of Moses in the Passage
According to Exodus 19:20, "The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the top of the mountain. So Moses went up."
Step 4: Match the Actions of Moses with the Given Options
He went down from the mountain: This is incorrect. After the thunder and lightning, Moses went up the mountain, not down.
He brought the people out of the camp to meet God: This is not accurate; the people were already at the base of the mountain, and Moses went up alone.
He went up to meet God: This is correct. The passage indicates that Moses went up the mountain to meet God.
He called the elders of the people to receive the commandment: This is incorrect as Moses himself went up the mountain, not the elders.
Answer: He went up to meet God.
This accurately reflects the action of Moses described in the biblical text following the incident of thunder and lightning.

questions.text: The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was a consequence of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Historical Context
The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II, the king of Babylon, occurred in 586 BC. This event was a significant part of the Babylonian Exile.
Step 2: Identify Key Historical and Biblical Figures
Hezekiah: King of Judah who reigned before Nebuchadnezzar's invasion. His death did not directly lead to the destruction of Jerusalem.
Josiah: King of Judah known for his religious reforms. Although his reforms were significant, they were not the direct cause of Jerusalem's destruction.
Israel's stubbornness to God: The Bible attributes Jerusalem’s destruction to the persistent disobedience and idolatry of the Israelites, which led to God's judgment.
Zedekiah: The last king of Judah before the Babylonian conquest. His rebellion against Babylon was a contributing factor to the destruction.
Step 3: Match the Cause with the Given Options
Hezekiah's death: Not directly related to the destruction.
Josiah's reforms: Although important, they were not the direct cause.
Israel's stubbornness to God: This is directly related to the biblical reason for the destruction, as described in the Bible.
Zedekiah's rebellion against Babylon: This was a direct contributing factor to the destruction but not the sole reason.
Answer: Israel's stubbornness to God.
The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was primarily a consequence of Israel's stubbornness to God, which led to divine judgment, with Zedekiah's rebellion being a significant immediate cause but not the overarching reason.

questions.text: The vision which Peter saw directing him to go to the house of Cornelius was to
options: extend the gospel to the Gentiles
prevent the persecution of the disciples
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This question refers to an event recorded in the book of Acts, specifically in Acts 10. Cornelius was a Roman centurion and a Gentile (non-Jew). Peter, a Jewish apostle, was given a vision by God that led him to visit Cornelius and share the gospel with him and his household.
"Demonstrate the power of God": Explanation: While God's power is indeed demonstrated throughout the Bible, including in this story, the primary purpose of the vision Peter received was not merely to showcase God's power. The vision had a more specific goal related to the spreading of the gospel.
"Prepare the apostles for evangelism"
Explanation: The apostles were already engaged in evangelism, sharing the message of Jesus Christ with others. However, up to this point, their focus had been primarily on the Jewish people. The vision Peter received was more about expanding the scope of their evangelism, specifically to include the Gentiles.
"Extend the gospel to the Gentiles": Explanation: This option directly reflects the purpose of the vision. In Acts 10, Peter sees a vision of a sheet descending from heaven with various animals, some considered unclean by Jewish law. A voice tells him to "kill and eat," but Peter refuses, saying he has never eaten anything unclean. The voice responds, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean" (Acts 10:15). This vision was God’s way of showing Peter that the gospel was not just for Jews but for Gentiles as well. As a result, Peter goes to the house of Cornelius, where the Holy Spirit is poured out on the Gentiles, signifying that the gospel is for all people.
"Prevent the persecution of the disciples": Explanation: This option does not fit the context of the vision. The vision Peter received was not about preventing persecution but about expanding the reach of the gospel.
Answer: Extend the gospel to the Gentiles.
The vision Peter saw was specifically intended to extend the gospel to the Gentiles. It marked a significant turning point in the early Christian church, emphasizing that the message of Jesus Christ was for all people, not just the Jews.
This answer accurately captures the purpose of Peter's vision, as it opened the door for the inclusion of Gentiles in the early Christian community, signifying the universal nature of the gospel message.

questions.text: According to Mark, the preaching of John the Baptist centred on
options: a rebuke of the scribes for misinterpreting the Law
a call on the Jews to forsake idolatry
repentance for the forgiveness of sins
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The Gospel of Mark introduces John the Baptist early in the narrative as a forerunner to Jesus Christ. John's role was to prepare the way for Jesus by preaching to the people and calling them to a specific response.
"A rebuke of the scribes for misinterpreting the Law": Explanation: While John the Baptist did have strong words for the religious leaders, particularly the Pharisees and Sadducees, this was not the central theme of his preaching. His primary focus was not on correcting their interpretation of the Law but on calling people to a deeper, more fundamental spiritual change.
"A call on the Jews to forsake idolatry": Explanation: Idolatry had been a significant issue in Israel's history, but by the time of John the Baptist, the Jewish people were more focused on strict monotheism and adherence to the Law. John's message did not center on forsaking idolatry but on something broader and more fundamental to spiritual life.
"Baptism and good works": Explanation: While John did emphasize baptism, it was not just baptism for its own sake or accompanied by a general call to good works. The baptism he preached was a symbolic act tied to a specific spiritual condition—repentance. Thus, the focus was not just on outward actions (good works) but on an inner transformation.
"Repentance for the forgiveness of sins": Explanation: This option aligns directly with the description in the Gospel of Mark. Mark 1:4 states, "And so John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." This phrase encapsulates the core of John's message: he called people to repent (turn away from their sins) and be baptized as a sign of their repentance, which would lead to the forgiveness of their sins.
Answer: Repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
According to the Gospel of Mark, the central theme of John the Baptist's preaching was repentance for the forgiveness of sins. His call was for the people to turn away from their sinful ways and prepare their hearts for the coming of the Messiah.
This answer accurately reflects the essence of John the Baptist's message as portrayed in the Gospel of Mark, emphasizing the need for a spiritual change as a preparation for the coming of Jesus.

questions.text: Before the feeding of the five thousand people the disciples told Jesus to send the people away because
options: there was no place for them to buy food
they could not get enough food for them
it was late in the evening
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The story of Jesus feeding the five thousand is found in all four Gospels, including the Gospel of Matthew (Matthew 14:13-21), Mark (Mark 6:30-44), Luke (Luke 9:10-17), and John (John 6:1-14). This miracle is one of the most well-known events in Jesus' ministry.
"There was no place for them to buy food": Explanation: While the location of the event was indeed remote, and there were no nearby places to buy food, this is not the primary reason the disciples gave when suggesting that the people be sent away.
"They could not get enough food for them": Explanation: The disciples did express concern about the lack of sufficient food to feed such a large crowd, which is why they suggested sending the people away. However, this was more of a follow-up issue than the initial reason they suggested sending the crowd away.
"It was late in the evening": Explanation: This is the key point. In the Gospel accounts, the disciples specifically mention that it was getting late. In Mark 6:35-36, for example, it says, "By this time it was late in the day, so his disciples came to him. 'This is a remote place,' they said, 'and it's already very late. Send the people away so that they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.'" The fact that it was late in the day was the primary concern that prompted the disciples to suggest dismissing the crowd.
"They were hungry and tired": Explanation: While it's logical to assume that the crowd might have been hungry and tired after a long day, this is not explicitly stated as the reason the disciples asked Jesus to send them away. The disciples were more concerned about the time of day and the logistical challenge of feeding such a large group.
Answer: It was late in the evening.
The primary reason the disciples told Jesus to send the people away before the feeding of the five thousand was because it was late in the evening. They were concerned that it would be too late for the people to find food if they stayed any longer.
This answer aligns with the Gospel accounts, where the disciples were concerned about the time and suggested sending the crowd away so they could find food before it got too late.

questions.text: According to Matthew, the disciples of Jesus fell on their faces during the Transfiguration when
options: they heared a voice from the cloud
Jesus face shone like the sun
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The Transfiguration of Jesus is a significant event described in the Gospels, where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, and there He is transfigured before them. This event is recounted in Matthew 17:1-9.
"Jesus' garment became white": Explanation: During the Transfiguration, it is mentioned that Jesus' clothes became dazzling white, as noted in Matthew 17:2. However, this event alone did not cause the disciples to fall on their faces.
"They heard a voice from the cloud"
Explanation: This is the key moment. According to Matthew 17:5-6, while Jesus was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my Son, whom I love; with him, I am well pleased. Listen to him!" When the disciples heard this, they were terrified and fell facedown to the ground. This indicates that it was hearing the voice of God from the cloud that caused them to fall on their faces.
"Jesus' face shone like the sun": Explanation: Matthew 17:2 describes how Jesus' face shone like the sun during the Transfiguration. This was a remarkable and awe-inspiring event, but the disciples did not fall on their faces at this point.
"They saw Moses and Elijah": Explanation: Moses and Elijah did appear with Jesus during the Transfiguration, as noted in Matthew 17:3. However, the appearance of these figures did not cause the disciples to fall on their faces. Their reaction was prompted specifically by hearing the voice from the cloud.
Answer: They heared a voice from the cloud.
The disciples of Jesus fell on their faces during the Transfiguration when they heard a voice from the cloud. This voice was understood to be the voice of God, which filled the disciples with awe and fear, leading them to fall facedown.
"They heard a voice from the cloud"
This answer is consistent with the account in Matthew 17:5-6, where the disciples' reaction of falling facedown is directly linked to hearing the divine voice from the cloud.

questions.text: Hosea said that when Israel returned to the Lord, they would dwell
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The book of Hosea in the Old Testament is a prophetic book that addresses the unfaithfulness of Israel and God's promise of restoration if they return to Him. Hosea uses various metaphors and imagery to describe Israel's relationship with God and the blessings that would follow their repentance.
"Among nations peacefully"
Explanation: While peace is often a result of God's blessings, Hosea does not specifically mention that Israel would dwell "among nations peacefully" as a consequence of their return to the Lord. This option is more of a general blessing rather than a specific promise mentioned by Hosea.
"In His house forever"
Explanation: Dwelling in the house of the Lord forever is a theme found in other parts of the Bible, particularly in the Psalms (e.g., Psalm 23). However, Hosea’s focus is different. This option does not directly align with the specific language Hosea uses regarding Israel's return to God.
"Beneath His shadow": Explanation: This option closely reflects the language used by Hosea. In Hosea 14:7, it says, "Those who live in his shadow will again raise grain, and they will blossom like the vine; his renown will be like the wine of Lebanon." The imagery of dwelling "beneath His shadow" symbolizes living under God's protection and care, receiving His blessings and flourishing as a result.
"In Jerusalem without molestation": Explanation: While the idea of safety and peace in Jerusalem is a common theme in prophetic literature, Hosea does not specifically mention that Israel would dwell in Jerusalem without molestation. This option does not directly correspond with Hosea's prophecy.
Answer: Beneath His shadow.
Hosea said that when Israel returned to the Lord, they would dwell beneath His shadow. This phrase emphasizes the protection, care, and flourishing that come from being under God's guidance and favor.
This answer accurately reflects the imagery used in Hosea 14:7, which conveys the blessings and protection that Israel would experience upon returning to the Lord.

questions.text: What did the apostles do when they heard that Samaria had received the word of God through Philip?
options: they sent Stephen to go and exhort them
they sent Peter and John to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit
they sent James and John to supervise the election of the seven deacons
they sent Barnabas and Saul to go and baptize them
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This event is recorded in the book of Acts, specifically in Acts 8:14-17. Philip, one of the seven deacons, had gone to Samaria and preached the gospel, and many Samaritans believed and were baptized. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard about this, they took action.
"They sent Stephen to go and exhort them": Explanation: Stephen was indeed a significant figure in the early church and one of the seven deacons, but he was not sent to Samaria. Stephen had already been martyred by this point in Acts 7, so this option cannot be correct.
"They sent Peter and John to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit": Explanation: This is the correct answer. According to Acts 8:14-17, when the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When Peter and John arrived, they prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had simply been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
"They sent James and John to supervise the election of the seven deacons": Explanation: This event (the election of the seven deacons) occurred earlier in Acts 6, and it is unrelated to the events in Samaria. Additionally, James and John were not involved in that specific event. Therefore, this option is not correct.
"They sent Barnabas and Saul to go and baptize them": Explanation: While Barnabas and Saul (later known as Paul) were key figures in the spread of Christianity, they were not sent to Samaria for this purpose. This event specifically involved Peter and John.
Answer: They sent Peter and John to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit.
When the apostles heard that Samaria had received the word of God through Philip, they sent Peter and John to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit.
This answer aligns with the biblical account in Acts 8:14-17, where Peter and John were sent to Samaria to lay hands on the new believers so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

questions.text: The disciples of Jesus were not able to heal the boy who had a dumb spirit because
options: the spirit refused to obey them
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This event is recorded in the Gospels, particularly in Mark 9:14-29. A father brings his son, who is possessed by a spirit that makes him mute, to Jesus' disciples for healing, but they are unable to cast out the spirit. Later, when Jesus arrives, He successfully heals the boy and explains the reason for the disciples' inability to do so.
"They had not prayed enough": Explanation: In Mark 9:29, after Jesus had healed the boy, the disciples asked Him privately why they couldn't cast out the spirit. Jesus replied, "This kind can come out only by prayer." Some manuscripts also add "and fasting." This indicates that the disciples might have lacked the necessary spiritual preparation or reliance on God through prayer, which was crucial for dealing with this particular kind of spirit.
"The spirit refused to obey them": Explanation: While the spirit did resist being cast out, the ultimate reason for the disciples' failure was not simply the spirit's refusal but rather something lacking in the disciples themselves—specifically their faith and their reliance on prayer.
"The boy was already dead": Explanation: This option is not correct. The boy was not dead; he was possessed by a spirit that caused him to be mute and also threw him into convulsions. Jesus healed him while he was still alive.
"They had no faith": Explanation: In Mark 9:19, Jesus expresses frustration with the disciples' lack of faith when He says, "O unbelieving generation, how long shall I stay with you? How long shall I put up with you? Bring the boy to me." Faith is a critical element in the ability to perform miracles, as demonstrated throughout the Gospels. The disciples' lack of faith contributed to their inability to heal the boy.
Answer: They had no faith.
The correct understanding combines both the need for faith and prayer. While "they had not prayed enough" is also a contributing factor according to Jesus' explanation, the broader reason is rooted in their lack of faith.
This answer captures the essence of Jesus' critique of His disciples. Their failure was due to a lack of sufficient faith, which hindered their ability to cast out the spirit, as well as a lack of prayer, which Jesus emphasized as necessary for dealing with such a powerful spirit.

questions.text: Pilate wondered greatly during the trial of Jesus before him because
options: Jesus gave him no answer to a single charge
the Jews asked that the notorious prisoner be released
Jesus agreed that He was the king of the Jews
his wife warned him to have nothing to do with Jesus
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The trial of Jesus before Pontius Pilate is recorded in all four Gospels, with details varying slightly between them. In Matthew 27:11-14, we see a key moment where Pilate is struck by something unusual during the proceedings.
"Jesus gave him no answer to a single charge": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In Matthew 27:12-14, when Jesus was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer. Pilate then asked Him, "Don't you hear the testimony they are bringing against you?" But Jesus made no reply, not even to a single charge, to the great amazement of the governor. Pilate was astonished because it was highly unusual for someone accused of serious crimes, particularly one facing possible execution, to remain silent in the face of such accusations.
"The Jews asked that the notorious prisoner be released": Explanation: This refers to the custom of releasing a prisoner during the Passover, and indeed the crowd chose Barabbas, a notorious prisoner, over Jesus. However, while this choice was significant, it is not specifically what caused Pilate to "wonder greatly" during the trial.
"Jesus agreed that He was the king of the Jews": Explanation: When Pilate asked Jesus if He was the king of the Jews, Jesus responded, "You have said so" (Matthew 27:11). While this statement was important, it was not the cause of Pilate's great amazement.
"His wife warned him to have nothing to do with Jesus": Explanation: Pilate’s wife did indeed send him a message urging him to avoid involvement with Jesus because of a troubling dream (Matthew 27:19). This event might have concerned Pilate, but it is not what caused him to "wonder greatly."
Answer: Jesus gave him no answer to a single charge.
Pilate's great amazement during the trial of Jesus was specifically because Jesus gave him no answer to a single charge. This silence in the face of serious accusations was unexpected and left Pilate greatly puzzled.
This answer reflects the key moment in the trial that caused Pilate to be astonished, as recorded in Matthew 27:12-14.

questions.text: The gifts offered Jesus at His birth by the wise men were
questions.explanation:
The gifts offered to Jesus at His birth by the wise men, according to the Gospel of Matthew, were gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
In Matthew 2:11, it is recorded that the wise men (also known as the Magi) visited Jesus after His birth and "opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh."
Gold: Symbolizes kingship and is often associated with wealth and royalty.
Frankincense: An aromatic resin used in incense and perfumes, symbolizing deity and worship.
Myrrh: Another resin used in embalming and perfumes, symbolizing suffering and death, as it was used in burial practices.
These gifts were symbolic of Jesus' identity and the roles He would fulfill.
Answer: Gold,frankincense and myrrh.

questions.text: Following the resurrection of Jesus, the Chief Priest and elders took counsel and bribed the guards to
options: say that the disciples stole the body of Jesus
keep the information away from His disciples
report the matter immediately to the rulers
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
After Jesus' resurrection, the guards who had been stationed at His tomb reported the miraculous events to the Chief Priests. This account is found in the Gospel of Matthew, specifically in Matthew 28:11-15.
"Say that the disciples stole the body of Jesus": Explanation: This is the correct answer. According to Matthew 28:12-13, after hearing the guards' report, the Chief Priests and elders took counsel and gave the soldiers a large sum of money, instructing them to say, "His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep." This was an attempt to cover up the resurrection by spreading a false story.
"Keep the information away from His disciples": Explanation: While the Chief Priests and elders wanted to prevent the spread of the truth about the resurrection, the specific action they took was to spread a false narrative rather than simply withholding information from the disciples.
"Report the matter immediately to the rulers": Explanation: The Chief Priests and elders did not instruct the guards to report the matter to the rulers. Instead, they bribed the guards to lie about what happened.
"Keep the matter among themselves": Explanation: The Chief Priests and elders did not just keep the matter private; they actively spread a false story to discredit the resurrection and prevent people from believing in it.
Answer: Say that the disciples stole the body of Jesus.
The Chief Priests and elders bribed the guards to say that the disciples stole the body of Jesus. This was part of their effort to suppress the truth about Jesus' resurrection and to maintain control over the narrative.
This answer accurately reflects the actions taken by the religious leaders as recorded in Matthew 28:12-13, where they bribed the guards to spread a false story about the disciples stealing Jesus' body.

questions.text: In the Sermon on the Mount, what did Jesus teach His disciples to do when they faced persecution?
options: They should leave vengeance to God
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The Sermon on the Mount, found in Matthew chapters 5-7, includes Jesus' teachings on various aspects of Christian life, including how to respond to persecution. In this sermon, Jesus provides specific guidance on how His followers should react when they are mistreated for their faith.
"They should pray and fast": Explanation: While prayer and fasting are important practices in the Christian faith, this is not the specific instruction Jesus gave regarding persecution in the Sermon on the Mount.
"They should take immediate vengeance": Explanation: This option directly contradicts Jesus' teachings. Jesus taught against taking vengeance. Instead, He encouraged His followers to love their enemies and to turn the other cheek when wronged.
"They should leave vengeance to God": Explanation: While this principle aligns with biblical teaching (Romans 12:19), it is not the specific instruction Jesus gave in the Sermon on the Mount regarding persecution.
"They should leap for joy": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In Matthew 5:11-12, Jesus says, "Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of me. Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you." Jesus teaches His disciples to respond to persecution with joy, recognizing that it brings a heavenly reward.
Answer: They should leap for joy.
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught His disciples that when they faced persecution, they should rejoice and be glad—essentially, they should leap for joy because their reward in heaven would be great.
This answer aligns with Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount, where He encouraged His followers to respond to persecution with joy, knowing that they are blessed and will receive a great reward in heaven.

questions.text: Jesus raised to life the son of the widow of Nain because He
options: wanted the whole of Judea to know about Him
wanted to show that He was a great prophet
loved the young man that died
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The account of Jesus raising the son of the widow of Nain is found in the Gospel of Luke 7:11-17. In this passage, Jesus encounters a funeral procession outside the town of Nain, where a widow's only son had died.
"Wanted the whole of Judea to know about Him": Explanation: While the miracle certainly did spread Jesus' fame throughout the region, the text does not indicate that this was Jesus' primary motivation for raising the young man.
"Wanted to show that He was a great prophet": Explanation: After the miracle, the people did recognize Jesus as a great prophet, but this is not presented as the reason for His action. The text emphasizes Jesus' compassion rather than a desire to prove Himself.
"Had compassion on the mother": Explanation: This is the correct answer. Luke 7:13 explicitly states, "When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her and he said, 'Don’t cry.'" Jesus was moved by compassion for the grieving mother, who had lost her only son, which led Him to perform the miracle.
"Loved the young man that died": Explanation: The text does not mention a specific relationship between Jesus and the young man. The emphasis is on Jesus' compassion for the mother rather than on His affection for the young man.
Answer: Had compassion on the mother.
Jesus raised the son of the widow of Nain to life because He had compassion on the mother. The passage in Luke emphasizes Jesus' deep compassion as the motivation for this miracle.
This answer aligns with the account in Luke 7:13, where Jesus' compassion for the grieving widow is highlighted as the reason for the miracle.

questions.text: Jesus washed the feet of His disciples because
options: He was soon to be glorified
He wanted to serve by example
it was a sign of holiness
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The event of Jesus washing His disciples' feet is recorded in the Gospel of John 13:1-17. This act took place during the Last Supper, just before Jesus was crucified. Washing the feet was typically a servant's task, so this action by Jesus carried deep symbolic meaning.
"He was soon to be glorified": Explanation: While it is true that Jesus was aware that His crucifixion and subsequent glorification were imminent, this was not the specific reason He washed the disciples' feet. The washing had a more immediate purpose related to teaching and exemplifying humility and service.
"He wanted to serve by example": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In John 13:14-15, Jesus explicitly explains the purpose of His action: "Now that I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you." Jesus washed their feet to model humility and servanthood, teaching them to serve one another in the same way.
"It was a sign of holiness": Explanation: While holiness is a key aspect of Jesus' ministry, the act of washing the disciples' feet was not primarily about holiness. It was about demonstrating humility and love through service.
"They needed to be washed"
Explanation: Although the disciples' feet were physically dirty from walking, the deeper purpose of the washing was not simply cleanliness but rather to teach a spiritual lesson about humility and service.
Answer: He wanted to serve by example.
Jesus washed the feet of His disciples because He wanted to serve by example. The action was intended to teach His disciples about the importance of humility and serving others.
This answer aligns with the explanation Jesus Himself provided in John 13:14-15, where He emphasized that His action was meant to be an example for His disciples to follow in serving one another.

questions.text: "...As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Jesus made the statement above on the occasion of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The phrase "I am the light of the world" is a significant declaration made by Jesus, and it appears specifically in the Gospel of John. Understanding the context in which this statement was made will help identify the correct occasion.
"Healing the man born blind": Explanation: This is the correct answer. The statement "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world" is directly linked to the event where Jesus heals a man who was blind from birth. This account is found in John 9:1-7. Jesus encounters a man who has been blind from birth, and before performing the miracle of restoring his sight, Jesus makes this declaration to emphasize His role in bringing spiritual and physical light to the world. After this statement, He proceeds to heal the man by making mud with His saliva, applying it to the man's eyes, and instructing him to wash in the Pool of Siloam.
"Raising Lazarus from the dead": Explanation: While this event is another significant miracle performed by Jesus, the statement "I am the light of the world" is not made in this context. The story of Lazarus being raised from the dead is found in John 11, where Jesus speaks about being "the resurrection and the life," but the specific statement about being the light of the world is not connected to this event.
"Restoring sight to blind Bartimaeus": Explanation: Blind Bartimaeus was another individual healed by Jesus, as recorded in Mark 10:46-52. However, the statement "I am the light of the world" is not made during this occasion. Bartimaeus calls out to Jesus as the "Son of David," and Jesus heals him, but the specific context of the statement in question is not linked to this event.
"Walking on the sea before daybreak"
Explanation: Jesus walking on the sea is recorded in multiple Gospels (e.g., Matthew 14:22-33, Mark 6:45-52, John 6:16-21), but the statement "I am the light of the world" is not made during this event. This miracle demonstrates Jesus' power over nature, but it is not associated with the declaration about being the light of the world.
Answer: Healing the man born blind.
The statement "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world" was made by Jesus in the context of healing the man born blind. This miracle, described in John 9, serves to illustrate Jesus' role as the one who brings both physical and spiritual light to humanity.
This answer is directly supported by the context in the Gospel of John, where Jesus makes the declaration right before performing the miracle of giving sight to a man who had been blind from birth.

questions.text: Peter enjoins Christians to wait in expectation of the new heavens and the new earth in which
options: there will be no more corruption
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This reference is found in 2 Peter 3:13, where the Apostle Peter encourages Christians to look forward to God's promise of a new creation after the current heavens and earth pass away.
"Evil will be destroyed": Explanation: While it's true that evil will be ultimately destroyed in the final judgment, this is not the specific emphasis Peter makes when describing the new heavens and the new earth.
"There will be no more corruption": Explanation: The absence of corruption could be inferred in a world where righteousness prevails, but Peter's description of the new heavens and new earth does not specifically mention the absence of corruption as the defining feature.
"There will be perfection": Explanation: Although the new heavens and the new earth will be characterized by perfection, Peter does not use this specific term in his description.
"Righteousness dwells"
Explanation: This is the correct answer. In 2 Peter 3:13, Peter specifically says, "But according to His promise, we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells." This phrase highlights that the defining characteristic of the new creation will be the presence of righteousness.
Answer: Rightecousness dwells.
Peter enjoins Christians to wait in expectation of the new heavens and the new earth where righteousness dwells. This is the key characteristic that Peter emphasizes in his letter, encouraging believers to look forward to a world where God's righteousness is fully manifest.
"Righteousness dwells"
This answer directly aligns with the wording in 2 Peter 3:13, where Peter encourages believers to anticipate the new creation as a place where righteousness will reign.

questions.text: What does Paul advise Roman Christians to do to those who persecute them?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The relevant passage is found in Romans 12:14, where Paul provides specific instructions on how Christians should respond to persecution.
"Give them drink when thirsty": Explanation: While Paul does encourage Christians to do good to their enemies, including giving them food and drink (Romans 12:20), this is not the specific advice given in relation to those who persecute them in Romans 12:14.
"Forgive them": Explanation: Forgiveness is a central Christian teaching, and while it's implied in how Christians should respond to persecution, the specific instruction Paul gives in Romans 12:14 is not about forgiveness.
"Bless them": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In Romans 12:14, Paul explicitly says, "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." This instruction highlights the importance of responding to persecution with kindness and a positive attitude, rather than seeking revenge or harboring resentment.
"Feed them when hungry": Explanation: Similar to giving drink to the thirsty, feeding the hungry is part of Paul's broader teaching on how to treat one's enemies, but the specific instruction for dealing with persecution is to bless them, as stated in Romans 12:14.
Answer: Bless them.
Paul advises Roman Christians to bless those who persecute them. This instruction is directly given in Romans 12:14, emphasizing the need to respond to persecution with grace and kindness.
This answer aligns with Paul's teaching in Romans 12:14, where he encourages believers to respond to persecution not with retaliation, but by blessing those who cause them harm.

questions.text: Peter admonishes that Christians should endure suffering because anyone who has suffered in the flesh
options: shall live the rest of his life in peace
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The relevant passage is found in 1 Peter 4:1-2, where Peter discusses the significance of suffering in the life of a Christian.
"Shall live the rest of his life in peace": Explanation: While enduring suffering can lead to a deeper sense of peace in a spiritual sense, this is not the specific reason Peter gives for enduring suffering in the flesh.
"Shall cloth himself with humility": Explanation: Although humility is a key virtue that Peter discusses elsewhere (e.g., 1 Peter 5:5), this is not the specific outcome Peter associates with suffering in the flesh in the passage in question.
"Has ceased from sin": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In 1 Peter 4:1, Peter writes, "Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same purpose, because he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin." Peter is emphasizing that enduring suffering, particularly for one's faith, has a purifying effect, helping a person to break away from sinful behaviors and live a life more aligned with God's will.
"Has overcome death": Explanation: Overcoming death is a concept related to eternal life through Christ's resurrection, but Peter does not specifically tie this idea to enduring suffering in the flesh in the passage in question.
Answer: Has ceased from sin.
Peter admonishes that Christians should endure suffering because anyone who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin. This emphasizes the transformative power of suffering, particularly in helping believers break free from sinful patterns.
This answer aligns with 1 Peter 4:1, where Peter discusses how suffering in the flesh can lead to a cessation of sinful behaviors, encouraging believers to live more fully in accordance with God's will.

questions.text: Which of the following are opposed to each other according to Galatians?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to this question, according to the book of Galatians, is:
Flesh and Spirit
In Galatians 5:16-17, Paul writes, "So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are in conflict with each other, so that you are not to do whatever you want."
This passage highlights the internal struggle between the desires of the flesh (which represent our sinful nature) and the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Paul teaches that these two forces are opposed to each other, and Christians are called to live by the Spirit rather than being controlled by the flesh.
Answer: Flesh and Spirit.

questions.text: According to Peter, God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him is
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
This statement from Peter is found in the book of Acts, specifically in Acts 10:34-35. Peter makes this statement after he has a vision and is led by the Holy Spirit to visit the house of Cornelius, a Gentile. This event marks a significant moment in the early church, demonstrating that the message of the Gospel is for all people, not just the Jews.
"Diligent before Him": Explanation: While diligence is an important quality in the Christian faith, it is not the specific term Peter uses to describe those who fear God.
"Acceptable to Him": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In Acts 10:34-35, Peter says, "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable to Him." Peter is emphasizing that God accepts people from every nation, regardless of their ethnic background, if they fear Him and do what is right.
"Holy before Him": Explanation: Holiness is a key aspect of Christian living, and those who follow God are called to be holy. However, in this specific passage, Peter does not use the term "holy" to describe those who fear God.
"Righteous before Him": Explanation: Righteousness is certainly an important concept in the Bible, but again, this is not the term Peter uses in this context. Peter is focusing on the fact that those who fear God and do what is right are acceptable to Him.
Answer: Acceptable to Him.
According to Peter in Acts 10:34-35, God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him is acceptable to Him. This statement emphasizes that God’s acceptance is not based on nationality or ethnicity, but on a person's reverence for God and their commitment to doing what is right.
This answer directly aligns with Peter’s statement in Acts 10:34-35, where he explains that God accepts all who fear Him and do what is right, regardless of their background.

questions.text: 'He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your resources...' The statement above by Paul was made in respect of

The statement "He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your resources..." by Paul was made in respect of Christian attitude to giving.
This statement is found in 2 Corinthians 9:10. In this chapter, Paul is encouraging the Corinthians to be generous in their giving. He assures them that God, who provides both seed for the sower and bread for food, will also provide for their needs and increase their ability to give. Paul's teaching emphasizes that when Christians give generously, they can trust that God will continue to supply their needs and even multiply their resources so that they can continue to be generous.
Answer: Christian attitude to giving.
This answer reflects the context in which Paul made this statement, as he was encouraging believers to give generously, knowing that God would provide for them abundantly.

questions.text: According to Corinthians, it is necessary for a Christian to forgive so as to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The reference to forgiveness and its importance in the Christian life is discussed by Paul in 2 Corinthians 2:10-11. Paul is writing to the Corinthian church, addressing the need for forgiveness within the community.
"Maintain brotherly affection": Explanation: While forgiveness does indeed help maintain brotherly affection, this is not the specific reason Paul gives in the passage from Corinthians.
"Emulate the life of Paul": Explanation: Paul does encourage believers to follow his example as he follows Christ, but in this specific context, he does not suggest that forgiveness is necessary simply to emulate his life.
"Maintain good neighbourliness": Explanation: Maintaining good relationships with others, including neighbors, is an important aspect of Christian living. However, this is not the reason Paul emphasizes the necessity of forgiveness in the context of Corinthians.
"Keep Satan from gaining advantage": Explanation: This is the correct answer. In 2 Corinthians 2:10-11, Paul says, "Anyone you forgive, I also forgive. And what I have forgiven—if there was anything to forgive—I have forgiven in the sight of Christ for your sake, in order that Satan might not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes." Here, Paul is emphasizing that unforgiveness can give Satan a foothold in the church, allowing him to create division and strife. By forgiving one another, Christians close the door on Satan's attempts to take advantage of any situation.
Answer: Keep Satan from gaining advantage.
According to Corinthians, it is necessary for a Christian to forgive to keep Satan from gaining advantage. Paul highlights that forgiveness is a critical component in preventing Satan from exploiting situations to cause harm within the Christian community.
This answer is based on Paul's teaching in 2 Corinthians 2:10-11, where he emphasizes the importance of forgiveness in thwarting Satan's schemes and maintaining unity within the church.

questions.text: According to Romans, good citizenship involves
questions.explanation:
To answer the question about what constitutes "good citizenship" according to the book of Romans
Step 1: Understand the Context
Romans 13: This chapter of Romans is where Paul discusses the relationship between Christians and governing authorities. He emphasizes that all authority comes from God and that Christians have a duty to be good citizens by respecting and obeying these authorities.
Step 2: Analyze Each Statement
Reporting criminals in society: Explanation: While Romans 13 emphasizes the role of governing authorities in maintaining order and punishing wrongdoers (Romans 13:4: "For the one in authority is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for rulers do not bear the sword for no reason"), it does not explicitly command individuals to report criminals.
Alignment: This is more of an implication rather than a direct teaching. Reporting criminals could be seen as part of supporting the government's role, but it's not explicitly mentioned in Romans.
Supporting the poor: Explanation: Supporting the poor is a common theme in Christian teachings, but in Romans 13, the focus is more on the relationship with authorities rather than direct acts of charity. However, supporting the poor is addressed elsewhere in Paul's writings (e.g., Romans 12:13: "Share with the Lord’s people who are in need. Practice hospitality").
Alignment: While supporting the poor is an important Christian duty, Romans 13 specifically does not focus on this aspect as part of "good citizenship."
Obedient to those in authority: Explanation: Romans 13:1-2 clearly states that Christians must be subject to governing authorities because all authority comes from God: "Let everyone be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which God has established." This includes paying taxes and showing respect to those in positions of power.
Alignment: This directly aligns with the teaching in Romans 13.
Participation in governance: Explanation: Romans 13 does not specifically mention participation in governance. It emphasizes obedience and respect for authorities but does not require Christians to actively participate in government functions.
Alignment: This idea is not explicitly supported by Romans 13. The focus is more on submission to authority rather than active participation.
Answer: Obedient to those in authority.
Based on the breakdown:
The idea of reporting criminals in society is not directly mentioned in Romans 13 but could be implied as part of supporting the governing authorities.
Supporting the poor is an important Christian teaching, but it is not the primary focus of Romans 13 regarding citizenship.
Obedient to those in authority is the most directly supported statement according to Romans 13.
Participation in governance is not discussed in Romans 13.
According to Romans, good citizenship involves obedience to those in authority. The other options, while they may be good practices or Christian duties in other contexts, are not the primary focus of Paul's teaching on citizenship in Romans.

questions.text: The four people that left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan were
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to this question, we need to review the biblical account of who left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan, as recorded in the book of Genesis.
Step 1: Review the Biblical Account
The story of the journey from Ur of the Chaldeans is found in Genesis 11:27-31. This passage describes the genealogy of Terah and the family’s move from Ur of the Chaldeans to Canaan.
Step 2: Identify the People Who Left Ur
According to Genesis 11:31:
Terah: He is the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. He led the family out of Ur.
Abram: Terah’s son, who later became known as Abraham.
Sarai: Abram’s wife, who later became known as Sarah.
Lot: The son of Haran, Abram’s nephew.
The verse says, "Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of his son Abram, and together they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan."
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Nahor, Abram, Haran, and Lot: Explanation: This option is incorrect because Nahor and Haran did not leave Ur. Haran had died before the journey began, and Nahor stayed behind.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Abram, Sarai, Lot, and Haran: Explanation: This is incorrect because Haran had already died in Ur before the family left for Canaan (Genesis 11:28).
Alignment: Incorrect.
Terah, Abram, Lot, and Nahor
Explanation: This is incorrect because Nahor did not leave Ur with the others; he stayed behind.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Terah, Abram, Lot, and Sarai: Explanation: This is the correct option because these are the individuals explicitly mentioned in Genesis 11:31 as leaving Ur together.
Alignment: Correct.
Answer: Terah, Abram, Lot and Sarai.
The correct answer is Terah, Abram, Lot, and Sarai. These are the four individuals who left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan, as described in Genesis 11:31.

questions.text: The third sign which God performed through Moses in Egypt was
options: sprinkling dust in the air to become gnats
pouring Nile water on dry land to become blood
putting his hand in his armpit to become leprous
casting down his rod to become a snake
questions.explanation:
To answer the question about the third sign that God performed through Moses in Egypt, we need to review the sequence of miraculous signs described in the book of Exodus.
Step 1: Review the Sequence of Signs in Exodus
The signs that God performed through Moses in Egypt are documented in Exodus 7-9. Here's the order of the first few signs:
Casting down his rod to become a snake: (Exodus 7:10-12): This was the first sign that Moses performed before Pharaoh, where Aaron’s rod turned into a serpent.
Turning the Nile water into blood: (Exodus 7:19-21): This was the second sign, where the waters of the Nile turned to blood.
Plague of frogs: (Exodus 8:1-15): This was the third plague, where frogs swarmed the land of Egypt. However, this option is not listed among the choices in your question.
After the first two signs, we need to identify the next significant sign that is listed in the options.
Step 2: Analyze the Options
Sprinkling dust in the air to become gnats: Explanation: This event occurred later as the third plague (Exodus 8:16-19). Although this is not the third sign overall, it is the third plague specifically.
Alignment: This is not the third sign overall, but the third plague. Since the question asks for the "third sign," this is not the best answer based on a strict reading.
Pouring Nile water on dry land to become blood: Explanation: This was a sign God told Moses to perform before the Israelites to show them that he was sent by God (Exodus 4:9). It’s significant, but in Egypt, the actual turning of the Nile into blood was the second sign Moses performed before Pharaoh.
Alignment: Incorrect as the third sign in Egypt.
Putting his hand in his armpit to become leprous: Explanation: This was another sign given to Moses to convince the Israelites that God had appeared to him (Exodus 4:6-7), but this sign was not performed in Egypt before Pharaoh.
Alignment: Incorrect as the third sign in Egypt.
Casting down his rod to become a snake: Explanation: This was the first sign, not the third.
Alignment: Incorrect as the third sign.
Answer: Sprinkling dust in the air to become gnats.
Given the options provided and based on the biblical sequence:
Sprinkling dust in the air to become gnats: This event, though not the third sign overall, was indeed the third plague in Egypt (Exodus 8:16-19).
Therefore, the best answer among the given options is sprinkling dust in the air to become gnats. While this was the third plague, it can be considered the third significant sign that God performed through Moses in Egypt.

questions.text: The man who first saw Absalom hanging did not kill him because he was
options: not armed enough to do so
met by the Commander-in-Chief of David's army
aware that David did not want Absalom killed
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer
Step 1: Review the Context
Absalom, the son of King David, had rebelled against his father and was eventually defeated in battle. As Absalom was fleeing on his mule, his hair got caught in the branches of a tree, leaving him hanging there. One of David's men saw Absalom in this vulnerable position but did not kill him.
Step 2: Analyze the Options Based on the Biblical Text
Not armed enough to do so: Explanation: The man did not cite being unarmed or lacking the weapons necessary to kill Absalom as his reason for not doing so.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Afraid of Absalom's army: Explanation: There is no indication in the text that the man refrained from killing Absalom because he feared Absalom’s army.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Met by the Commander-in-Chief of David's army: Explanation: The man did later encounter Joab, the Commander-in-Chief of David's army, but this was after he had already chosen not to kill Absalom. This encounter was not the reason he didn’t kill Absalom.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Aware that David did not want Absalom killed: Explanation: The correct answer is found in 2 Samuel 18:12. The man who saw Absalom hanging in the tree explicitly said to Joab, "Even if I had the weight of a thousand shekels of silver in my hand, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son. For in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake, protect the young man Absalom.'" The man was aware that King David had commanded his commanders to deal gently with Absalom, and he feared the repercussions of disobeying the king's orders.
Alignment: Correct.
Answer: Aware that David did not want Absalom killed.
The man refrained from killing Absalom because he knew King David had specifically commanded that Absalom's life be spared, despite Absalom's rebellion.

questions.text: The covenant which God made with the Israelites was ratified when

Moses built an altar at the foot of Mount Horeb

the young men offered burnt and peace offerings
