questions.text: The disciples of Jesus could not heal the boy with epilepsy because they
questions.explanation:
To answer this question correctly, we need to refer to the biblical account where the disciples of Jesus were unable to heal a boy with epilepsy.
Step 1: Identify the Story
This story is found in the Gospels, specifically in Matthew 17:14-20 and Mark 9:14-29. It involves a father bringing his son, who suffers from seizures (often interpreted as epilepsy), to Jesus after the disciples were unable to heal him.
Step 2: Analyze the Possible Reasons
The question provides four possible reasons for why the disciples could not heal the boy:
Were powerless: This suggests they lacked the ability or authority. However, Jesus had previously given His disciples the power to cast out demons and heal the sick (Matthew 10:1), so this option doesn’t align with what we know from earlier in the scriptures.
Did not pray: Prayer is an essential part of spiritual practices, but whether or not they prayed is not explicitly mentioned as the reason in the immediate context.
Did not fast: Fasting is a practice of self-denial that is sometimes associated with spiritual power, but it is not mentioned directly in the context of this story.
Had little faith: This option directly relates to what Jesus said to the disciples after He healed the boy.
Step 3: Refer to Jesus' Explanation
After Jesus healed the boy, the disciples asked why they couldn’t cast out the demon. Jesus responded, "Because of your little faith" (Matthew 17:20, ESV). He also added that with faith as small as a mustard seed, they could move mountains. In some versions of this story, like in Mark 9:29, Jesus also mentions that "this kind can come out only by prayer" (and some manuscripts add "and fasting"), but the primary reason He highlights is their little faith.
Answer: Had little faith.
The correct answer, according to the biblical account, is that the disciples of Jesus could not heal the boy because they had little faith.

questions.text: Demolishing of the temple and rebinding it in three days was to seamy the death of Jesus for hour many days
questions.explanation:
Answer: 3 days.
The statement about demolishing the temple and rebuilding it in three days was made by Jesus in John 2:19. This statement was a metaphorical reference to His own death and resurrection.
In John 2:19 (KJV), Jesus says:
> "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."
Jesus was speaking about His body as the "temple." He was predicting that He would be crucified (the "demolishing" of the temple) and then be resurrected on the third day.
Eternal day (This does not fit the context of the three days).
7 days (This is not the correct time frame for Jesus' resurrection).
3 days: (This is the correct time frame, referring to the period between Jesus' death and His resurrection).
A day (This is not the correct time frame for Jesus' resurrection).
The reference to demolishing the temple and rebuilding it in three days was a symbolic way of referring to the death and resurrection of Jesus, which occurred over three days.

questions.text: According to Matthew, true wisdom is
options: to beware of false prophets and teachings
seeking God's kingdom and His righteousness
knowing the truth and doing it all the time
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer,
Step 1: Understand the context
The Gospel of Matthew contains several teachings of Jesus that provide insight into what true wisdom entails. These teachings often emphasize not just knowing what is right, but also doing it.
Step 2: Identify the relevant passages
One key passage in Matthew that discusses wisdom is found in Matthew 7:24-27. Here, Jesus tells the parable of the wise and foolish builders. The wise builder is described as the one who hears Jesus' words and puts them into practice. This suggests that wisdom involves both understanding and action.
Matthew 7:24 (NIV version) states:
> "Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock."
Step 3: Analyze the options
Beware of false prophets and teachings
Obeying fully the ten commandments
Seeking God's kingdom and His righteousness
Knowing the truth and doing it all the time
Step 4: Select the correct answer
The passage from Matthew indicates that true wisdom is about knowing the truth (hearing Jesus' words) and doing it (putting them into practice). This aligns directly with the fourth option.
Answer: Knowing the truth and doing it all the time.
According to Matthew, true wisdom is not just about knowledge but about consistently applying that knowledge in daily life.

questions.text: According to Romans, individuals that manifest spiritual gifts should
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to refer to the teachings in the Book of Romans where Paul discusses how individuals who manifest spiritual gifts should conduct themselves.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The relevant passage is found in Romans 12:3-8. In this passage, Paul discusses the proper attitude and behavior for those who have spiritual gifts.
Romans 12:3 (NIV) says: "For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you."
Romans 12:6 (NIV) continues: "We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with your faith..."
Step 2: Understand the Emphasis on Humility
Paul emphasizes that those who manifest spiritual gifts should do so with humility. He warns against thinking too highly of oneself because of the gifts received, emphasizing that all gifts are from God and should be used in accordance with His will.
Step 3: Match the Instruction with the Answer Choices
Always give generously: - While giving is important, this specific instruction is more about how spiritual gifts should be exercised with humility.
Show humility: - This is correct, as Paul specifically emphasizes the need for humility when exercising spiritual gifts.
Exhibit genuine love: - Genuine love is also a key principle in Romans 12, particularly in the broader context (Romans 12:9), but the specific instruction regarding spiritual gifts focuses on humility.

questions.text: What punishment did God give Solomon for his unwise policies?

Contextual Understanding

questions.text: What did Saul do after his defeat of the Amalekites?
options: he set up a monument for himself
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context of the Question
After defeating the Amalekites, Saul had to respond to the aftermath of his military victory. This was an opportunity to demonstrate his adherence to God's commands.
Step 2: Examine Each Option
He returned to Shiloh: Shiloh was a significant location for the Israelites, but there is no specific biblical record of Saul returning to Shiloh after this battle. His actions following the defeat were more directly linked to other locations and events.
He set up a monument for himself: According to 1 Samuel 15:12, Saul set up a monument for himself in Carmel. This act was a display of pride and self-glorification, which contrasted with the expected humility and focus on God’s glory.
He offered sacrifices to God: Although Saul did offer sacrifices to God at other times, the specific biblical account of his actions after defeating the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:21-22) focuses on his setting up the monument rather than offering sacrifices.
He repented of his sins: Saul’s repentance is a theme in other parts of the Bible, but after the defeat of the Amalekites, he did not show genuine repentance. Instead, he made excuses and did not fully acknowledge his disobedience.
Step 3: Review the Biblical Account
1 Samuel 15:12 describes Saul setting up a monument for himself. This act was criticized by the prophet Samuel and seen as indicative of Saul’s pride and failure to fully obey God's command.
Answer: He set up a monument for himself.
Saul set up a monument for himself is the correct answer. This action was significant in the biblical narrative as it illustrated Saul’s pride and disobedience, which led to his rejection by God as king.

questions.text: Summarily, St Paul in his teaching on 'New Life In Christ' advised Christains to ______
options: Endeavor to be baptized by immersion
Pray for the Grace of God
Dwell richly in the word of God
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct summary of St. Paul’s teaching on "New Life in Christ,"
Step 1: Understand Paul’s Teaching on "New Life in Christ"
Paul’s teaching on "New Life in Christ" emphasizes that believers are transformed through their faith in Christ. This transformation leads them to live according to the Spirit, displaying the fruits of the Spirit, and walking in righteousness. Paul frequently encourages believers to immerse themselves in the teachings of Christ and to allow the Word of God to shape their lives.
Colossians 3:16: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God."
Romans 12:2: "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect."
Paul's teaching encompasses more than avoiding specific sins like adultery and murder. Instead, it encourages a holistic transformation that involves dwelling richly in the Word of God.
Step 2: Evaluate the Options
Endeavor to be baptized by immersion: While baptism is important, it is not the central focus of Paul's teaching on new life in Christ.
Pray for the Grace of God: While praying for grace is important, Paul’s teaching on new life in Christ is more about the transformation that occurs when the Word of God dwells in believers.
Forsake only adultery and murder: This is too narrow and does not encompass the broader call to live a transformed life.
Dwell richly in the word of God: This is correct. Paul advises believers to allow the Word of God to dwell in them richly, guiding their thoughts, actions, and overall conduct as they live out their new life in Christ.
Answer: Dwell richly in the word of God.
St. Paul, in his teaching on "New Life in Christ," advises Christians to immerse themselves in the Word of God, allowing it to transform and guide every aspect of their lives.

questions.text: King Josiah defiled Topheth which was in the valley of the sons of Hinnom during his reform in Israel so that
options: no one might sacrifice human beings again to Molech
he might pull down Topheth and break Molech into pieces
he might revive the worship of the sun god
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to refer to the biblical account of King Josiah’s reforms in Israel, specifically focusing on his actions in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, also known as Topheth. This event is described in the Old Testament, particularly in the book of 2 Kings.
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage can be found in 2 Kings 23:10. This chapter details King Josiah’s extensive religious reforms aimed at purging Israel and Judah of idolatry and false worship practices.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: 2 Kings 23:10.
Situation: As part of his reform, King Josiah sought to eliminate idolatry and practices that were against the worship of the true God. One of the most detestable practices was the worship of Molech, which involved human sacrifice, specifically the sacrifice of children.
Step 3: Examine What Josiah Did
2 Kings 23:10: "He defiled Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, so that no one might burn his son or his daughter as an offering to Molech."
This verse clearly indicates that Josiah defiled Topheth to prevent the continuation of child sacrifices to Molech, a Canaanite deity associated with this gruesome practice.
Step 4: Compare the Answer Choices
No one might sacrifice human beings again to Molech: This directly matches the reason given in 2 Kings 23:10.
He might pull down Topheth and break Molech into pieces: While Josiah did destroy many idolatrous sites, the specific act of defiling Topheth was to stop the human sacrifices.
He might revive the worship of the sun god: This is contrary to Josiah's reforms, which were aimed at abolishing idolatry, not reviving it.
No one would worship Molech: While this is related, the specific reason given is to prevent human sacrifices, not just general worship.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: No one might sacrifice human beings again to Molech.
The text in 2 Kings 23:10 confirms that the primary reason for defiling Topheth was to prevent the horrific practice of child sacrifice to Molech.

questions.text: "...And I will say to my soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; take your ease, eat, drink, be merry..." God's response to the statement above was that
options: his soul was required of him
his soul should be satisfied with his increase
he should lay up more treasures for himself
the servant should enter into the rest of his Lord
questions.explanation:
Answer: His soul was required of him.
"
This statement comes from the Parable of the Rich Fool, which is found in Luke 12:16-21. In this parable, Jesus tells the story of a rich man who, after accumulating a large amount of wealth, decides to store it up and live a life of ease, without regard for God or the future.
Luke 12:20 states:
"But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?'"
This response from God emphasizes the futility of focusing solely on material wealth without being "rich toward God."
His soul was required of him: This directly matches the response given by God in Luke 12:20.
His soul should be satisfied with his increase: This is not the response given by God; the emphasis is on the futility of hoarding wealth.
He should lay up more treasures for himself: This is the opposite of the lesson of the parable.
The servant should enter into the rest of his Lord: This phrase is not found in this parable; it is more related to the parable of the talents.
God's response to the rich man in the parable was that his soul was required of him that very night, underscoring the suddenness of death and the importance of spiritual richness.

questions.text: The conditions for justification according to Paul is_______________

Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
Paul's teaching on justification is a central theme in his letters, especially in Romans and Galatians. According to Paul:
Romans 3:28: "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law."
Galatians 2:16: "Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ."
Paul consistently emphasizes that justification comes through faith in Christ crucified and not through works, merit, or the ability to keep the law.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Merit and favour: This is incorrect. Paul teaches that justification is not based on human merit or earning God's favor.
Ability to keep God's commandments: This is incorrect. Paul argues that no one can be justified by the law because no one can perfectly keep God's commandments.
Possession of spiritual gifts: This is incorrect. Spiritual gifts are important, but they are not the basis for justification.
Faith in Christ crucified: This is correct. Paul teaches that justification is by faith in Christ alone, based on His sacrificial death and resurrection.
Answer: Faith in Christ crucified.
According to Paul, the condition for justification is faith in Christ crucified.

questions.text: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus The statement above was made by Paul to the Church at
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Question
The question asks us to identify which church Paul was addressing when he made the specific statement about God supplying every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
Step 2: Recognize the Source of the Statement
The statement in question is a verse from the New Testament, specifically from one of Paul's letters to the early Christian churches. Knowing this, we need to locate the exact verse to identify which church was being addressed.
Step 3: Locate the Verse in the Bible
The statement, "And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus," is found in Philippians 4:19. This indicates that the statement is part of Paul's letter to the Philippians.
Step 4: Contextual Understanding
In his letter to the Philippians, Paul was expressing his gratitude to the believers in Philippi for their financial support and generosity. He reassures them that, just as they have met his needs, God will also meet their needs through His divine provision.
Step 5: Match the Statement to the Church
Now that we know the verse is from the Book of Philippians, we can confirm that the church Paul was addressing when he made this statement was the Church at Philippi.
Step 6: Verify Against the Answer Choices
Galatia: Paul wrote the letter to the Galatians, but the statement in question is not found there.
Philippi: This is the correct match, as the statement is found in Philippians 4:19.
Ephesus: Paul wrote a letter to the Ephesians, but this statement does not appear in that letter.
Corinth: Paul also wrote letters to the Corinthians, but the statement is not found in those letters either.
Step 7: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Philippi.
Paul made the statement "And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus" to the Church at Philippi. This is found in Philippians 4:19. Therefore, the correct answer is Philippi.

questions.text: Jesus' reply to the Devil's command to throw Himself down from the pinnacle of the temple was

...You shall not tempt the Lord your God"
...You shall worship the Lord your God and Him only shall you serve"
He will give his anges charge of you."
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to this question is found in the account of Jesus' temptation in the wilderness, specifically during the second temptation where the Devil challenges Jesus to throw Himself down from the pinnacle of the temple.
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is found in Matthew 4:5-7 and Luke 4:9-12.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: Matthew 4:5-7 and Luke 4:9-12.
Situation: During the second temptation, the Devil takes Jesus to the pinnacle of the temple and challenges Him to throw Himself down, quoting Psalm 91:11-12, which says that God will command His angels to protect Him.
Step 3: Examine Jesus' Reply
Matthew 4:7: "Jesus said to him, 'Again it is written, You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
Luke 4:12: "And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
In both accounts, Jesus responds by quoting Deuteronomy 6:16, emphasizing that one should not test God.
Step 4: Compare and Eliminate Incorrect Options
"Man shall not live by bread alone": This was Jesus' response to the first temptation, where the Devil challenged Him to turn stones into bread.
"You shall not tempt the Lord your God": Correct. This was Jesus' response to the Devil's challenge to throw Himself down from the pinnacle of the temple.
"You shall worship the Lord your God and Him only shall you serve": This was Jesus' response to the third temptation, where the Devil offered Him all the kingdoms of the world if Jesus would worship him.
"He will give His angels charge of you": This is part of the scripture the Devil quoted, not Jesus' reply.
Answer: ...You shall not tempt the Lord your God".
The correct answer is “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

questions.text: Why did God accept David who killed Uriah and took his wife but rejected Saul who spared King Agag?
options: David humbled himself when he realized his sin but Saul was stubborn
David was a singer of praises while Saul was not
David was a man after God's heart while Saul was His enemy
David was from the favoured tribe of Judah while Saul was from Benjamin
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to understand the key differences in how David and Saul responded to their sins and how their hearts were aligned with God’s will.
Step 1: Understand David’s Actions and Response
David committed serious sins by arranging for the death of Uriah and taking Bathsheba, Uriah's wife. However, when the prophet Nathan confronted David about his sin in 2 Samuel 12, David immediately recognized his wrongdoing, confessed his sin, and sought God's forgiveness.
2 Samuel 12:13 (NIV) says, "Then David said to Nathan, 'I have sinned against the Lord.' Nathan replied, 'The Lord has taken away your sin. You are not going to die.'"
David’s heart was repentant, and he genuinely sought to restore his relationship with God.
Step 2: Understand Saul’s Actions and Response
Saul, on the other hand, disobeyed God by sparing King Agag and taking spoils after a victory when he was explicitly instructed to destroy everything. When confronted by the prophet Samuel in 1 Samuel 15, Saul initially tried to justify his actions rather than immediately confessing his wrongdoing. His repentance was superficial, and he was more concerned with his own reputation than with truly obeying God.
1 Samuel 15:22-23 (NIV) says, "But Samuel replied: 'Does the Lord delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the Lord? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed is better than the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance like the evil of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has rejected you as king.'"
Step 3: Compare Their Hearts and Relationship with God
The key difference is that David had a heart that was truly repentant and aligned with God, while Saul’s heart was stubborn and disobedient.
Step 4: Match the Explanation with the Answer Choices
David humbled himself when he realized his sin but Saul was stubborn: - This is correct. David’s humility and genuine repentance distinguished him from Saul’s stubbornness and superficial repentance.
David was a singer of praises while Saul was not: - While David was known for his psalms and praises, this is not the reason for God accepting him and rejecting Saul.
David was a man after God's heart while Saul was His enemy: - This partially touches on the truth, but the critical issue was their responses to sin, not merely their labels.
David was from the favored tribe of Judah while Saul was from Benjamin: - This is incorrect. God's judgment was based on their actions and hearts, not on their tribal affiliations.
Answer: David humbled himself when he realized his sin but Saul was stubborn.

questions.text: 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" The statement above was made by the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context of the Statement
The statement "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" is a direct quote from the Bible. This is a crucial clue that points us toward the New Testament, where many miracles performed by Jesus are recorded.
Step 2: Understand the Meaning of "Make Me Clean"
The phrase "make me clean" is often associated with healing from a condition that made someone ritually unclean according to Jewish law. In biblical terms, being "unclean" could mean a number of things, but it most commonly referred to someone who had a skin disease, particularly leprosy.
Step 3: Match the Statement to the Correct Biblical Story
Now,
Centurion's Servant: This story is found in the Gospels (e.g., Matthew 8:5-13), where a Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant. The centurion shows great faith by telling Jesus that He doesn't even need to come to his house to heal the servant; a word from Jesus is enough. However, this story does not involve the phrase "make me clean."
Epileptic Boy: This account is in the Gospels (e.g., Mark 9:14-29). A father brings his epileptic son to Jesus and asks for healing. The phrase "make me clean" is not used here either.
Leper: In the Gospels (e.g., Matthew 8:1-4, Mark 1:40-45, Luke 5:12-16), there is a story where a leper approaches Jesus and says, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." This matches the statement exactly.
Paralytic: This story is also in the Gospels (e.g., Matthew 9:1-8, Mark 2:1-12), where a paralyzed man is brought to Jesus, and Jesus heals him. However, the man does not say the phrase "make me clean."
Answer: Leper.
Based on the context and matching the phrase to the correct biblical story, the person who made the statement "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean" is the leper.

questions.text: "...Whoever does not bear his cross and comes after me cannot be my disciple... This statement by Jesus entails that
options: following Him leads to death on the cross
following him demands total surrender and commitment
one must be prepared to disown his parents
His followers must carry a cross
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context of the statement
The statement, "Whoever does not bear his cross and comes after me cannot be my disciple," is found in the Gospels (e.g., Luke 14:27). Jesus is speaking to the crowd about the cost of discipleship. In this context, "bearing one's cross" is a metaphorical expression. During Roman times, carrying a cross was associated with a person condemned to crucifixion, symbolizing a path of suffering and sacrifice.
Step 2: Analyze each option
Following Him leads to death on the cross: Explanation: This option suggests that every follower of Jesus must physically die by crucifixion. While Jesus himself died on the cross, and some of his disciples faced martyrdom, this statement is not meant to be understood literally for all followers.
Relevance: This interpretation is too literal and doesn't capture the metaphorical meaning of Jesus' statement.
Following Him demands total surrender and commitment: Explanation: This option reflects the idea that to be a true disciple of Jesus, one must be willing to surrender everything—personal ambitions, comforts, relationships, and even life itself. "Bearing the cross" here symbolizes the willingness to endure hardship, sacrifice, and complete commitment to following Jesus.
Relevance: This interpretation aligns well with the overall message of Jesus about the cost of discipleship. It emphasizes the level of commitment and sacrifice required to be a true follower.
One must be prepared to disown his parents: Explanation: This option suggests that following Jesus requires disowning one's family. While Jesus does speak about the division that might come as a result of following him (e.g., "I have come to set a man against his father..."), the focus of this specific statement is broader than just familial relationships.
Relevance: This is a narrower interpretation and does not capture the full scope of what "bearing the cross" entails.
His followers must carry a cross: Explanation: This option implies that every follower of Jesus must physically carry a cross. While it reflects the literal image of Jesus carrying his cross, the statement is meant to be understood metaphorically rather than as a physical requirement.
Relevance: This option misses the metaphorical nature of the statement, which is about the willingness to face sacrifices and challenges in following Jesus.
Step 3: Identify the best answer
The correct understanding of the statement is that following Jesus demands a level of commitment that might involve significant sacrifice and self-denial. The metaphor of "bearing the cross" is about embracing the challenges, hardships, and even potential suffering that come with being a disciple.
Answer: Following him demands total surrender and commitment.
This is the correct answer, as it best captures the meaning of Jesus' statement about the cost of discipleship. It emphasizes the need for complete dedication and willingness to endure whatever is required to follow Jesus faithfully.

questions.text: Paul reminded the Thessalonians that he did not eat anyone's bread without paying for it. This statement teaches
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to this question is found in Paul's letters to the Thessalonians, where he discusses his conduct among them.
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is 2 Thessalonians 3:7-8.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: 2 Thessalonians 3:7-8.
Situation: In this passage, Paul is reminding the Thessalonians of the example he set for them when he was with them. He emphasizes that he did not rely on others for food without paying for it but instead worked hard to support himself, setting an example for the believers to follow.
Step 3: Examine Paul's Teaching
2 Thessalonians 3:7-8: "For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you."
This passage highlights the importance of hard work and not being a burden on others. Paul worked to support himself, demonstrating a work ethic that he encouraged others to follow.
Step 4: Compare and Eliminate Incorrect Options
Self-respect: While self-respect is important, the focus of this passage is on the value of hard work.
Creativity: Creativity is not the lesson being taught in this context.
Hard work: Correct. Paul emphasizes the importance of working hard and not being a burden on others, which is the primary lesson in this passage.
Humility: While humility is a Christian virtue, the emphasis here is specifically on working hard and paying for what one consumes.
Answer: Hardwork.
The correct answer is “hard work.”

questions.text: The reason for the first Apostolic Council in Jerusalem was that
options: circumcision was enjoined on the Gentile converts as necessary for salvation
the Gentiles were discriminated against at the fellowship meals
the widows of the Hellenistic Jews were discriminated against in the daily ministration.
questions.explanation:
To determine the reason for the first Apostolic Council in Jerusalem, we need to analyze the relevant biblical context and evaluate the options provided.
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Event
The first Apostolic Council, also known as the Council of Jerusalem, is recorded in Acts 15. This council was a significant event in the early church, where the apostles and elders gathered to resolve a major theological issue.
Step 2: Understand the Context
The reason for the Council of Jerusalem was a dispute that arose because some Jewish Christians were teaching that Gentile converts must be circumcised and required to follow the Law of Moses to be saved. This teaching caused confusion and disagreement, especially as Paul and Barnabas had been preaching to Gentiles without imposing these requirements.
Acts 15:1-2: "Certain people came down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the believers: 'Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.' This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute and debate with them. So Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question."
The council was convened to address whether circumcision and adherence to the Mosaic Law were necessary for Gentile converts to Christianity.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Paul's apostleship was in dispute: This is incorrect. While Paul's authority was questioned at times, the council was not convened to address this issue.
Circumcision was enjoined on the Gentile converts as necessary for salvation: This is correct. The central issue that prompted the council was whether Gentile converts needed to be circumcised and follow the Mosaic Law to be saved.
The Gentiles were discriminated against at the fellowship meals: This issue did arise in the early church (as seen in Galatians 2), but it was not the reason for the Council of Jerusalem.
The widows of the Hellenistic Jews were discriminated against in the daily ministration: This issue is addressed in Acts 6, where the seven deacons were appointed, but it was not related to the Council of Jerusalem.
Answer: Circumcision was enjoined on the Gentile converts as necessary for salvation.
The first Apostolic Council in Jerusalem was convened to resolve this specific theological dispute.

questions.text: "..the soul that sins shall die". The statement above by Prophet Ezekiel means that
options: God will judge the soul of a sinner
a sinner shall not escape punishment
every person is responsible for his own sin
the wages of sin is death
questions.explanation:
Answer: Every person is responsible for his own sin.
"
The statement "the soul that sins shall die" is found in Ezekiel 18:4 and Ezekiel 18:20. This chapter discusses the principle of individual responsibility for sin, countering the idea that children are punished for the sins of their parents or vice versa.
Ezekiel 18:20 states:
"The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself."
This emphasizes that each person is responsible for their own actions and sins.
God will judge the soul of a sinner: While this is true, it doesn't fully capture the specific meaning of Ezekiel's statement.
A sinner shall not escape punishment: This is implied, but it's not the primary focus of Ezekiel's message here.
Every person is responsible for his own sin: This directly matches the context of Ezekiel 18, where the emphasis is on individual responsibility.
The wages of sin is death: This is a related concept found in the New Testament (Romans 6:23), but it is not the exact meaning of Ezekiel's statement.
The statement by Prophet Ezekiel means that every person is responsible for their own sin, as explained in Ezekiel 18.

questions.text: Because David sought God's will to pursue the Amalekites who had invaded Ziklag,he was rewarded with victory and
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context
The story is found in 1 Samuel 30. After discovering that the Amalekites had attacked Ziklag, burned it down, and taken captive the women and children, David sought the Lord's guidance on whether he should pursue them. God instructed David to pursue the Amalekites, assuring him of victory.
Step 2: Examine the relevant passage
In 1 Samuel 30:18-20, after pursuing and defeating the Amalekites, David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. Additionally, David and his men collected a significant amount of spoil (or plunder), which they brought back from the Amalekites.
Step 3: Analyze each option
Many prisoners of war: Explanation: While David rescued all the captives taken by the Amalekites, the focus in the biblical text is on the recovery of the people and the spoils. The mention of prisoners of war as a reward does not align with the narrative.
Relevance: This option is not the best description of the reward given to David.
Favour: Explanation: Although David was undoubtedly favored by God in this situation, the passage specifically emphasizes the material spoils that David and his men collected after the victory.
Relevance: This option is not as specific as the narrative's emphasis on spoils.
Many new territories: Explanation: There is no mention in the biblical text that David gained new territories as a result of this victory. The focus is on the recovery of the captives and the spoils from the Amalekites.
Relevance: This option does not align with the biblical narrative.
Spoils: Explanation: After the victory, David and his men took the spoils from the Amalekites. The spoils included livestock and other goods, which were distributed among David’s men and the elders of Judah (1 Samuel 30:20-26).
Relevance: This option directly reflects the reward described in the biblical passage.
Step 4: Identify the correct answer
The correct answer is that David was rewarded with victory and spoils.
Answer: Spoils.
This is the correct answer, as it accurately reflects the reward David received after pursuing and defeating the Amalekites, as described in 1 Samuel 30.

questions.text: During the giving of the law at mount Sinai, the Israelites wanted Moses to speak to them instead of God because_____________
options: the people were afraid and trembled
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The event is recorded in Exodus 20:18-19. After God gave the Ten Commandments, the people were terrified by the thunder, lightning, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoke on the mountain. As a result, they were afraid and said to Moses:
“You speak to us, and we will listen. But do not let God speak to us, lest we die.”
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
They thought they will die: This is correct. The Israelites were terrified by God's presence and voice, and they feared they would die if He continued to speak directly to them.
They did not consecrate themselves: While the Israelites were commanded to consecrate themselves before the event (Exodus 19:10-11), this was not the reason they wanted Moses to speak to them instead of God.
The people were afraid and trembled: This is also correct and aligns with the biblical text, as the people were indeed afraid. However, the more specific reason was their fear of dying if God spoke directly to them.
Moses was their spokesman: While Moses acted as their mediator, the specific reason the Israelites wanted Moses to speak instead of God was their fear of death.
Answer: They thought they will die.
The most accurate answer is:
The Israelites wanted Moses to speak to them instead of God because they were afraid they would die if God continued to speak directly to them.

questions.text: "...Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father upon us, and we will serve you," This request was made to Rehoboam because
options: the people had another person in mind
the people wanted to test his wisdom
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is found in 1 Kings 12:1-4. This section discusses the request made by the people to Rehoboam after he became king.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: 1 Kings 12:1-4.
Situation: After Solomon's death, his son Rehoboam became king. The people of Israel approached Rehoboam with a request to lighten the heavy burdens that had been placed upon them during Solomon's reign.
Step 3: Examine the Specific Request
1 Kings 12:4: "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."
The people were asking for relief from the heavy labor and high taxes that had been imposed on them during Solomon's reign. They were not threatening revolt or testing Rehoboam's wisdom; rather, they were seeking a reduction in their burdens so they could continue to serve the new king.
Step 4: Compare the Answer Choices
The people had another person in mind: This is not directly related to the specific request; although, later, the dissatisfaction leads to the selection of Jeroboam as king by the northern tribes.
The people wanted to test his wisdom: There is no indication in the text that the request was made as a test of Rehoboam's wisdom.
Of an impending revolt: While a revolt did eventually occur, this was not the reason for the initial request; the request was about seeking relief.
The people wanted some relief: This directly matches the context and the request made in 1 Kings 12:4.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: The people wanted some relief.
The text in 1 Kings 12:4 clearly indicates that the people were asking for relief from the heavy burdens imposed during Solomon’s reign.

questions.text: "Leave the dead to bury their own dead..." Jesus statement above to the man He asked to follow Him was indicative of
options: His desire to save the man
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer,
Step 1: Understand the context
The statement "Leave the dead to bury their own dead" is found in the Gospel of Matthew 8:21-22 and Luke 9:59-60. In this passage, a man expressed his desire to follow Jesus but asked to first go and bury his father. Jesus responded with this statement, indicating the urgency and priority of following Him.
Step 2: Identify the meaning
Jesus' statement is often interpreted as emphasizing the cost of discipleship. It underscores the idea that following Him requires total commitment, even to the point of prioritizing His call over traditional social and familial obligations. The phrase suggests that the spiritual call to follow Jesus must take precedence over earthly concerns, even those as important as burying a loved one.
Step 3: Match with the given options
His desire to save the man
His power over death
The cost of discipleship
The futility of life
Answer: The cost discipleship.
The cost of discipleship
Jesus' statement "Leave the dead to bury their own dead" was indicative of the cost of discipleship, highlighting the need for absolute commitment to following Him above all else.

questions.text: "Take heart, it is I, fear not." This statement was made by Jesus when
options: He appeared to two disciples on the way to Emmaus
He was walking on the sea in the night
Mary Magdalene saw Him at the sepulchre
the woman saw Him after resurrection
questions.explanation:
To solve this question,
Step 1: Understand the context
The statement "Take heart, it is I, fear not" is associated with a moment when Jesus reassures His disciples during a time of fear or uncertainty.
Step 2: Identify the specific event
This statement is found in the New Testament, specifically in the Gospels. The event being referred to is when Jesus walked on water. The disciples were in a boat at night, and they saw Jesus walking toward them on the sea. They were terrified, thinking they were seeing a ghost, but Jesus reassured them with the words, "Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid."
Step 3: Recall or research the exact wording
The relevant passage is from Mark 6:50 (NIV version), where it says:
> "Immediately he spoke to them and said, 'Take courage! It is I. Don’t be afraid.'"
This event occurs when Jesus is walking on the sea at night.
Step 4: Match with the given options
He appeared to two disciples on the way to Emmaus
He was walking on the sea in the night: Mary Magdalene saw Him at the sepulchre
The woman saw Him after resurrection
Step 5: Select the correct answer
The correct context for the statement is when Jesus was walking on the sea at night and reassured His disciples.
Answer: He was walking on the sea in the night.
This statement was made by Jesus when He was walking on the sea at night and comforting His disciples who were afraid.

questions.text: A parable that teaches a lesson on the demands of the kingdom is that of the
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer,
Step 1: Understand the context of the parables
The Parable of the Weeds (Matthew 13:24-30): This parable, also known as the Parable of the Wheat and Tares, teaches about the kingdom of heaven and the coexistence of good and evil in the world until the final judgment. It emphasizes the patience required and the final separation of the righteous from the wicked.
The Parable of the Lost Coin (Luke 15:8-10): This parable focuses on the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, highlighting God's love and the value He places on each person.
The Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32): This parable illustrates God's forgiveness and the joy of reconciliation when a sinner repents and returns to God.
The Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37): This parable teaches about loving one's neighbor, regardless of social or ethnic boundaries, and emphasizes compassion and mercy.
Step 2: Identify the parable that focuses on the demands of the kingdom
The Parable of the Weeds is specifically about the kingdom of heaven and the ultimate judgment that awaits, making it the parable that directly addresses the demands and expectations of the kingdom.
Answer: Weeds.
The Parable of the Weeds teaches a lesson on the demands of the kingdom, specifically the need for patience and the final judgment when the righteous and the wicked will be separated.

questions.text: After healing the man at the pool of Bethzatha, the Jews sought all the more to kill Jesus because
options: they hated the man that was healed
they were unhappy that He healed the man
He claimed that God His father was still working
He did this on the Sabbath
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context of the Healing
The event in question is the healing of a man at the Pool of Bethzatha (also known as Bethesda) described in John 5:1-18. Jesus healed the man who had been an invalid for 38 years.
Step 2: Identify the Reaction of the Jews
After healing the man, the Jews sought to kill Jesus. The reason for their intense reaction is detailed in John 5:16-18.
Step 3: Review the Reasons Given
They hated the man that was healed: Not mentioned as a reason. The focus is on Jesus, not on the healed man.
They were unhappy that He healed the man: While they were not happy about the healing, the primary issue was related to the specific actions of Jesus.
He claimed that God His father was still working: In John 5:17, Jesus said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” This claim implied that Jesus had a unique relationship with God and was doing God’s work, which aggravated the Jews.
He did this on the Sabbath: In John 5:9-10, it is explicitly noted that the healing took place on the Sabbath. The Jews were particularly upset because Jesus performed the healing on this day, which they considered a violation of Sabbath laws.
Step 4: Match the Correct Reason with the Given Options
They hated the man that was healed: Incorrect.
They were unhappy that He healed the man: Partially correct, but not the main reason.
He claimed that God His father was still working: Partially correct, but this was not the primary reason.
He did this on the Sabbath: Correct. The Jews were most upset because Jesus healed the man on the Sabbath, which they considered a breach of the law.
Answer: He did this on the Sabbath.
This explains why the Jews sought to kill Jesus after the healing at the Pool of Bethzatha.

questions.text: The Last Supper took place during the Passover on the first day of
questions.explanation:
Answer: Unleavened bread.
The Last Supper took place during the Jewish festival of Passover, specifically on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread. This is clearly stated in the Gospels. The Feast of Unleavened Bread is a significant part of the Passover celebration and begins immediately after the Passover meal.
Context of the Event
The Last Supper, which is also known as the Passover meal, was shared by Jesus and His disciples on the evening before His crucifixion.
The Passover meal commemorated the Israelites' exodus from Egypt, and it was observed during the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Biblical Reference
In Matthew 26:17, it states: "Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, 'Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?'"
This indicates that the Last Supper took place on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
Analyze the Options
The week: This option is too general and does not specifically describe the context of the Last Supper.
Unleavened Bread: This is the correct answer. The Last Supper occurred during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is part of the Passover celebration.
Abstinence from blood: This is not related to the timing of the Last Supper.
The month: This option is too vague. The timing of the Last Supper is specifically tied to the Feast of Unleavened Bread, not just the beginning of a month.
Conclusion
The Last Supper took place during the Passover on the first day of Unleavened Bread.

questions.text: "...Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies...because they have become a thing for destruction..." Israel become a thing for destruction in the statement above because
options: she had devoted things in her midst
her soldiers refused to cooperate with the captain
the captain of her army was terrified
she had sent a few soldiers to battle
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to understand the context in which the statement was made, as recorded in the Old Testament.
Step 1: Identify the Story
The statement is found in the Book of Joshua, specifically in Joshua 7. This chapter deals with the aftermath of Israel's defeat at Ai, which occurred because of a sin committed by one of the Israelites, Achan.
Step 2: Understand the Reason for Israel's Defeat
In Joshua 7:11-12 (NIV), God tells Joshua:
Joshua 7:11-12 (NIV): "Israel has sinned; they have violated my covenant, which I commanded them to keep. They have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen, they have lied, they have put them with their own possessions. That is why the Israelites cannot stand against their enemies; they turn their backs and run because they have been made liable to destruction. I will not be with you anymore unless you destroy whatever among you is devoted to destruction."
The Israelites became "a thing for destruction" because they had taken some of the devoted things, which were supposed to be destroyed or dedicated to God, and kept them for themselves. This disobedience led to their defeat.
Step 3: Match the Reason with the Answer Choices
She had devoted things in her midst: - This is correct, as the reason for their defeat was that someone in Israel (Achan) had taken and hidden devoted things.
Her soldiers refused to cooperate with the captain: - This is incorrect; the issue was not about cooperation with the captain.
The captain of her army was terrified: - This is incorrect; the problem was not the fear of the captain.
She had sent a few soldiers to battle: - While Israel did send a small force to battle at Ai, the main reason for their defeat was the sin involving the devoted things.
Answer: She had devoted things in her midst.
"

questions.text: God's pardon of the people of Nineveh teaches a lesson on the benefits of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context of the question
The story of Nineveh is found in the Book of Jonah in the Bible. Jonah was sent by God to the city of Nineveh to warn the people that their wickedness had reached a point where God was going to destroy the city. However, after hearing Jonah's message, the people of Nineveh, from the king down to the common citizens, repented of their sins. They fasted, wore sackcloth, and turned from their evil ways. In response to their repentance, God showed mercy and decided not to destroy the city.
Step 2: Analyze each option
Tolerance: Explanation: Tolerance refers to the willingness to accept or endure someone else's beliefs or practices. While God showed mercy to the Ninevites, the focus of the story is not on tolerance but on the people's response to Jonah's warning.
Relevance: The story is more about the people turning away from their sins rather than God tolerating their sins.
Repentance: Explanation: Repentance is the act of feeling remorse for one's sins and turning away from those sins. The people of Nineveh repented after hearing Jonah's message, and it was this repentance that led God to forgive them and spare the city.
Relevance: This directly aligns with the lesson of the story. The benefits of repentance are clearly shown in how God responded to the Ninevites' change of heart.
Justice: Explanation: Justice involves the fair and impartial application of the law. While justice is an important concept, the story of Nineveh is focused on mercy and forgiveness rather than strict justice, as God chose to spare the city rather than punish it as initially planned.
Relevance: The lesson here is more about mercy and forgiveness rather than justice.
Forgiveness: Explanation: Forgiveness is the act of pardoning someone for their offenses. God forgave the people of Nineveh after they repented, demonstrating His mercy.
Relevance: While forgiveness is certainly a part of the story, it is the repentance of the Ninevites that prompted God's forgiveness.
Step 3: Identify the best answer
The story of God's pardon of the people of Nineveh teaches a powerful lesson about the benefits of repentance. Their sincere repentance led to God's forgiveness and the sparing of their city.
Answer: Repentance.
This is the correct answer, as the central lesson of the story is that genuine repentance can lead to God's mercy and forgiveness.

questions.text: After Saul had realized that God would have nothing to do with him, he sought the help of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The situation occurs after Saul realizes that God has turned away from him. This is described in 1 Samuel 28.
Step 2: Review Saul’s Actions
In 1 Samuel 28:7-8, Saul seeks the help of a medium, specifically the medium at Endor, to summon the spirit of Samuel for guidance.
Step 3: Match the Help Sought with the Given Options
A medium: Correct. Saul consulted the medium at Endor to seek counsel after God had stopped communicating with him.
Achish: Incorrect. Achish was the Philistine king whom Saul had previously sought refuge with.
Samuel: Incorrect. Saul sought Samuel’s spirit through a medium, as Samuel was deceased.
A prophet: Incorrect. Saul had already been rejected by God and was not seeking a living prophet.
Answer: A medium.
Saul sought the help of a medium after realizing that God would no longer provide guidance.

questions.text: "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh..." When Moses resisted God's call with the statement above, it portrayed his
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
This statement is made by Moses in Exodus 3:11. Moses is expressing hesitation and doubt about his ability to fulfill God's command to confront Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
Step 2: Evaluate Each Option
Stubbornness: This would imply a deliberate resistance or unwillingness to follow God's command despite knowing it is correct. However, Moses's reluctance is more about self-doubt than outright defiance.
Incompetence: This would suggest Moses feels he lacks the necessary skills or qualifications for the task. While Moses does express concern about his ability, this option doesn't fully capture his deeper feelings of inadequacy.
Lack of Strength: This would indicate physical or emotional weakness. Moses’s concern is not about physical strength but about his role and capability in the mission.
Lack of Eloquence: This option is related to Moses’s concern about his ability to speak effectively. In Exodus 4:10, Moses specifically mentions his lack of eloquence or speaking ability.
Step 3: Determine the Most Accurate Option
Moses’s resistance is primarily due to his feeling of inadequacy regarding his speaking abilities, as he explicitly mentions his lack of eloquence in Exodus 4:10. This aligns with his concern about not being able to effectively communicate with Pharaoh.
Conclusion:
Answer: Lack of eloquence.
This is correct as it most accurately represents Moses’s concern and hesitation about the task at hand.

questions.text: 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble and mounted on an ass..." The prophecy in the statement above was fulfilled during Jesus
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Prophecy's Origin
The statement in the question is a prophecy. The key to answering the question correctly is to first identify where this prophecy comes from in the Bible.
This prophecy is from the Old Testament, specifically Zechariah 9:9, which says, "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey."
Step 2: Identify the Event in the Life of Jesus
Next, you need to recall an event in the New Testament that matches this prophecy. The event should involve Jesus fulfilling the prophecy by riding a donkey.
The triumphal entry refers to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem shortly before His crucifixion. In this event, Jesus deliberately rides on a donkey to fulfill the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9. The people of Jerusalem greet Him with palm branches, shouting "Hosanna," recognizing Him as their King. This event is recorded in all four Gospels: Matthew 21:1-11, Mark 11:1-11, Luke 19:28-40, and John 12:12-19.
Step 3: Eliminate Other Options
Now, let's briefly review the other options to ensure they do not fit the prophecy:
Baptism by John: This event marks the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry but does not involve a donkey or any fulfillment of this specific prophecy.
Birth in a manger: This event signifies Jesus’ humble birth but, again, does not involve a donkey in this context, nor does it directly fulfill the prophecy in question.
Transfiguration: This event is where Jesus reveals His divine glory to three disciples on a mountain, which also does not involve a donkey or the fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9.
Answer: Triumphal entry.
Given the prophecy and the events in the life of Jesus, the triumphal entry is the correct event where this prophecy was fulfilled.
This methodical approach ensures that you understand not only what the correct answer is but also why it is the correct answer based on the biblical context.

questions.text: According to Paul in Philippians, Jesus demonstrated humility when He
options: had pity on the possessed man
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context
The question is referring to a passage in the book of Philippians where Paul describes how Jesus demonstrated humility. This passage is found in Philippians 2:5-8, which is part of what is often called the "Christ Hymn."
Step 2: Identify the specific passage
The relevant verses are Philippians 2:5-8. In these verses, Paul encourages the believers in Philippi to have the same mindset as Christ Jesus, who demonstrated the ultimate humility.
Step 3: Recall or research the exact wording
Philippians 2:5-8 (NIV version) states:
> "In your relationships with one another, have the same mindset as Christ Jesus: Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness. And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death—even death on a cross!"
Step 4: Analyze the key concept
In this passage, Paul highlights that Jesus demonstrated humility by taking the form of man and becoming obedient to death on the cross. Although Jesus was in the very nature God, He did not cling to His divine status but instead humbled Himself by becoming human.
Step 5: Match with the given options
Likened Himself to God
Had pity on the possessed man
Took the form of man: Forgave those who crucified Him
Step 6: Select the correct answer
The correct answer, according to Philippians 2:5-8, is that Jesus demonstrated humility by taking the form of man.
Answer: Took the form of man.
According to Paul in Philippians, Jesus demonstrated humility when He took the form of man, choosing to humble Himself and become obedient to death on the cross.

options: "we are going to obey the LORD our God"
"the LORD is our God, we shall obey Him"
"all the words which the LORD has spoken we will do"
"we shall keep all the commandments of God
questions.explanation:

This event is described in Exodus 24:3-7, where Moses recounts the covenant terms to the people, and they respond affirmatively.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
"We are going to obey the LORD our God": This phrase does not directly match the specific wording used by the people in the biblical text.
"The LORD is our God, we shall obey Him": While this statement expresses a commitment to obedience, it is not the exact wording from the biblical account.

questions.text: When prophet Isaiah saw the lord of host in the temple he_______
options: Was ashamed of himself and his people
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
Context: The vision of Isaiah in the temple is described in Isaiah 6:1-8. In this vision, Isaiah sees the Lord seated on a throne, and the seraphim are praising God.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Condemned himself and his people: This is partially correct. Isaiah does acknowledge his unworthiness and the sinfulness of his people, but condemnation is not the primary focus of his reaction.
Was ashamed of himself and his people: This is also partially correct. Isaiah expresses his unworthiness and the sinfulness of his people, reflecting a sense of shame.
Praised His Glory: Although Isaiah does acknowledge the Lord’s glory, his initial reaction is more focused on his own unworthiness.
Prayed fervently: Isaiah does not explicitly pray fervently in the vision, but he does respond with confession and willingness to serve.
Answer: Condemned himself and his people.
When Isaiah saw the Lord of Hosts in the temple, he condemned himself and his people by acknowledging his uncleanliness and the sinfulness of his people. This self-awareness led to his subsequent purification and commission to speak for God.

questions.text: The Jews asked Jesus whether they should pay tax or not because they wanted to
options: help him and his disciples to pay their taxes
questions.explanation:
To determine why the Jews asked Jesus whether they should pay tax or not,
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Event
This event is recorded in Matthew 22:15-22, Mark 12:13-17, and Luke 20:20-26. The question about paying taxes to Caesar was posed to Jesus by the Pharisees and Herodians.
Step 2: Understand the Biblical Context
The Pharisees and Herodians asked Jesus, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?" Their intention was to trap Jesus in a dilemma:
If Jesus said yes, He could alienate the Jewish people who resented Roman rule and the taxes imposed by the Romans.
If Jesus said no, He could be accused of rebellion against Rome, giving the authorities grounds to arrest Him.
Matthew 22:15: "Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words."
The purpose of asking the question was to entrap Jesus, hoping that His answer would put Him at odds with either the Roman authorities or the Jewish people.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Entrap him in his talk: This is correct. The primary motive of the Pharisees and Herodians was to trap Jesus with a question that could lead to His downfall, no matter how He answered.
Praise his teaching: This is incorrect. The question was not asked to praise Jesus, but rather to challenge Him.
Help him and his disciples to pay their taxes: This is incorrect. The question was not asked with genuine concern about Jesus or His disciples' taxes.
Evade paying taxes: This is incorrect. The intent was not about evading taxes but about trapping Jesus in a difficult situation.
Answer: Entrap him in his talk.
The Jews asked Jesus whether they should pay tax or not because they wanted to trap Him in a situation where His answer could be used against Him.

questions.text: The disciples were for the first time called Christians in____________
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The Bible records the first instance of the disciples being called Christians in Acts 11:26. This passage specifically states:
"And when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. So it was that for a whole year they assembled with the church and taught a great many people. And the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch."
Step 2: Understand the Context
In Acts 11, Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Saul (who is also known as Paul). He then brought Saul to Antioch. They both stayed there for a year, teaching large numbers of people. It was during this time that the disciples in Antioch were first called Christians.
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
Jerusalem: While Jerusalem was the starting point of the early church, it is not where the disciples were first called Christians.
Judea: Judea is a region, but it is not where the term "Christian" was first used.
Tarsus: Tarsus is where Saul (Paul) was from, but it is not where the disciples were first called Christians.
Antioch: This is the correct answer. According to Acts 11:26, the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
Answer: Antioch.
The disciples were for the first time called Christians in Antioch.

questions.text: According to Gospel of John, when Jesus appeared to the disciples on the evening of the first day of the week He
options: narrated to them how he suffered
questions.explanation:
In the Gospel of John, when Jesus appeared to the disciples on the evening of the first day of the week (which was the day of His resurrection), He greeted them in a specific way.
Contextual Understanding
This event takes place in John 20, where Jesus appears to His disciples after His resurrection. The disciples were gathered together in a room with the doors locked because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders.
Scriptural Reference
John 20:19 (NIV): "On the evening of that first day of the week, when the disciples were together, with the doors locked for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said, ‘Peace be with you!’"
Understanding Jesus' Actions
When Jesus appeared to His disciples, the first thing He did was pronounce peace upon them. He said, "Peace be with you," offering them comfort and reassurance after His resurrection.
Identify the Correct Option
Answer: Pronounced peace upon them.
" This is what Jesus did when He first appeared to the disciples after His resurrection.
According to the Gospel of John, when Jesus appeared to the disciples on the evening of the first day of the week, He pronounced peace upon them.

questions.text: According to Paul, just as the law came to increase trespass, so sin came to increase
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in Romans 5:20, where Paul discusses the relationship between the law, sin, and grace.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 5:20 states, “Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
Step 3: Match the Concept with the Given Options
Ungodliness: Incorrect. The passage does not discuss ungodliness in this context.
Punishment: Incorrect. The focus is on the increase of grace rather than punishment.
Righteousness: Incorrect. The passage contrasts sin with the increase of grace, not righteousness.
Grace: Correct. The passage states that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.
Answer: Grace.
Paul teaches that while the law increased trespass, the increase of sin led to an even greater increase of grace.

questions.text: The four people that left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan were
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
Context: The departure from Ur of the Chaldeans is described in Genesis 11:31 and Genesis 12:1-4. The key figures involved are Terah and his family.
Step 2: Review the Relevant Passage
Genesis 11:31 (NIV): “Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of his son Abram, and together they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan.”
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
Nahor, Abram, Haran and Lot: Nahor is not mentioned as having left Ur with the others in this context.
Terah, Abram, Lot and Sarai: This is correct. Terah (Abram’s father), Abram (later named Abraham), Sarai (Abram’s wife, later named Sarah), and Lot (Abram’s nephew) are the ones who left Ur.
Abram, Sarai, Lot and Haran: Haran was already deceased by the time of the departure from Ur, so he did not leave with them.
Terah, Abram, Lot and Nabor: Nabor (often spelled Nahor) was not part of the departure from Ur to Canaan.
Answer: Terah, Abram, Lot and Sarai.
The four people who left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan were Terah, Abram, Lot, and Sarai.

questions.text: St Paul's teaching on spiritual gifts was directed to _______
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Question
The question asks which group of early Christians St. Paul directed his teachings on spiritual gifts toward. To answer this, we need to identify the specific letters or epistles in which Paul discusses spiritual gifts and determine to whom these letters were addressed.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Biblical Passage
St. Paul’s most detailed and extensive teaching on spiritual gifts is found in 1 Corinthians 12-14. In these chapters, Paul provides instructions and clarification about the nature and use of spiritual gifts within the Christian community.
Step 3: Analyze the Context of 1 Corinthians 12-14
1 Corinthians 12: Paul explains the variety of spiritual gifts given by the Holy Spirit, such as wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, speaking in tongues, and interpretation of tongues. He emphasizes that all these gifts come from the same Spirit and are meant to benefit the entire church.
1 Corinthians 13: Known as the "Love Chapter," Paul emphasizes that love is greater than any spiritual gift. He teaches that even the most impressive gifts are meaningless without love.
1 Corinthians 14: Paul gives practical instructions on how to use spiritual gifts, particularly speaking in tongues and prophecy, in a way that builds up the church rather than causing confusion.
Step 4: Determine the Audience of the Teaching
The entire letter of 1 Corinthians is addressed to the church in Corinth, which was struggling with various issues, including the misuse of spiritual gifts. Therefore, it is clear that Paul’s teachings on spiritual gifts were directed specifically to the Corinthians.
Step 5: Evaluate the Other Options
Thessalonians: Paul’s letters to the Thessalonians focus on issues like the second coming of Christ, living a holy life, and encouragement, but they do not address spiritual gifts in detail.
Galatians: In Galatians, Paul addresses the issues of justification by faith versus works of the law. There is no detailed discussion of spiritual gifts.
Macedonians: The Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea) received letters from Paul, but these letters do not focus on spiritual gifts.
Answer: Corinthians.
St. Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts was directed to the Corinthians, specifically in his first letter to them (1 Corinthians 12-14). This teaching was crucial for guiding the Corinthian church in the proper use of spiritual gifts.

questions.text: "...But let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an overflowing stream." Amos' statement above suggests that the society was terribly
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The statement in the question comes from the Book of Amos, a prophetic book in the Old Testament. Amos was a prophet who spoke out against the social injustices of his time. He was particularly concerned with the exploitation and oppression of the poor by the wealthy and powerful in Israel.
Step 2: Analyzing the Options
Vindictive: This option suggests that the society was characterized by a desire for revenge. While Amos does speak against various forms of moral decay, "vindictiveness" specifically is not the primary concern in this context.
Abusive: This option implies that the society was characterized by abuse, which can be a broader term. While there was certainly abuse, especially towards the poor and vulnerable, the word "abusive" alone does not fully capture the systemic nature of the injustice Amos was addressing.
Oppressive: This option suggests that the society was marked by oppression, where the powerful exploited and mistreated the weak, particularly the poor. This directly aligns with the message of Amos, who was condemning the leaders and the wealthy for their oppressive practices. Amos called for justice and righteousness in response to the oppression he witnessed.
Destructive: This option implies that the society was engaged in actions that were causing destruction. While this could be a result of the oppression, the primary focus of Amos' statement is on the social injustice and the need for justice and righteousness, rather than on destruction itself.
Answer: Oppressive.
Amos' statement, "But let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an overflowing stream," is a call for an end to the oppression and injustice that was rampant in society. He was urging the people to practice justice and righteousness instead of exploiting and oppressing the vulnerable.

questions.text: Paul told the Athenians that they were very religious because
options: some of their poets said that men are the offsprings
they dedicated an alter to the unknown God
their Epicurean and Stoic philosophers always discussed religious issues
the city was full of idols and symbols of religious devotion.
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to the question about why Paul told the Athenians that they were "very religious,"
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Information
The reference to Paul telling the Athenians that they were "very religious" comes from Acts 17:22-23. This occurs during Paul’s visit to Athens, where he delivers a sermon at the Areopagus.
Step 2: Understanding the Context
In Acts 17:22-23, it is written:
"So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
Here, Paul acknowledges that the Athenians are very religious based on their dedication of an altar to an "unknown god." He uses this observation as an opportunity to introduce them to the true God he preaches about.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Some of their poets said that men are the offspring of God: While Paul does reference Greek poets later in his speech (Acts 17:28), this is not why he initially calls the Athenians "very religious."
They dedicated an altar to the unknown God: This is the correct answer. Paul specifically mentions this altar as evidence of their religious devotion and uses it as a starting point to discuss the God he preaches.
Their Epicurean and Stoic philosophers always discussed religious issues: Although Paul debated with these philosophers (Acts 17:18), this is not the reason he calls the Athenians "very religious."
The city was full of idols and symbols of religious devotion: While Paul does observe that the city is full of idols (Acts 17:16), it is the altar to the unknown god that he highlights as the reason for calling the Athenians "very religious."
Answer: They dedicated an alter to the unknown God.
They dedicated an altar to the unknown God
Paul observed the altar with the inscription "To the unknown god" and used it as an opportunity to explain the God he was preaching about, acknowledging the Athenians' religious nature.

questions.text: What did the blind man by the roadside near Jericho do no receiving his sight?
options: he thanked Jesus for healing him
he gave praise to God for making him whole
he jumped for joy and went away
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is "he followed Jesus, glorifying God."
Step 1: Understand the Context
This event is described in Luke 18:35-43. A blind man, often identified as Bartimaeus in the parallel account in Mark, was sitting by the roadside near Jericho when he heard that Jesus was passing by. He called out to Jesus for mercy, and Jesus healed him.
Step 2: Analyze the Relevant Passage
Luke 18:43 states:
"And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God."
This indicates that the blind man, upon receiving his sight, chose to follow Jesus and glorify God.
Step 3: Compare with the Answer Choices
He thanked Jesus for healing him: While this would have been appropriate, the text specifically mentions that he followed Jesus and glorified God.
He gave praise to God for making him whole: This is partially correct, but the complete action described is following Jesus while glorifying God.
He jumped for joy and went away: There is no mention of him jumping for joy and going away in the passage.
He followed Jesus, glorifying God: This is the exact response recorded in Luke 18:43.
Answer: He followed Jesus, glorfying God.
He followed Jesus, glorifying God
Upon receiving his sight, the blind man by the roadside near Jericho followed Jesus, glorifying God, as recorded in Luke 18:43.
