questions.text: What did Gideon call the altar which he built to the LORD?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The story of Gideon is found in the Book of Judges, specifically in Judges 6. After the Angel of the Lord appeared to Gideon and gave him a mission to save Israel from the Midianites, Gideon built an altar to the LORD.
Step 2: Identifying the Name of the Altar
In Judges 6:24, it says:
> "Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, 'The LORD is Peace.' To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites."
This verse clearly indicates the name that Gideon gave to the altar.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
The LORD is merciful: This is not the name that Gideon gave to the altar.
The LORD is peace: This option is correct. Gideon named the altar "The LORD is Peace" (in Hebrew, "Yahweh Shalom").
Jehovah Jireh: "Jehovah Jireh" means "The LORD will provide," and this name is associated with Abraham's story in Genesis 22, not Gideon's altar.
The LORD is great: This is not the name given to the altar by Gideon.
Answer: The LORD is peace.
Gideon called the altar which he built to the LORD "The LORD is Peace" (Yahweh Shalom).

questions.text: "The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few..." Jesus made the statement above during the_________
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, "
Step 1: Understand the Context
This statement is recorded in two places in the Gospels:
Matthew 9:37-38: Jesus says, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest." This statement is made just before Jesus sends out His twelve disciples on their mission.
Luke 10:2: Jesus repeats the same words when He is sending out seventy (or seventy-two, depending on the manuscript) others to go ahead of Him into every town and place where He Himself was about to go.
Step 2: Analyze the Options
Commissioning of the seventy others: This is correct according to Luke 10:2. Jesus made this statement when He was sending out the seventy (or seventy-two) disciples.
Mission of the twelve: Although Jesus made a similar statement before sending out the twelve in Matthew 9:37-38, the phrasing of the question suggests a later event, which refers to the commissioning of the seventy others.
Sermon on the mount: This statement was not made during the Sermon on the Mount.
Triumphant entry: This statement was not made during the triumphant entry into Jerusalem.
Answer: Commissioning of the seventy others.
The statement "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few" was made by Jesus during the commissioning of the seventy others.

questions.text: According to Matthew, the stone on the tomb of Jesus was removed by
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The question refers to the events following the resurrection of Jesus, as recorded in the Gospel of Matthew. The stone covering the entrance to Jesus' tomb was found to be rolled away when some of His followers visited the tomb on the first day of the week after His crucifixion.
Step 2: Identifying Who Removed the Stone
In Matthew 28:2, it is written:
> "And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it."
This passage clearly states that the stone was removed by an angel.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
An angel: This option is correct. The Gospel of Matthew specifically mentions that an angel rolled back the stone.
A Roman soldier: There is no mention in Matthew's account of a Roman soldier removing the stone. In fact, the soldiers guarding the tomb were struck with fear when the angel appeared.
Mary Magdalene: Mary Magdalene was one of the women who visited the tomb, but she did not remove the stone. She found the stone already removed when she arrived.
Peter and John: Peter and John visited the tomb after Mary Magdalene reported that the stone had been removed, but they did not remove the stone themselves.
Answer: An angel.
According to Matthew, the stone on the tomb of Jesus was removed by an angel.

questions.text: St. Paul on 'Civic Responsibility' advised Christians not only to be law-abiding but also_________
options: to provide moral advice to those in authority
do what is expected of them
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer Paul's teachings on civic responsibility.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
St. Paul's teachings on civic responsibility are found in Romans 13:1-7. In this passage, Paul advises Christians to be subject to governing authorities because all authority comes from God. He emphasizes the importance of obeying the laws and doing what is right.
Step 2: Analyze the Key Points of Paul's Teaching
In Romans 13, Paul stresses that Christians should:
Be law-abiding: Submit to authorities as they are instituted by God.
Pay taxes: Fulfill financial obligations to the government.
Do what is expected of them: This includes respecting and honoring those in authority, as well as fulfilling civic duties.
Step 3: Evaluate Each Option
Provide moral advice to those in authority: Paul does not specifically advise Christians to provide moral advice to those in authority in this passage.
Do what is expected of them: This is correct. Paul emphasizes that Christians should fulfill their obligations, including paying taxes, giving respect, and honoring authorities.
Shun membership of unlawful societies: While it is good advice, this is not the focus of Paul’s teaching in Romans 13.
Resist any illegitimate government: Paul does not encourage resistance to government, even if it is perceived as illegitimate. Instead, he advises submission to governing authorities.
Answer: Do what is expected of them.
St. Paul advised Christians not only to be law-abiding but also to do what is expected of them in terms of fulfilling their civic responsibilities, including paying taxes and showing respect to authorities.

questions.text: For how long did the Lord supply the children of Israel with manna in the wilderness?
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to how long the Lord supplied the children of Israel with manna in the wilderness, we need to refer to the biblical account.
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The story of the manna is found in Exodus 16. The Israelites began receiving manna from God shortly after they left Egypt and continued to receive it throughout their journey in the wilderness until they reached the Promised Land.
In Exodus 16:35, it is stated: "The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land that was settled; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan."
Step 2: Analyzing Each Option
Step 3: Option 1: "Forty Years"
Analysis: This is the correct answer. The Israelites ate manna for 40 years, from shortly after they left Egypt until they entered the Promised Land.
Step 4: Option 2: "Thirty-eight years"
Analysis: This is incorrect. While the Israelites wandered for 38 years after leaving Kadesh Barnea, the total time of manna provision was 40 years.
Step 5: Option 3: "Eleven months"
Analysis: This is incorrect. The provision of manna lasted far longer than eleven months.
Step 6: Option 4: "Twenty-two years"
Analysis: This is incorrect. The duration was 40 years, not 22 years.
Answer: Forty Years.
The Lord supplied the children of Israel with manna in the wilderness for forty years until they reached the border of the Promised Land.

questions.text: The failure of Rehoboam to heed to the advice of the old men resulted in
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context of the question
Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, became king after Solomon's death. In 1 Kings 12, when the people of Israel came to Rehoboam to ask for lighter burdens, he sought advice on how to respond. The old men (the elders who had advised his father, Solomon) advised Rehoboam to be a servant to the people and speak kindly to them, which would secure their loyalty. However, Rehoboam rejected this advice and instead followed the counsel of the younger men, who advised him to make the burdens even heavier.
Step 2: Analyze each option
Famine in the land: Explanation: This suggests that the consequence of Rehoboam's actions led to a famine.
Relevance: There is no biblical account linking Rehoboam's decision to a famine. This option does not match the historical or biblical context.
Division of the kingdom: Explanation: This refers to the split of the united kingdom of Israel into two separate kingdoms: the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah).
Relevance: This is the direct result of Rehoboam's failure to heed the advice of the old men. His harsh response led to the ten northern tribes rebelling and making Jeroboam their king, resulting in the division of the kingdom.
The attack by the Philistines
Explanation: This suggests that Rehoboam's decision led to an attack by the Philistines.
Relevance: The Bible does not associate Rehoboam’s decision with an attack by the Philistines. This option is not relevant to the specific consequence mentioned in the question.
The war against Jeroboam: Explanation: This suggests that Rehoboam's decision led directly to a war with Jeroboam.
Relevance: While there was tension and eventual conflict between the kingdoms of Judah (led by Rehoboam) and Israel (led by Jeroboam), the primary and immediate consequence of Rehoboam’s decision was the division of the kingdom, not war.
Step 3: Identify the best answer
The Bible clearly states that Rehoboam's decision to follow the advice of the younger men led to the division of the kingdom, with ten tribes breaking away to form the northern kingdom under Jeroboam.
Answer: Division of the kingdom.
This is the correct answer, as it directly reflects the primary consequence of Rehoboam's failure to heed the advice of the old men, leading to the split of the united kingdom of Israel.

Step 2: Review Saul’s Promise

Step 3: Match the Promise with the Given Options
Giving the person part of his land: Not specifically mentioned.
Giving his daughter in marriage to the person: Correct. Saul promised to give his daughter in marriage to the person who defeated Goliath.

questions.text: The model example in St. Paul teaching on humility is _______
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to this question about the model example in St. Paul’s teaching on humility, we need to refer to Paul’s writings in the New Testament and identify the figure he uses as the ultimate example of humility.
Step 1: Understanding St. Paul’s Teaching on Humility
St. Paul discusses the topic of humility most explicitly in his letter to the Philippians. In Philippians 2:5-11, Paul presents Jesus Christ as the supreme model of humility. He describes how Jesus, though being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage. Instead, Jesus humbled himself by taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross.
This passage is known as the "Christ Hymn" and is central to Paul’s teaching on humility. It emphasizes that true humility involves self-sacrifice, service to others, and obedience to God.
Step 2: Analyzing Each Option
Step 3: Option 1: "Abraham"
Abraham is an important figure in the Bible, known for his faith and obedience to God, but he is not specifically cited by St. Paul as the model of humility.
Step 4: Option 2: "Prophet Elijah"
Elijah is a significant prophet, known for his zeal and miracles, but he is not referenced by Paul as an example of humility.
Step 5: Option 3: "None of the Above"
This could be the correct answer if none of the listed individuals is the model of humility according to St. Paul’s teachings.
Step 6: Option 4: "Noah"
Noah is known for his obedience in building the ark, but like Abraham and Elijah, he is not presented by Paul as the epitome of humility.
Answer: None of the Above.
St. Paul’s model example of humility is Jesus Christ, not Abraham, Elijah, or Noah. Since "Jesus Christ" is not listed among the options, the correct answer is:
Paul’s teaching on humility highlights Christ as the ultimate model, making "None of the Above" the correct choice.

Understanding the Commandment

Identify the Correct Option

" This is the new commandment that Jesus gave to His disciples.

questions.text: One of the following is not a condition for effective prayer according to St James_____
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to this question, James teaches about the conditions for effective prayer in the New Testament.
Step 1: Context of St. James' Teachings on Prayer
In the Epistle of James, particularly in James 1:5-8 and James 5:13-18, St. James outlines several conditions for effective prayer. He emphasizes the importance of faith, perseverance, and righteousness when praying.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Step 3: Option 1: "Faith"
Faith is a key condition for effective prayer according to St. James. In James 1:6, he advises, "But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind." Thus, faith is essential.
Step 4: Option 2: "Lowliness"
Lowliness or humility is a Christian virtue, but it is not specifically mentioned by St. James as a condition for effective prayer. St. James does stress the importance of humility in general (James 4:6), but this is not directly tied to his teachings on effective prayer.
Step 5: Option 3: "Steadfastness"
Steadfastness is closely related to perseverance. While James doesn't use the word "steadfastness" explicitly in relation to prayer, he does emphasize the importance of persistence and patience, which are similar in meaning.
Step 6: Option 4: "Perseverance"
Perseverance is emphasized by James, particularly in the context of enduring trials and remaining faithful. In James 5:16, he talks about the "effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man" which suggests perseverance in prayer.
Answer: Lowliness.
The condition for effective prayer not mentioned by St. James is:
While lowliness or humility is an important Christian virtue, it is not specifically listed by St. James as a condition for effective prayer in his epistle.

questions.text: Whose address led to the conversion of three thousand souls on the of Pentecost?

Step 2: Identify the specific passage
Acts 2:14-41 describes how Peter stood up with the Eleven and addressed the crowd, explaining the fulfillment of prophecy and proclaiming Jesus as the Messiah.

Acts 2:41 (NIV version) states:
> "Those who accepted his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to their number that day."
Step 4: Match with the given options
Peter's: James
Paul's
John's
Answer: Peter's.
Peter's address on the day of Pentecost led to the conversion of about three thousand souls.

questions.text: Who was Aaron to Moses in the bible?
questions.explanation:
In the Bible, Aaron was Moses' brother.
Aaron is introduced as the elder brother of Moses in the book of Exodus. He played a significant role in the story of the Israelites' exodus from Egypt. God appointed Aaron to be the spokesperson for Moses when Moses expressed concern about his ability to speak eloquently. Aaron later became the first high priest of the Israelites.
Step 1: Reference
Exodus 4:14: "Then the Lord's anger burned against Moses and he said, 'What about your brother, Aaron the Levite? I know he can speak well.'"
Exodus 7:1: "Then the Lord said to Moses, 'See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.'"
Answer: His brother.

questions.text: The most significant lesson at the scene of the Israelites' blame of Moses in their struggle and escape from Egypt is that___________
options: God hardened the heart of Pharaoh to pursue the Israelites
they would have perfered to stay back and die in Egypt
Moses' courage and confidence in God saved the entire situation
Moses' height of anger and intolerance was revealed
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Event
The event in question refers to the scene where the Israelites, after escaping from Egypt, found themselves trapped between Pharaoh's pursuing army and the Red Sea. In their fear, they blamed Moses for leading them out of Egypt, accusing him of bringing them to the desert to die. This is recorded in Exodus 14:10-14.
Step 2: Understand the Key Lessons from the Event
When the Israelites blamed Moses, he responded with great faith and courage, telling the people to "stand firm and see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today" (Exodus 14:13). Moses' faith in God led to the miraculous parting of the Red Sea, allowing the Israelites to escape.
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
God hardened the heart of Pharaoh to pursue the Israelites: While this is true, it is not the most significant lesson from the scene. The focus is on the response to the Israelites' fear and complaints.
They would have preferred to stay back and die in Egypt: The Israelites did express this sentiment, but it serves more as a reflection of their fear than the primary lesson.
Moses' courage and confidence in God saved the entire situation: This is the correct lesson. Moses' faith and leadership in the face of the Israelites' fear and complaints led to God's miraculous intervention, saving the Israelites from destruction.
Moses' height of anger and intolerance was revealed: This is incorrect. The passage does not highlight Moses’ anger or intolerance; rather, it emphasizes his faith and trust in God.
Answer: Moses' courage and confidence in God saved the entire situation.
The most significant lesson at the scene of the Israelites' blame of Moses is that Moses’ courage and unwavering confidence in God led to the miraculous deliverance of the Israelites from the Egyptian army.

questions.text: What did the Israelites do immediately David killed Goliath?
options: They plundered the tents of the Philistines
they rose up and pursued the Philistines
they withdrew from fighting their enemies
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to the question "What did the Israelites do immediately after David killed Goliath?" is "they rose up and pursued the Philistines."
Step 1: Context of the Battle
The event takes place in 1 Samuel 17, where the Israelites are at war with the Philistines. Goliath, the champion of the Philistines, had been challenging the Israelites to send a warrior to fight him in single combat, but no one dared to face him until David stepped forward.
Step 2: David Kills Goliath
David, a young shepherd, confronts Goliath with a sling and a stone. He strikes Goliath on the forehead with a stone, and Goliath falls to the ground. David then uses Goliath's own sword to kill him and cuts off his head (1 Samuel 17:49-51).
Step 3: Immediate Reaction of the Israelites
Upon seeing that Goliath was dead, the Philistines turned and ran away in fear (1 Samuel 17:51).
The Israelites’ Response: The men of Israel and Judah immediately rose up, shouting in triumph, and pursued the Philistines. They chased them all the way to the gates of Ekron and Gath, which were Philistine cities (1 Samuel 17:52).
Step 4: Outcome of the Pursuit
As the Israelites pursued the fleeing Philistines, they struck them down along the way. After the pursuit, they returned and plundered the Philistine camp (1 Samuel 17:53).
In summary, the immediate action taken by the Israelites after David killed Goliath was that "they rose up and pursued the Philistines." This marked the turning point in the battle, leading to a decisive victory for the Israelites.
Answer: They rose up and pursued the Philistines.

questions.text: What was Samson's major achievement as Israel's leader?
options: He captured the city of Jericho
He saved the Israelites from the Amorites
He secured permanent independence for Israel
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand Samson's Role
Samson was a judge of Israel known for his extraordinary strength, as described in the Book of Judges.
Step 2: Evaluate Each Option
Suppressed the Philistines: Samson is best known for his conflicts with the Philistines. His actions, such as pulling down the pillars of the Philistine temple, were significant in undermining Philistine power, though they did not fully suppress them.
Captured the City of Jericho: This was achieved by Joshua, not Samson. Jericho's capture is a significant event in the history of Israel but not related to Samson.
Saved the Israelites from the Amorites: This is not associated with Samson. The Amorites were not the primary adversaries of Samson.
Secured Permanent Independence for Israel: Samson's achievements did not result in permanent independence for Israel. His efforts were more about individual victories and struggles rather than establishing long-term independence.
Step 3: Determine the Most Accurate Option
Samson's major achievement was his role in suppressing Philistine influence through various acts of defiance and strength. While he did not fully end Philistine dominance, he had a significant impact on their control over Israel.
Conclusion:
Answer: He suppressed the Philistines.
This is correct as it most accurately reflects Samson’s major achievements and contributions as a leader of Israel.

questions.text: The reward for total obedience to the commandments of God is
questions.explanation: Answer: Wisdom.

questions.text: When the Babylonians captured king Zedekiah, they
options: assaulted his wives in his presence
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
Context: King Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, and his capture is described in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39.
Step 2: Review the Relevant Passage
2 Kings 25:7 (NIV): “They killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. Then they put out his eyes, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon.”
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
Killed him immediately: Zedekiah was not killed immediately; he was captured and later executed.
Assaulted his wives in his presence: There is no mention in the Bible that Zedekiah’s wives were assaulted in his presence.
Pulled out his eyes: This is correct. After killing his sons, the Babylonians pulled out Zedekiah’s eyes and took him to Babylon.
Took his sons to Babylon: Zedekiah’s sons were killed before his eyes, not taken to Babylon.
Answer: Pulled out his eyes.
When the Babylonians captured King Zedekiah, they pulled out his eyes.

questions.text: Although Josiah removed the vessels of Baal and Asherah from the Temple, God did not turn from the fierceness of His wrath because
options: the people did not remove them completely
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
King Josiah undertook significant reforms to rid Judah of idolatry, including removing the vessels of Baal and Asherah from the Temple (2 Kings 23). However, despite these efforts, God’s wrath was not fully averted.
Step 2: Evaluate Each Option
The People Did Not Remove Them Completely: Josiah made substantial efforts to remove idolatry, but it’s recorded that the people’s persistent sin and idolatry continued to provoke God’s anger.
Jehoahaz, Josiah’s Son, Had Provoked Him: Jehoahaz’s actions were after Josiah's death and not directly related to the cause of God’s wrath during Josiah’s reign.
Manasseh Had Provoked Him: Manasseh, Josiah’s grandfather, committed significant idolatry and evil practices, which led to God’s judgment on Judah. God’s wrath was not entirely mitigated by Josiah’s reforms due to Manasseh’s earlier actions (2 Kings 24:3-4).
The People Had Opposed Josiah: While opposition existed, it was not the primary reason for God’s continued wrath.
Step 3: Determine the Most Accurate Option
The lasting impact of Manasseh’s sins on the nation was a significant factor. Even though Josiah made efforts to reform, the long-term consequences of Manasseh’s actions contributed to God’s continued wrath.
Conclusion:
The correct answer is Manasseh had provoked Him, as the previous king’s sins had set in motion a divine judgment that continued despite Josiah’s reforms.
Answer: Manaddeh had provoked Him.

questions.text: "...The earth produces of itself, first the blade then the ear, then the full grain in the ear..." The statement above was made by Jesus in the parable of the
questions.explanation:
Answer: Seed growing secretly.
"
The statement "The earth produces of itself, first the blade then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" is part of a parable that Jesus told to illustrate the mysterious and gradual growth of the kingdom of God.
This specific statement is found in Mark 4:26-29, which is known as the Parable of the Seed Growing Secretly. In this parable, Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a man who scatters seed on the ground and then, without his knowing how, the seed sprouts and grows.
Mark 4:28 states:
"The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear."
Weeds: The Parable of the Weeds is about the coexistence of good and evil until the final judgment.
Seed growing secretly: This is the correct parable where the statement about the growth process of the seed is made.
Sower: The Parable of the Sower focuses on different types of soil and how they receive the seed.
Mustard seed: The Parable of the Mustard Seed describes the kingdom of God growing from a small beginning to something great.
The statement "The earth produces of itself, first the blade then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" was made by Jesus in the Parable of the Seed Growing Secretly, as recorded in Mark 4:26-29.

questions.text: The Lord protected the Israelites with all but one of the following when the Egyptians chased them
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to this question, we need to examine the biblical account of how the Lord protected the Israelites when the Egyptians chased them during the Exodus.
Step 1: Understanding the Biblical Account
The relevant story is found in Exodus 14, where the Israelites are fleeing from Egypt, and the Egyptian army is pursuing them. God provides several forms of protection to the Israelites during this time.
Pillar of Cloud: In Exodus 14:19-20, the Lord moved the pillar of cloud to stand between the Israelites and the Egyptians, creating a barrier. This cloud brought darkness to the Egyptians but light to the Israelites.
Pillar of Fire: The pillar of fire is also mentioned as guiding and protecting the Israelites, though it is not directly cited during the chase at the Red Sea in the specific instance of the barrier.
Angels: In Exodus 14:19, it is mentioned that the angel of God, who had been traveling in front of Israel’s army, withdrew and went behind them, providing additional protection.
Pillar of Darkness: There is no mention of a "pillar of darkness" specifically in the Bible. The darkness was a result of the cloud, not a separate pillar of darkness.
Pillar of Storm: There is no mention of a "pillar of storm" in the biblical account.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Step 3: Option 1: "Pillar of cloud"
This is correct. The pillar of cloud protected the Israelites by confusing the Egyptians and providing light to the Israelites.
Step 4: Option 2: "Pillar of darkness"
There is no mention of a "pillar of darkness" as a separate entity in the Bible. The darkness was part of the pillar of cloud, not a separate pillar.
Step 5: Option 3: "Angels"
Angels are indeed mentioned as protecting the Israelites by moving between them and the Egyptians.
Step 6: Option 4: "Pillar of storm"
There is no mention of a "pillar of storm" in the biblical narrative.
Answer: Pillar of storm.
This option is not mentioned in the Bible as a form of protection provided to the Israelites during their escape from the Egyptians.

questions.text: The new covenant God made with the house of Israel and the house of Judah was written on
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The "new covenant" is specifically mentioned in Jeremiah 31:31-34. This passage outlines the nature of the covenant God intended to make with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: Jeremiah 31:31-34 is the key passage where God speaks about a new covenant that is different from the old covenant made with the Israelites when they came out of Egypt.
Nature of the New Covenant: The old covenant was given in the form of laws written on tablets of stone (as seen with the Ten Commandments). The new covenant, however, would be different in how it is established and internalized by the people.
Step 3: Examine the Content of the New Covenant
In Jeremiah 31:33, God explains the nature of this new covenant:
Jeremiah 31:33: "This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel after that time," declares the LORD. "I will put my law in their minds and write it on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people."
From this passage, it’s clear that unlike the old covenant written on tablets of stone, the new covenant is characterized by the law being written directly on the hearts of the people.
Step 4: Compare the Answer Choices
Stones: This refers to the old covenant, where the Ten Commandments were written on stone tablets.
Tablets: Again, this refers to the old covenant, where the law was given on stone tablets.
Their foreheads: This is not mentioned in the context of the new covenant.
Their hearts: This is directly mentioned in Jeremiah 31:33, where God says He will write His law on their hearts.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Their hearts.
To be certain, Jeremiah 31:33 clearly states that the new covenant involves God's law being written on the hearts of the people, making it a deeply personal and internalized relationship with God.
”

questions.text: Jesus healed the lame man who had been sick for thirty-eight years at?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Event
The healing of the lame man who had been sick for thirty-eight years is recorded in John 5:1-15. This passage describes the healing of a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.
Step 2: Analyze the Relevant Biblical Passage
John 5:2-9: "Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades. In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed. One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, 'Do you want to be healed?' The sick man answered him, 'Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.' Jesus said to him, 'Get up, take up your bed, and walk.' And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked."
The healing took place at the pool called Bethesda in Jerusalem.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Capernaum: This is incorrect. Although Jesus performed many miracles in Capernaum, this particular healing did not occur there.
Samaria: This is incorrect. The healing did not take place in Samaria.
Galilee: This is incorrect. The healing did not take place in Galilee.
Bethesda: The correct name is Bethesda, not "Betsheba," but this option was closest if correctly spelled. However, since it was spelled incorrectly and Jerusalem would have been a better alternative, Bethesda is indeed the correct location.
Answer: Betsheba.
The correct answer, based on location, should have been Bethesda (correctly spelled) in Jerusalem. However, given the options, none of them exactly match the correct name or the location.

questions.text: "It is finished" The statement above by Jesus on the cross implies that
options: His association with the Jews is finished
His association with His Disciples is finished
His work of redemption is Finished
the work of the enemy is finished
questions.explanation:
Answer: His work of redemption is Finished.
The statement "It is finished," spoken by Jesus on the cross, is found in John 19:30. This phrase signifies the completion of Jesus' mission on earth, particularly His work of redemption. By saying "It is finished," Jesus was declaring that He had fulfilled all that was required for the salvation of humanity. This included living a sinless life, fulfilling the prophecies, and offering Himself as the ultimate sacrifice for sin.
Context of the Statement
Jesus uttered the phrase "It is finished" just before He died on the cross. This was the culmination of His earthly ministry and the purpose for which He came into the world: to redeem humanity from sin.
Meaning of "It is finished"
The phrase in Greek is "Tetelestai," which means "paid in full" or "completed." It signifies that the debt of sin has been fully paid, and the work required for redemption has been accomplished.
Analyze the Options
His association with the Jews is finished: While Jesus' earthly ministry to the Jewish people was coming to an end, this was not the primary focus of His statement.
His association with His Disciples is finished: Jesus’ relationship with His disciples was not the focus here; rather, it was about completing His mission.
His work of redemption is finished: This is the correct answer. Jesus was declaring that His work to provide salvation for humanity was complete.
The work of the enemy is finished: While Jesus’ victory over sin and death is implied, the specific statement is about completing His redemptive work.
Conclusion
Jesus’ statement "It is finished" on the cross signifies that His work of redemption is finished.

questions.text: Jesus directed those He healed of leprosy to offer gifts of cleansing because
options: without such offerings, the leprosy might come back
He did not want confrontation with the Pharisees
such offerings would serve as proof to the people
questions.explanation:
Answer: Such offerings would serve as proof to the people.
In the Gospels, when Jesus healed people of leprosy, He directed them to go and show themselves to the priest and offer the gifts prescribed by Moses as a testimony to the people. This is recorded in Matthew 8:4, Mark 1:44, and Luke 5:14.
Context of the Command
Leprosy was a serious disease, and according to the Law of Moses (found in Leviticus 14), anyone cured of leprosy had to go through a specific process involving the priest to be officially declared clean. This included offering certain sacrifices.
Jesus' Instruction
After healing a leper, Jesus would often say something like, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them" (Matthew 8:4).
Purpose of the Offering
The offering served as a "proof" or testimony to the people, especially to the priests, that the person had indeed been cleansed. This also ensured that the healing complied with the requirements of the Mosaic Law and allowed the healed person to be reintegrated into the community.
Analyze the Options
They needed to show appreciation: While showing appreciation is important, this was not the specific reason Jesus directed the healed individuals to make the offering.
Without such offerings, the leprosy might come back: There is no biblical basis for this idea; the offering was not about preventing the leprosy from returning.
He did not want confrontation with the Pharisees: Avoiding confrontation may have been a consideration, but the primary reason given in Scripture is different.
Such offerings would serve as proof to the people: This is the correct answer. The offering was a testimony to the priests and the people that the person had been healed and was now clean.
Conclusion
Jesus directed those He healed of leprosy to offer gifts of cleansing because such offerings would serve as proof to the people.

questions.text: When they returned from their mission, the Seventy reported that
options: even demons were subject to them
they saw Satan fall like lightning
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context of the Mission
The Seventy (or Seventy-Two, depending on the translation) were sent out by Jesus to heal the sick and preach the kingdom of God. Their mission is described in Luke 10:1-24.
Step 2: Review the Report by the Seventy
In Luke 10:17, the Seventy return and report to Jesus: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!”
They also mention that they saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven in Luke 10:18, which reflects the impact of their mission and the authority given to them.
Step 3: Match the Report with the Given Options
Even demons were subject to them: Correct. This is explicitly mentioned in Luke 10:17.
Even Samaritans accepted their message: This is not mentioned in the report.
They saw Satan fall like lightning: This is mentioned by Jesus in response to their report (Luke 10:18), but it is not the Seventy's report.
Their needs were fully met: Not explicitly mentioned in the report.
Answer: Even demons were subject to them.
This matches the specific report made by the Seventy upon returning from their mission.

questions.text: Jesus' reply to the devil's first temptation of Him was
options: "...man shall not live by bread alone..."
"...You shall not tempt the Lord your God..."
"...You shall worship the Lord your God..."
questions.explanation:
Jesus' reply to the devil's first temptation during His time in the wilderness is recorded in the Gospels, particularly in the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke.
Contextual Understanding
The first temptation occurs when Jesus has been fasting for forty days and nights, and the devil tempts Him to turn stones into bread to satisfy His hunger.
Scriptural Reference
Matthew 4:3-4 (NIV): "The tempter came to him and said, 'If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.' Jesus answered, 'It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’'"
Understanding Jesus' Response
In response to the devil's temptation to turn stones into bread, Jesus quotes Scripture, specifically Deuteronomy 8:3, stating that "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God."
Identify the Correct Option
The correct answer is "....man shall not live by bread alone..."
Answer: "...man shall not live by bread alone...".
Jesus' reply to the devil's first temptation of Him was "....man shall not live by bread alone...".

questions.text: Prophet Hosea named his second child Not Pitied because God would no more pity the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The prophet Hosea was instructed by God to give symbolic names to his children as a representation of God's message to Israel. In Hosea 1, Hosea's second child, a daughter, was named "Lo-Ruhamah," which means "Not Pitied" or "No Mercy."
Step 2: Identifying the Reason for the Name
In Hosea 1:6, it is written:
> "And she conceived again and bore a daughter. And the LORD said to him, 'Call her name No Mercy (Lo-Ruhamah), for I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel, to forgive them at all.'"
This passage clearly indicates that the name "Not Pitied" was given because God would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
Kings of Judah: This is not correct. The text specifically refers to the house of Israel, not the kings of Judah.
Kings of Israel: The focus is on the entire house of Israel, not just the kings.
House of Judah: This is not correct. The text specifically refers to the house of Israel, not Judah.
House of Israel: This option is correct. The name "Not Pitied" was given because God would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel.
Answer: House of Israel.
Prophet Hosea named his second child "Not Pitied" because God would no more pity the house of Israel.

questions.text: "Can any one forbid water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" The statement above was made by Peter at the conversion of
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The statement "Can anyone forbid water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" was made by Peter in the Book of Acts. This event occurred when Peter was preaching to a group of Gentiles, and the Holy Spirit came upon them just as it had on the Jewish believers at Pentecost.
Step 2: Identifying the Event
This event is recorded in Acts 10, where Peter visits the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion. Cornelius and his household received the Holy Spirit while Peter was speaking to them, and Peter recognized that they should be baptized, just as the Jewish believers were.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
Herod: Herod was a ruler who is mentioned in the Gospels and Acts, but he was not the one who converted or received the Holy Spirit in this context.
Lydia: Lydia is mentioned in Acts 16 as a woman who was converted by Paul’s preaching, not Peter’s, and she is not associated with this specific event.
Saul: Saul, who later became Paul, was converted on the road to Damascus, and his story is found in Acts 9. Peter was not involved in Saul’s conversion.
Cornelius: This option is correct. Cornelius was the Roman centurion whose conversion is described in Acts 10. Peter’s statement about baptizing those who had received the Holy Spirit was made in reference to Cornelius and his household.
Answer: Cornelius.
Peter made the statement "Can anyone forbid water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" at the conversion of Cornelius and his household.

questions.text: "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan... who oppress the poor, who crush the needy..." cows of Bashan in the statement above refer to the____________
questions.explanation:
The phrase "cows of Bashan" in the statement "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan... who oppress the poor, who crush the needy..." is found in the book of Amos 4:1. In this context, the "cows of Bashan" is a metaphorical expression used by the prophet Amos to refer to the women of Samaria.
Step 1: Understand the Context
Bashan was a region known for its fertile land and well-fed cattle. By referring to the women of Samaria as "cows of Bashan," Amos is critiquing their indulgent lifestyles and their role in oppressing the poor and needy through their luxurious living, which contributed to social injustice.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Wicked kings: While Amos does speak against the rulers of Israel, the "cows of Bashan" specifically refers to women.
False prophets: The phrase does not refer to false prophets.
Women of Samaria: This is the correct answer. Amos is addressing the women of Samaria who were living in luxury and contributing to the oppression of the poor.
Judges in Israel: The "cows of Bashan" does not refer to judges.
Answer: Women of Samaria.
The "cows of Bashan" in the statement refers to the women of Samaria who were oppressing the poor and crushing the needy.

questions.text: "I called to the Lord, out of my distress, and he answered me, out of the belly of shoel I cried and thou didst hear my voice..." Jonah's statement above implies that God_________
options: hears and answers prayers in times of distress
is happy when His servants are humble
expects total loyalty from His servants
expects conviction of sin from His servants
questions.explanation:
To answer this question,
Step 1: Understand the Context
The statement comes from the book of Jonah in the Old Testament, specifically Jonah 2:2. This is part of Jonah's prayer to God from inside the belly of the great fish. Jonah had been swallowed by the fish after trying to flee from God’s command to go to Nineveh. In his distress, Jonah prayed to God, acknowledging that even from "the belly of Sheol" (a metaphor for a place of death or deep despair), God heard and answered his prayer.
Step 2: Analyze the Key Message
The focus of Jonah's prayer is on God's responsiveness to prayer, even in the most desperate and hopeless situations. Jonah acknowledges that God heard him when he called out in his distress, demonstrating that God is attentive and responsive to the prayers of those who are in need, no matter how dire the circumstances.
Step 3: Analyze the Options
Hears and answers prayers in times of distress: This option directly aligns with the content of Jonah's prayer. Jonah's statement is a testimony to the fact that God listens and responds to those who call out to Him in distress.
Is happy when His servants are humble: While humility is important, this specific statement from Jonah does not emphasize God's happiness with humility but rather His responsiveness to prayer.
Expects total loyalty from His servants: Although God does expect loyalty, this is not the focus of Jonah's statement in this context.
Expects conviction of sin from His servants: Conviction of sin is significant in Jonah’s overall story, but the specific statement focuses on God's response to prayer, not on conviction of sin.
Answer: Hears and answers prayers in times of distress.
Jonah's statement implies that God hears and answers prayers in times of distress.

questions.text: Saul lent from Samuel's spirit that the LORD would
options: give the Philistines into his hands
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
This question refers to an event in the First Book of Samuel. After Saul disobeyed God's commands, God rejected Saul as king. Saul then sought guidance, and at one point, he visited the medium at Endor to summon the spirit of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 28:3-19). Saul wanted to know what would happen to him and his kingdom.
Step 2: Identifying the Message from Samuel's Spirit
When Samuel's spirit appeared, he delivered a grim message to Saul. In 1 Samuel 28:16-19, Samuel tells Saul that the LORD has become his enemy and that the kingdom will be torn from him and given to David. Additionally, Samuel foretells that the Israelites will be defeated by the Philistines, and Saul and his sons will die in battle the next day.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
Give the Philistines into his hands: This is incorrect. Samuel's spirit did not tell Saul that the Philistines would be defeated by him; in fact, the opposite was true—the Israelites would be defeated.
Afflict him with sickness: This is not mentioned in the message from Samuel's spirit.
Become his enemy: This option is correct. Samuel's spirit told Saul that the LORD had become his enemy because of Saul's disobedience.
Pardon his iniquity
This option is incorrect. There is no indication that Samuel's spirit told Saul that the LORD would pardon his iniquity. In fact, the message was quite the opposite, emphasizing the consequences of Saul's disobedience.
Answer: Become his enemy.
Saul learned from Samuel's spirit that the LORD would become his enemy due to his disobedience and that his kingdom would be taken from him and given to David.

questions.text: Paul declares that Christians have the same functions but they have gifts that differ according to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
This teaching is found in Romans 12:4-6, where Paul discusses the diversity of spiritual gifts within the Christian community.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Romans 12:6 states, "We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us."
Step 3: Match the Explanation with the Given Options
Their devotion to prayer: Incorrect. The passage does not attribute the differences in gifts to prayer.
Enablement by the Spirit: While the Spirit gives gifts, the specific wording in Romans 12 is "grace."
Their suffering and endurance: Incorrect. The passage does not relate gifts to suffering and endurance.
Grace given to them: Correct. The gifts differ according to the grace given to each individual, as stated in Romans 12:6.
Answer: Grace given to them.
Paul emphasizes that the differing gifts among Christians are due to the grace given by God.

questions.text: Prophet Ezekiel described the house of Israel as having a hard forehead and a stubborn heart because the people
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is found in Ezekiel 3:7.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: Ezekiel 3:4-7.
Situation: God is sending Ezekiel to the people of Israel, but He warns Ezekiel that the people are rebellious and will be resistant to his message.
Step 3: Examine the Specific Description
Ezekiel 3:7: "But the house of Israel will not listen to you, because they are not willing to listen to me; for all the house of Israel are impudent and hard-hearted."
The phrase "hard forehead and stubborn heart" refers to the people's unwillingness to listen to God and their persistent rebellion against His commands. They are described as being obstinate and resistant to God's message delivered through Ezekiel.
Step 4: Compare and Eliminate Incorrect Options
Lacked confidence in him: While the people may not have trusted Ezekiel, the description specifically focuses on their refusal to listen to him, which is a broader issue than just lacking confidence.
Refused to listen to him: This directly aligns with the passage in Ezekiel 3:7, which states that the people were unwilling to listen to Ezekiel because they were not willing to listen to God.
Had taken God for granted: While this may be true in a broader sense, the specific issue mentioned in the text is their refusal to listen.
Had endured suffering: This does not match the description given in the text; their hard-heartedness was not due to suffering but to their rebellious nature.
Answer: Refused to listen to him.

questions.text: What was Herod's reaction when he heard the news about Jesus birth?
questions.explanation:

Herod was troubled because he perceived the birth of Jesus as a threat to his rule.

questions.text: Speaking in tongues by the disciples at Pentecost was the fulfillment of a prophecy by
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to identify the prophet who foretold the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which was manifested by the disciples speaking in tongues at Pentecost.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The relevant event is recorded in Acts 2:1-4. When the Holy Spirit descended on the disciples at Pentecost, they began to speak in other tongues.
Acts 2:16-17 (NIV) records Peter's explanation of the event: "No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: 'In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams.'"
Step 2: Understand the Fulfillment of Prophecy
Peter directly connects the event of speaking in tongues at Pentecost with the prophecy given by the prophet Joel. Joel had prophesied about the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in the last days, which Peter says is being fulfilled at Pentecost.
Step 3: Match the Prophecy with the Answer Choices
Joel: - This is correct, as Peter specifically cites the prophecy of Joel as being fulfilled at Pentecost.
Micah: - This is incorrect; Micah did not prophesy about the event at Pentecost.
Amos: - This is incorrect; Amos did not prophesy about the event at Pentecost.
Hosea: - This is incorrect; Hosea did not prophesy about the event at Pentecost.
Answer: Joel.

questions.text: God instructed Moses on Mount Sinai to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passages
The relevant passages that detail God’s instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai are primarily found in Exodus 19 and Exodus 20.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: Exodus 19:10-14, Exodus 20.
Situation: The Israelites had arrived at Mount Sinai, and God called Moses up the mountain to give him the Ten Commandments and other laws. Before this, God gave specific instructions to Moses concerning the preparation of the people to receive His presence.
Step 3: Examine the Specific Instructions
Consecrate the People: In Exodus 19:10-11, God instructed Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. Have them wash their clothes and be ready by the third day, because on that day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people."
This passage shows that God’s instruction to Moses on Mount Sinai included consecrating the people in preparation for God's presence.
Step 4: Compare and Eliminate Incorrect Options
Speak to the rock: This instruction was given later, in Numbers 20:8, when the Israelites were in the wilderness, not at Mount Sinai.
Strike the rock: This instruction was given earlier, in Exodus 17:6, when the Israelites needed water, but it also was not at Mount Sinai.
Consecrate the people: This is the correct answer, as it directly aligns with God's instruction to Moses in Exodus 19:10-11 on Mount Sinai.
Pray for the people: While Moses often interceded for the people, the specific instruction at Mount Sinai was to consecrate the people.
Answer: Consecrate the people.

questions.text: The effect of Stephen's death on the Early Church was that
options: it weakened the faith of the apostles
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context of Stephen's death
Stephen was one of the first deacons of the Early Church and became the first Christian martyr when he was stoned to death, as recorded in Acts 7. His death was a significant event for the Early Church, leading to a series of consequences.
Step 2: Analyze each option
Christianity was spread to non-Jews: Explanation: After Stephen's death, a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, causing many believers to scatter to different regions, including Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1). This scattering led to the spread of Christianity beyond the Jewish community to non-Jews (Gentiles). For instance, Philip went to Samaria and preached the gospel there.
Relevance: This directly aligns with the effect of Stephen's death, as it catalyzed the spread of Christianity to a wider audience.
It united the church: Explanation: While the church did remain united in faith, the immediate effect of Stephen's death was not primarily about uniting the church but about the scattering of believers due to persecution.
Relevance: This option does not capture the main consequence of Stephen's death.
It weakened the faith of the apostles: Explanation: There is no biblical evidence that Stephen's death weakened the faith of the apostles. On the contrary, the apostles continued to preach with boldness despite the persecution.
Relevance: This option is not supported by the biblical account.
The believers were arrested: Explanation: While persecution and arrests did occur, the more significant effect of Stephen's death was the dispersion of believers, leading to the spread of the gospel.
Relevance: This is not the primary effect of Stephen's death, though persecution did increase.
Step 3: Identify the best answer
The best answer is that Christianity was spread to non-Jews as a result of Stephen's death. His martyrdom led to the scattering of believers, which in turn led to the spread of the gospel beyond the Jewish community.
Answer: Christianity was spread to non-jews.
This is the correct answer, as it accurately reflects the significant impact of Stephen's death on the Early Church.

questions.text: The way in which various people hear the word of God is described in the parable of the ______

The correct answer can be determined by analyzing the parables mentioned and their content.
Step 1: Understand the context
The question asks about a parable that describes how different people hear and respond to the word of God. This is a reference to one of Jesus' parables that categorizes the different ways people receive God's message.
Step 2: Identify the specific parable
The relevant parable is the Parable of the Sower, which is found in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke. In this parable, Jesus describes a sower who scatters seeds on different types of ground, each representing a different response to hearing the word of God.
Step 3: Recall or research the exact wording
In the Parable of the Sower, the seed represents the word of God, and the different types of soil represent different kinds of hearers: some are receptive, some are distracted, and some are resistant.
Step 4: Match with the given options
Wheat and tares
Sower: Love of God
Weeds

The Parable of the Sower is the one that describes the various ways people hear and respond to the word of God.

questions.text: Paul returned Philemon's slave back to him to ensure that
options: he would be welcome when he left prison
the slave can complete his service time
Philemon forgave and accepted the slave
he could boast of Philemon's obedience.
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer,
Step 1: Understand the context
The letter to Philemon is a personal letter from Paul regarding Onesimus, a slave who had run away from Philemon and later encountered Paul. During his time with Paul, Onesimus became a Christian. Paul then sends Onesimus back to Philemon with the letter, asking Philemon to receive Onesimus not just as a slave, but as a brother in Christ.
Step 2: Identify the specific passage
The key verse is found in Philemon 1:15-16, where Paul appeals to Philemon to welcome Onesimus back.
Step 3: Recall or research the exact wording
Philemon 1:15-16 (NIV version) states:
> "Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a little while was that you might have him back forever—no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother. He is very dear to me but even dearer to you, both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord."
Paul also expresses his confidence in Philemon's obedience to this appeal in verse 21:
> "Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask."
Step 4: Analyze the key concept
Paul's primary reason for sending Onesimus back was to ensure that Philemon would forgive and accept him, not merely as a slave but as a brother in Christ. Paul wanted to mend the relationship and ensure that there was reconciliation.
Step 5: Match with the given options
He would be welcome when he left prison
The slave can complete his service time
Philemon forgave and accepted the slave: He could boast of Philemon's obedience
Step 6: Select the correct answer
The correct answer is that Paul returned Onesimus to Philemon to ensure that Philemon forgave and accepted the slave as a brother in Christ.
Answer: Philemon forgave and accepted the slave.
Paul returned Philemon's slave, Onesimus, to ensure that Philemon would forgive and accept him as a brother in Christ, highlighting the importance of reconciliation and Christian love.

questions.text: David's victory over the Amalekites who raided Ziklag was due to
options: the great army that followed him to fight the Amalekites
his swearing to the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites not to kill or harm him
his prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them
the fact that David was a might man in battle
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context
The context is found in 1 Samuel 30, where David’s victory over the Amalekites is described.
Step 2: Review the Factors Leading to the Victory
The great army that followed him to fight the Amalekites: David did have a strong group of men, but the victory was not solely attributed to the size of his army.
His swearing to the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites not to kill or harm him: David did make a promise to the Egyptian servant to spare his life, but this was not the primary reason for the victory.
His prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them: Correct. David sought God's guidance through prayer before pursuing the Amalekites, and God instructed him to pursue and assured him of success (1 Samuel 30:8).
The fact that David was a mighty man in battle: David was indeed a skilled warrior, but the victory was ultimately due to his seeking God’s approval and guidance.
Answer: His prayer in seeking the approval of God before pursuing them.
David's victory was attributed to his seeking God's guidance and following His direction.

questions.text: Peter in his epistle, charged his fellow elders to
questions.explanation:
Understand the Context
In 1 Peter 5:1-3, Peter gives instructions to the elders in the Church, emphasizing their responsibilities and the manner in which they should lead.
Analyze Each Option
Option 1: Take care of their families:
While taking care of one’s family is important, Peter’s instructions to the elders focus more on their role in the church rather than their family responsibilities.
Option 2: Be strong in their faith:
This is a general exhortation for all believers, but Peter’s specific charge to the elders in this passage is about their pastoral responsibilities.
Option 3: Have compassion on the weak:
Compassion is important, but Peter’s specific instructions to elders in this context focus on their leadership role rather than general compassion.
Option 4: Tend the flock of God:
This option is correct. Peter charges the elders to "tend the flock of God," which means to shepherd and care for the church (1 Peter 5:2). This encompasses guiding, leading, and caring for the spiritual needs of the congregation.
Select the Correct Answer
Peter in his epistle charged his fellow elders to tend the flock of God, which reflects their pastoral and leadership responsibilities. Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4: tend the flock of God.
Answer: Tend the flock of God.
Peter in his epistle charged his fellow elders to tend the flock of God, emphasizing their responsibility to shepherd and care for the church. The final answer is Option 4: tend the flock of God.

questions.text: To whom did God reveal himself to as the almighty God?
questions.explanation:
Answer: Abram.
God revealed Himself as "the Almighty God" (El Shaddai) to Abram in Genesis 17:1. This was before God changed Abram's name to Abraham.
Genesis 17:1 (KJV) states:

This passage marks the moment when God made a covenant with Abram and gave him the promise of many descendants. Shortly after this, in Genesis 17:5, God changes Abram's name to Abraham.
The children of Israel (While God did reveal Himself to the Israelites in various ways, He specifically revealed Himself as the Almighty God to Abram).
Abram: (This is the correct answer, as God revealed Himself as the Almighty God to Abram before his name was changed to Abraham).

questions.text: " Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." Jesus made the statement above to one of the criminals because he
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
This statement was made by Jesus during His crucifixion, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke, specifically in Luke 23:39-43. Two criminals were crucified alongside Jesus, and one of them had a significant interaction with Him.
Step 2: Analyzing the Options
Respected Him: While respect might have been part of the criminal's attitude, this alone is not the reason Jesus promised him a place in paradise.
Praised Him: The criminal did not explicitly praise Jesus in the recorded dialogue, so this option is not accurate.
Rebuked his partner: The criminal did indeed rebuke the other criminal who was mocking Jesus, saying that they were being justly punished while Jesus had done nothing wrong. However, while this rebuke shows a change in heart, it is not the sole reason for Jesus' promise.
Was repentant: This option best aligns with the text. The criminal acknowledged his own guilt and recognized Jesus' innocence. He expressed faith in Jesus by asking Him to remember him when He came into His kingdom (Luke 23:42). This act of repentance and faith led Jesus to assure him that he would be with Him in paradise.
Answer: Was repentant.
Jesus made the statement to the criminal because he demonstrated repentance and faith in Jesus, acknowledging his own sins and recognizing Jesus' righteousness.

questions.text: Laxity in disciplining children is dangerous both the family and society as exemplified by
questions.explanation:
Answer: Absalom.
The story of Absalom, the son of King David, is a clear example of how laxity in disciplining children can lead to severe consequences for both the family and society. Absalom's actions led to significant turmoil within David's family and caused a rebellion against David's rule, which affected the entire nation of Israel.
Context of Absalom’s Story: Absalom was one of King David's sons. After his sister Tamar was violated by their half-brother Amnon, Absalom took matters into his own hands by killing Amnon. David failed to take strong disciplinary action against Absalom for this murder.
Later, Absalom rebelled against his father, King David, attempting to take the throne by force. This rebellion led to a civil war in Israel, resulting in much bloodshed and Absalom’s eventual death.
Analyze the Options
Jonathan: Jonathan, the son of King Saul, was a loyal friend to David and is not an example of poor discipline leading to negative outcomes.
Tamar: Tamar was a victim of wrongdoing, not an example of lax discipline.
Absalom: This is the correct answer. Absalom's story exemplifies how a lack of proper discipline can lead to disastrous consequences for both the family and society.
Ahikam: Ahikam is a lesser-known figure in the Bible and is not associated with issues of discipline or the consequences of laxity in parenting.
Conclusion
Absalom's story is a powerful example of how laxity in disciplining children can lead to severe consequences for both the family and society.

questions.text: The effect of Stephen's death on the early church was that
options: the gospel was spread to non-jews
it weakened the faith of the apostles
questions.explanation:
Answer: The gospel was spread to non-jews.
The death of Stephen, the first Christian martyr, had a significant impact on the early church. After Stephen was stoned to death, a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem. This persecution caused many believers to scatter to different regions, and as they went, they preached the gospel in new areas, including to non-Jews (Gentiles).
Context of Stephen's Death
Stephen was one of the seven deacons chosen by the early church to help with the distribution of food and other needs (Acts 6:1-6).
He was a powerful preacher and performed great wonders and signs among the people. However, his bold preaching led to his arrest and eventual stoning by the Jewish authorities (Acts 7:54-60).
Effect on the Church
After Stephen’s death, Acts 8:1-4 describes how a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem. As a result, many believers fled the city and went to different regions, including Judea and Samaria.
As these believers were scattered, they began to preach the gospel wherever they went. This led to the spread of Christianity beyond the Jewish community, reaching non-Jews (Gentiles) as well.
Analyze the Options
The believers were arrested: While there was persecution and arrest of believers, the main effect highlighted in Acts is the spread of the gospel.
The gospel was spread to non-Jews: This is the correct answer. The scattering of believers led to the spread of the gospel to new regions and to non-Jews.
It united the church: While the church remained united in mission, the immediate result of Stephen's death was not about uniting the church but about the spread of the gospel.
It weakened the faith of the apostles: This is incorrect. The apostles and believers continued to be strong in their faith, and the gospel continued to spread.
Conclusion
The effect of Stephen's death on the early church was that the gospel was spread to non-Jews.

questions.text: Daniel became distinguished above all other Presidents and satraps because
options: an excellent spirit was in him
the spirit of Darius was in him
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
This question refers to the biblical character Daniel, who served in the court of King Darius in the Book of Daniel in the Old Testament. Daniel was one of the Jewish exiles taken to Babylon, and he rose to a high position in the Babylonian and Medo-Persian empires due to his wisdom and ability to interpret dreams and visions.
Step 2: Analyzing the Options
An excellent spirit was in him: This option suggests that Daniel was distinguished because of an "excellent spirit" within him. This phrase is directly linked to the biblical text in Daniel 6:3, which states that Daniel had an excellent spirit, making him stand out among the other officials. This implies that his character, wisdom, and possibly his connection with God were what set him apart.
The spirit of Darius was in him: This option suggests that Daniel had the spirit of King Darius within him. However, there is no biblical reference or support for this idea. The Bible does not mention anything about Daniel possessing the spirit of Darius. Therefore, this option is incorrect.
He was a good administrator: While Daniel was indeed a capable administrator, and his administrative skills contributed to his success, the Bible emphasizes that it was the "excellent spirit" within him that truly distinguished him. This option alone does not fully capture the reason for Daniel's distinction.
He was highly educated: This option suggests that Daniel's distinction came from his education. While Daniel was indeed educated and skilled in knowledge and learning, the Bible does not attribute his distinction solely to his education. The emphasis is more on his character and spirit.
Answer: An excellent spirit was in him.
This answer is consistent with Daniel 6:3, where it explicitly states that Daniel was preferred above the presidents and satraps because an excellent spirit was in him. This "excellent spirit" likely refers to his exceptional character, wisdom, and the divine favor he had, which led to his high standing in the kingdom.

questions.text: God called Jonah and sent him to the people of Nineveh to
options: pray to Him for their forgiveness
questions.explanation:

The context is found in the book of Jonah, where God gives Jonah a specific mission.
Step 2: Review the Passage
Jonah 1:2 states, “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.”
Step 3: Match the Mission with the Given Options
Pray to Him for their forgiveness: Incorrect. God did not send Jonah to pray for forgiveness but to deliver a message.
Pray for their repentance: Incorrect. Jonah’s mission was not to pray but to deliver a message of judgment.
Preach His word to them: Partially correct, but more specifically, Jonah was sent to cry out against the city.
Cry against their wickedness: Correct. Jonah was sent to call out against the wickedness of Nineveh.
Answer: Cry against their wickedness.
Jonah was sent to deliver a message of judgment to Nineveh due to its wickedness.

questions.text: Asa removed the abominable image his mother made for Asherah and burnt it at
questions.explanation:
To answer this question,
Step 1: Understand the Context
The story of King Asa removing the abominable image is found in 1 Kings 15:13 and 2 Chronicles 15:16. Asa was a king of Judah who did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, and he took strong actions to rid the land of idolatry, including removing the image his mother (or grandmother) had made for the worship of Asherah.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Passage
1 Kings 15:13 says:
"He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron."

The brook Kidron: This is the correct answer. According to 1 Kings 15:13, Asa burned the abominable image at the brook Kidron.
Ramah: This was a city in the territory of Benjamin, but it is not the location mentioned in this context.
Tirzah: Tirzah was a city that served as the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel at one point, but it is not related to Asa’s actions.
Answer: The brook kidron.
Asa removed the abominable image his mother made for Asherah and burned it at the brook Kidron.

questions.text: The disciple who replaced Judas Iscariot was
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
After Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus and subsequently died, the remaining eleven apostles decided to select a replacement to restore their number to twelve. This event is recorded in the Book of Acts, specifically in Acts 1:15-26.
Step 2: Identifying the Disciple Who Replaced Judas
In Acts 1:23-26, two men were proposed as candidates: Joseph called Barsabbas (who was also known as Justus) and Matthias. The apostles prayed and cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was then added to the eleven apostles.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
Justus: Justus, also known as Joseph called Barsabbas, was one of the candidates considered to replace Judas, but he was not chosen.
Stephen: Stephen was one of the first deacons and the first Christian martyr (Acts 6-7), but he was not involved in the selection process to replace Judas.
Mathias: This option is correct. Matthias was the disciple chosen by the casting of lots to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the twelve apostles.
Luke: Luke was the author of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles, but he was not one of the twelve apostles and was not involved in the replacement of Judas.
Answer: Mathias.
Matthias was the disciple who replaced Judas Iscariot as one of the twelve apostles.

questions.text: According to Thessalonians, the second coming of the Lord will be
options: like a theif in the night
with the blowing of a trumpet
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, let's focus on what Paul writes in his letters to the Thessalonians about the second coming of the Lord.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Passage
In 1 Thessalonians 5:2, Paul describes the nature of the second coming of the Lord:
"For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night."
Step 2: Analyze the Options
Based on the passage:
When the elements are dissolved: This phrase is not from Thessalonians but is found in 2 Peter 3:10, where it describes the day of the Lord. However, it's not the phrase used in Thessalonians.
Like a thief in the night: This is the correct answer. Paul explicitly uses this simile to describe the sudden and unexpected nature of the Lord's return in 1 Thessalonians 5:2.
With the blowing of a trumpet: While the blowing of a trumpet is mentioned in connection with the second coming (e.g., 1 Corinthians 15:52 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16), the specific phrase related to the timing and suddenness of the event in Thessalonians is "like a thief in the night."
After scoffers have come: This refers to another biblical passage (2 Peter 3:3) and is not directly connected to the description of the second coming in Thessalonians.
Answer: Like a theif in the night.
According to 1 Thessalonians, the second coming of the Lord will be like a thief in the night.

questions.text: "What have you to do with us O son of God"? Have you come here to torment us before the time? This statement reveals that the demoniacs in the country of Gadarenes_________
options: were threatened by the power of Jesus
did not expect Jesus to come to them at that time
recognized the supreme power of Jesus
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, This event is recorded in the New Testament in the book of Matthew 8:28-34, Mark 5:1-20, and Luke 8:26-39.
Step 1: Understand the Context
The statement, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” was made by the demons possessing two men in the region of the Gadarenes. When Jesus approached them, the demons immediately recognized who He was and acknowledged His authority. They were aware of His power to cast them out and were frightened by the possibility of their destruction or torment, which they expected to happen "before the time" (likely referring to the final judgment).
Step 2: Analyze the Implications of the Statement
The statement indicates that:
The demons recognized Jesus as the "Son of God," which shows an acknowledgment of His divine identity and power.
They feared that Jesus could torment them, which indicates that they were threatened by His presence and power.
The mention of "before the time" suggests that the demons were aware of an appointed time for their ultimate judgment and were surprised by Jesus’s early arrival.
Step 3: Analyze the Options
Wanted to question Jesus's authority: The demons did not question His authority; instead, they acknowledged it.
Were threatened by the power of Jesus: This is true. The demons were clearly afraid that Jesus had come to torment them, showing that they felt threatened by His power.
Did not expect Jesus to come to them at that time: While they mentioned "before the time," the focus was more on the fear of Jesus’s power than surprise at His arrival.
Recognized the supreme power of Jesus: This is also true. The demons recognized and acknowledged Jesus as the "Son of God," which directly indicates they understood His supreme authority and power.
Answer: Recognized the supreme power of Jesus.
The statement made by the demoniacs reveals that they recognized the supreme power of Jesus and felt threatened by it.
