questions.text: Daniel and others opted for vegetables and water in place of the King's food and wine because
options: the King's food would defile them
the King's food was not palatable
God was not happy with Israel's situation
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the context
The story of Daniel and his companions choosing vegetables and water instead of the king’s food is found in the book of Daniel, chapter 1. Daniel and his three friends (Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah) were among the young men taken from Judah to serve in the Babylonian king's palace. They were offered food and wine from the king’s table, but they chose not to partake in it.
Step 2: Identify the specific passage
The relevant passage is found in Daniel 1:8.
Step 3: Recall or research the exact wording
Daniel 1:8 (NIV version) states:
> "But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the royal food and wine, and he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself this way."
Step 4: Analyze the key concept
Daniel and his companions refused the king's food because they believed it would defile them. This could be due to several reasons, including that the food may have been offered to idols or did not comply with Jewish dietary laws. Daniel wanted to remain faithful to God's commandments, even in a foreign land.
Step 5: Match with the given options
They were fasting for Israel
The King's food would defile them: The King's food was not palatable
God was not happy with Israel's situation
Step 6: Select the correct answer
The correct reason for Daniel and his companions choosing vegetables and water is that the king's food would defile them.
Answer: The King's food would defile them.
Daniel and others opted for vegetables and water instead of the king's food and wine because they believed the king's food would defile them, and they wanted to remain faithful to their religious convictions.

questions.text: In Luke, at the last Supper, Jesus revealed His
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The Last Supper is an important event in the Gospels, where Jesus shares a final meal with His disciples before His crucifixion. During this meal, Jesus makes several important revelations and prepares His disciples for what is to come.
Step 2: Identifying the Specific Revelation
In the Gospel of Luke, particularly in Luke 22:14-23, Jesus shares the Last Supper with His disciples. During this meal, He specifically speaks about His imminent suffering and death.
In Luke 22:15-16, Jesus says:
> "And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'"
Later, He speaks about His body being given and His blood being poured out for them (Luke 22:19-20), which directly refers to His upcoming suffering and crucifixion.
Step 3: Analyzing the Options
Resurrection: While Jesus does speak about His resurrection at various points, the specific focus at the Last Supper in Luke is on His imminent suffering.
Imminent sufferings: This option is correct. Jesus clearly speaks about His impending suffering and death during the Last Supper.
Love for His disciples: While Jesus' love for His disciples is evident throughout His ministry, and He shows it during the Last Supper, the specific revelation He makes during this meal is about His upcoming suffering.
Ascension: The ascension is discussed later in the Gospels and Acts, but it is not the focus of the Last Supper in Luke.
Answer: Imminent sufferings.
At the Last Supper in Luke, Jesus revealed His imminent sufferings, preparing His disciples for the events that were about to unfold, including His crucifixion.

questions.text: In paul's letter to the Thessalonians, believers were admonishing to prepare for the second coming of Christ by
questions.explanation:

"
In Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, he addresses the need for believers to be prepared for the second coming of Christ.

Encouraging idlers to work hard: While Paul does encourage work in other parts of his letters, this is not the specific advice given for preparing for the second coming.
Preaching peace and tolerance: Although important, this is not the specific admonition given in relation to preparing for Christ's return.
Keeping awake and being sober: This directly aligns with the instruction in 1 Thessalonians 5:6.
Praying and fasting: While these practices are important in Christian life, they are not specifically mentioned in this context for preparing for the second coming.
In Paul's letter to the Thessalonians, believers were admonished to prepare for the second coming of Christ by keeping awake and being sober, as stated in 1 Thessalonians 5:6.

questions.text: Jesus encouraged His followers to rejoice when they were persecuted because
options: great would be their reward in heaven
angels would come to their aid
they would not lack anything good
all their sins would be forgiven
questions.explanation:
Understand the Context
Jesus' encouragement to rejoice during persecution is discussed in the New Testament, specifically in Matthew 5:10-12, part of the Sermon on the Mount. It emphasizes the spiritual reward for enduring hardships for righteousness.
Analyze Each Option
Option 1: Great would be their reward in heaven:
This option aligns with Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:12, where He says, "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven." This implies that enduring persecution for righteousness is rewarded with a significant blessing in the afterlife.
Option 2: Angels would come to their aid:
While angels assisting believers is mentioned in other parts of the Bible, it is not the specific reason given by Jesus for rejoicing during persecution in this context.
Option 3: They would not lack anything good:
Although God provides for believers, this is not the direct reason given by Jesus for rejoicing in the context of persecution.
Option 4: All their sins would be forgiven:
Forgiveness of sins is a core message of Christianity, but it is not specifically linked to rejoicing in the face of persecution in this context.
Select the Correct Answer
The correct reason Jesus gives for rejoicing during persecution is that there is a great reward in heaven for those who endure such trials. Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1: great would be their reward in heaven.
Answer: Great would be their reward in heaven.
Jesus encouraged His followers to rejoice in persecution because it signifies a future, substantial reward in heaven for those who remain steadfast.

questions.text: "...The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge..." The parable above in the land of Israel means that
options: parents are punished for the sins of their children
children are punished for the sins of their parents
parents are punished for the sins of their grandparents
great grandchildren are punished for the sins of their forefathers
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Biblical Context
This proverb is found in Ezekiel 18:2. It reflects a common belief in ancient Israel that the consequences of sin were inherited by subsequent generations.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Parents are punished for the sins of their children: This is incorrect. The proverb suggests the reverse, where the consequences of one generation's actions affect the next.
Children are punished for the sins of their parents: This is the correct interpretation. The proverb reflects the belief that children suffer the consequences of their parents' sins.
Parents are punished for the sins of their grandparents: This does not fit the context of the proverb, which focuses on the direct consequences between parents and children.
Great grandchildren are punished for the sins of their forefathers: While this concept appears in other contexts, the proverb specifically addresses the immediate impact on children.
Step 3: Select the Most Accurate Answer
The parable means that children are punished for the sins of their parents.
Answer: Children are punished for the sins of their parents.
This reflects the belief that the consequences of sins are passed from one generation to the next, as described in the proverb.

questions.text: Now the sons of Eli were sons of _______ they knew not the Lord.
questions.explanation:

This phrase is found in 1 Samuel 2:12. The verse describes the sons of Eli, the high priest, who were corrupt and did not follow God's ways.
1 Samuel 2:12 (KJV) states:

Lucifer (Not the term used in this context)

Nature (This doesn't fit the context)

questions.text: Which of these is not time about Stephen
options: he was stoned for telling lie
he was full of the holy ghost
he prayed for the people that stoned him
questions.explanation:
Answer: He was stoned for telling lie.
He was stoned for telling a lie
Stephen is a significant figure in the New Testament, particularly in the book of Acts. He was one of the seven deacons chosen to serve the early Christian community (Acts 6:5). He is known for being the first Christian martyr, being full of the Holy Spirit, and praying for those who were stoning him.
How was the first martyr: This is true. Stephen is recognized as the first Christian martyr, as recorded in Acts 7.
He was stoned for telling a lie: This is false. Stephen was stoned for boldly proclaiming the truth about Jesus Christ, not for telling a lie. His speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7) was a powerful defense of his faith, which led to his martyrdom.
He was full of the Holy Ghost: This is true. Acts 6:5 specifically mentions that Stephen was "full of faith and of the Holy Ghost."
He prayed for the people that stoned him: This is true. In Acts 7:60, Stephen prayed, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them," as he was being stoned.
He was stoned for telling a lie
This statement is not true about Stephen. Stephen was stoned for boldly proclaiming the truth about Jesus, not for telling a lie.

questions.text: My father Chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpion. Who said this?

questions.text: A promise made by king Saul to anyone that could face and defeat Goliath was______________

giving his daughter in marriage to the person
giving the person part of his land
making the person captain of his army

questions.text: What did the demons in the region of the Gadarenes do when they saw Jesus?
options: They Pleaded for Jesus to send them to the herds of pigs
They Requested to follow him as a disciple
They Acknowledged him as the son of the Most High God D
They Pleaded that a miracle be performed to cleanse him
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
Context: The encounter is described in Mark 5:1-13 and Luke 8:26-33. Jesus meets a man possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes.
Step 2: Review the Relevant Passage
Mark 5:6-12 describes how the demons recognized Jesus and acknowledged His divine authority. They begged Jesus not to send them out of the region but instead to send them into a herd of pigs.
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
They Pleaded for Jesus to send them to the herds of pigs: This is correct. The demons requested to be sent into the pigs rather than being sent away from the region.
They Requested to follow him as a disciple: This is incorrect. The demons did not ask to follow Jesus as disciples.
They Acknowledged him as the son of the Most High God: While the demons did acknowledge Jesus' divine nature, their primary action was to beg Him to send them into the pigs.
They Pleaded that a miracle be performed to cleanse them: This is incorrect. The demons did not ask for a miracle to cleanse them but for permission to enter the pigs.
Answer: They Pleaded for Jesus to send them to the herds of pigs.
When the demons in the region of the Gadarenes saw Jesus, they pleaded for Jesus to send them to the herds of pigs.

questions.text: According to St James, 'He who keeps the whole law and fails in one is guilty of...'
options: Breaking the new commandment of Christ
Breaking that particular love and should pray for grace
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer, James regarding the law.
Step 1: Understanding the Context
The statement in question is derived from James 2:10, where St. James writes, "For whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it." This verse highlights the comprehensive and interconnected nature of the law. St. James emphasizes that the law is a unified whole, and breaking even one commandment is equivalent to breaking the entire law.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Step 3: Option 1: "Breaking the new commandment of Christ"
Analysis: This option is not directly correct. The "new commandment" generally refers to Christ's command to love one another (John 13:34). However, St. James is discussing the law in its entirety rather than just this specific commandment.
Step 4: Option 2: "Breaking that particular law and should pray for grace"
Analysis: While it is true that one should seek grace when failing, this option does not capture the full implication of St. James' teaching. He emphasizes that failing in one part of the law makes one guilty of breaking the entire law, not just the particular law that was broken.
Step 5: Option 3: "Breaking the whole law"
Analysis: This is the correct interpretation. St. James teaches that the law is indivisible, meaning that breaking one part is equivalent to breaking the whole law. This reflects the severity and totality of the law’s demands.
Step 6: Option 4: "Breaking the ten commandments"
Analysis: While the Ten Commandments are part of the law, St. James is referring to the entire Mosaic Law, not just the Ten Commandments. The emphasis is on the entire body of law, not specifically the Ten Commandments.
Answer: Breaking the whole law.
St. James teaches that anyone who fails in even one part of the law is guilty of breaking the entire law, highlighting the comprehensive and unified nature of the law.

Step 2: Analyze the Meaning of "Faults"
The "faults" the chief butler is referring to are his forgetting Joseph after being released from prison, despite Joseph's accurate interpretation of his dream. questions.text: The workmen who repaired the house of the LORD during Josiah"s religious reforms were not made to account for the money given them because they
options: did not receive the money directly
questions.explanation:
Answer: Were honest workmen.
During the reign of King Josiah, a significant religious reform took place, which included the repair of the Temple. The workmen who were responsible for repairing the house of the Lord were not required to account for the money given to them because they were considered honest and trustworthy. This is mentioned in 2 Kings 22:7.
Context of the Reforms
King Josiah initiated a series of religious reforms, including the repair of the Temple in Jerusalem. The priests collected money from the people to fund the repairs.
Key Verse
2 Kings 22:7 states, "But they did not require an accounting from those to whom they gave the money to pay the workers, because they acted with complete honesty."
Reason for Not Requiring an Accounting
The reason given in the scripture for not requiring an accounting from the workmen was their honesty. They were trusted to use the money appropriately without the need for oversight.
Analyze the Options
Did not receive the money directly: This is incorrect; the workmen did receive the money for the repairs.
Lacked accounting capabilities: There is no indication that the workmen lacked the ability to account for the money. The issue was their honesty, not their capability.
Bribed the Temple officials: This is incorrect and not mentioned in the text. The scripture emphasizes their honesty, not corruption.
Were honest workmen: This is the correct answer. The Bible explicitly states that the workmen were not required to account for the money because they were honest.
Conclusion
The workmen who repaired the house of the Lord during Josiah's religious reforms were not made to account for the money given them because they were honest workmen.

nsure that proper baptism must be in a river

Jesus' baptism does serve as an example for believers, but the explicit reason given by Jesus in the text was to fulfill all righteousness.
Fulfill all righteousness
This option directly aligns with Jesus' explanation in Matthew 3:15. Jesus stated that His baptism was necessary "to fulfill all righteousness," indicating that it was part of God's plan and an act of obedience.

Jesus' baptism by John in the River Jordan was to fulfill all righteousness, signifying His obedience to God's will and His identification with humanity.

The correct reason Joseph was made prime minister is interpreted Pharaoh's dream and counseled him on what to do.

questions.text: "It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it" what was to be divided?
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to this question, we need to identify the context and origin of the phrase, "It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it."
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Phrase
The phrase "It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it" is found in the Bible in the story of King Solomon’s wisdom. This story is a famous example of Solomon’s judgment and is recounted in 1 Kings 3:16-28.
Step 2: Understanding the Story
In this story, two women come to King Solomon, both claiming to be the mother of a living baby. One of the babies had died, and each woman claimed the living child as her own. To resolve the dispute, Solomon proposed to cut the living baby in half and give each woman half of the child. The true mother immediately begged the king to give the baby to the other woman, revealing her maternal love, while the false mother agreed to have the baby divided.
The phrase “It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it” was spoken in the context of this story, highlighting the false mother's willingness to see the baby killed rather than let the true mother have him.
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
Step 4: Option 1: "Elijah's mantle"
Elijah’s mantle is not related to this story. The mantle was a symbol of Elijah’s prophetic authority, passed to Elisha, but there is no mention of it being divided.
Step 5: Option 2: "Jesus' garment"
Jesus’ garment was divided among the soldiers who crucified him (John 19:23-24), but this event is not related to the phrase in question.
Step 6: Option 3: "Live Baby"
This is the correct answer. The live baby in the story of Solomon was the subject of the proposed division, which led to the revelation of the true mother.
Step 7: Option 4: "Solomon's Kingdom"
Solomon’s kingdom is not related to this phrase. The kingdom was not divided during Solomon's reign, but after his death under his son Rehoboam.
Answer: Live Baby.
The phrase "It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it" refers to King Solomon’s judgment in the case of the two women claiming to be the mother of a living baby. Solomon's proposal to divide the baby revealed the true mother, demonstrating his wisdom.

questions.text: What effect did the decision of the Council of Jerusalem have on the early Church?
options: The Church experienced freedom from persecution
The Jews became leaders of the community
Gentiles were free to be members of the Church
questions.explanation:
Understand the Context
The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15, was a significant meeting of early Church leaders to address whether Gentile converts needed to follow Jewish laws, particularly circumcision, to be part of the Church.
Analyze Each Option
Option 1: Members became more united:
While the decision contributed to unity, it was not the primary focus of the council's decision. The council addressed a specific doctrinal issue, and unity was a byproduct rather than the direct effect.
Option 2: The Church experienced freedom from persecution:
The council’s decision did not directly lead to freedom from persecution. Persecution continued despite the decision, which mainly focused on doctrinal issues related to Gentile membership.
Option 3: The Jews became leaders of the community:
The council did not change the leadership structure in favor of Jews specifically. The decision was more about doctrinal issues related to Gentile converts rather than altering leadership dynamics.
Option 4: Gentiles were free to be members of the Church:
This option is correct. The council decided that Gentile converts did not need to follow Jewish laws, such as circumcision, to be accepted into the Church. This decision made it clear that Gentiles could become members without adhering to Jewish customs, significantly impacting the early Church's expansion.
Select the Correct Answer
The Council of Jerusalem’s decision allowed Gentiles to join the Church without following Jewish laws, which was a major development for the early Church. Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4: Gentiles were free to be members of the Church.
Answer: Gentiles were free to be members of the Church.
The decision of the Council of Jerusalem had the effect of allowing Gentiles to become members of the Church without needing to follow Jewish laws, facilitating the Church’s expansion and inclusivity. The final answer is Option 4: Gentiles were free to be members of the Church.

In this passage, Paul and Barnabas encounter a man named Elymas (also known as Bar-Jesus), who was a magician and false prophet. Elymas opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, away from the faith. In response, Paul rebuked Elymas with the words, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy."
Step 2: Analyzing the Options
Elymas, the magician
This option is correct. Elymas was the magician who opposed Paul and Barnabas and was subsequently rebuked by Paul with the statement in question.
Paulus, the proconsul: This option is incorrect. Paulus, or Sergius Paulus, was the proconsul who was interested in hearing the word of God, and Paul did not rebuke him.
Simon, the magician
Simon the Magician (also known as Simon Magus) is another figure mentioned in Acts (Acts 8), but he is not the one Paul rebuked with this statement. Simon was rebuked by Peter for trying to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.
Demetrius, the silversmith
Demetrius is a different figure mentioned in Acts 19:24-27. He was a silversmith in Ephesus who opposed Paul because his trade of making silver shrines of Artemis was threatened by the spread of Christianity. This option does not fit the context of the statement.
Answer: Elymas, the magican.
Elymas, the magician
Paul's rebuke was directed at Elymas, the magician, who was trying to oppose the spread of the Gospel.

questions.text: In his exhortation to elders, Peter describes himself as
options: the first disciple to be called by Jesus
a witness of the sufferings of Christ
one of the closest disciples of Jesus
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to look at how Peter describes himself in his exhortation to the elders, which is found in one of his epistles.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The relevant passage is found in 1 Peter 5:1.
1 Peter 5:1 (NIV) says: "To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed."
Step 2: Understand How Peter Describes Himself
In this verse, Peter describes himself as a witness of the sufferings of Christ. He does not emphasize his position as the first disciple to be called, or his close relationship with Jesus, or any leadership role among the apostles. Instead, he focuses on his personal witness of Christ's sufferings and his shared responsibility with other elders.
Step 3: Match Peter's Description with the Answer Choices
The first disciple to be called by Jesus: - This is incorrect; Peter does not describe himself this way in this passage.
A witness of the sufferings of Christ: - This is correct, as Peter explicitly identifies himself as a witness of Christ's sufferings.
One of the closest disciples of Jesus: - While Peter was indeed one of the closest disciples, this is not how he describes himself in this context.
The leader of the apostles: - Although Peter was a prominent leader among the apostles, he does not use this title in his exhortation.
Answer: A witness of the sufferings of Christ.

questions.text: According to Paul's letter to the Philippians, Christ demonstrated His humility by
options: taking the form of a servant
washing the feet of His disciples
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is found in Philippians 2:5-8. This section is often referred to as the "Christ Hymn" and focuses on Christ's humility and obedience.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Location in the Bible: Philippians 2:5-8.
Situation: Paul is encouraging the Philippians to adopt the same mindset as Christ, who, despite His divine nature, humbled Himself for the sake of humanity.
Step 3: Examine How Christ Demonstrated His Humility
Philippians 2:6-7: "Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness."
Philippians 2:8: "And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death—even death on a cross!"
In these verses, Paul highlights that Christ demonstrated His humility in two key ways:
Taking the form of a servant: Christ, though God, took on human nature and lived as a servant.
Becoming obedient to death on a cross: Christ's ultimate act of humility was His willingness to die a shameful death on the cross.
Step 4: Compare the Answer Choices
Taking the form of a servant: This directly aligns with Philippians 2:7, where Paul explains that Christ demonstrated His humility by taking the form of a servant.
Praying for His enemies: While this is an act of humility and love that Christ did, it is not the specific focus of Paul's teaching on humility in Philippians.
Dying on the cross: This is another key aspect of Christ's humility mentioned in Philippians 2:8, but the primary demonstration of humility that Paul emphasizes is taking the form of a servant.
Washing the feet of His disciples: This act is recorded in John 13 and is a significant demonstration of humility, but it is not mentioned in Philippians.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Based on the analysis, the most direct answer that aligns with Paul's teaching in Philippians is:
Taking the form of a servant.
Step 6: Confirm with the Text
The text in Philippians 2:7 clearly states that Christ demonstrated His humility by taking the form of a servant.
Answer: Taking the form of a servant.

questions.text: The religious tension in Israel during the reign of King Ahab was caused by
options: Prophet Nathan's prophecy about Israel's doom
Ahab's heed to the advice of the elders
Elijah's insistence on God to punish Israel
questions.explanation:
The religious tension in Israel during the reign of King Ahab was primarily caused by Jezebel's introduction of idol worship.
Jezebel, Ahab's wife, was a Phoenician princess who introduced and promoted the worship of Baal in Israel. This led to a significant conflict between the worship of Yahweh (the God of Israel) and the worship of Baal, causing widespread religious tension.
Jezebel’s influence led Ahab to build a temple for Baal in Samaria and to support the prophets of Baal and Asherah, which directly opposed the worship of Yahweh.
The tension culminated in the famous confrontation between the prophet Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, where Yahweh demonstrated His power by sending fire from heaven to consume the sacrifice, proving that He alone is God (1 Kings 18).
Answer: Jezebel's introduction of idol worship.
Jezebel's introduction of idol worship was the main cause of the religious tension in Israel during the reign of King Ahab.

questions.text: Ezra was able to gain favour before the king of Persia because
options: he was a scribe and the King's friend
he was skilled in the law of Moses
the hand of the Lord was upon him
Aaron was his great grand father
questions.explanation:
Answer: The hand of the Lord was upon him.
Ezra, a skilled scribe and teacher of the Law of Moses, was able to gain favor before the king of Persia primarily because "the hand of the Lord his God was upon him." This phrase is repeated several times in the Book of Ezra to emphasize that it was God's favor and blessing that enabled Ezra to succeed in his endeavors.
Specifically, in Ezra 7:6, it states:
"This Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the Lord, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the Lord his God was upon him."
Option 1 - He was a scribe and the King's friend: While Ezra was indeed a scribe, there is no indication that he was a personal friend of the king. His favor was due to God's intervention, not personal connections.
Option 2 - He was skilled in the law of Moses: Although Ezra was skilled in the Law of Moses, the Bible attributes his success to God's favor rather than his own skills alone.
Option 3 - The hand of the Lord was upon him: This is the correct answer. The repeated emphasis in the Book of Ezra is that God’s favor ("the hand of the Lord") was the key reason for Ezra’s success before the king.
Option 4 - Aaron was his great grandfather: While Ezra was a descendant of Aaron, this is not the reason given for his favor with the king.

The king punished all the violent people in the land: This is not mentioned in the text as the reason for God's pity.
They turned from their evil way

They made sacrifices of sin offering to God: The text does not mention that they made sacrifices; instead, it emphasizes their repentance and turning from evil.

questions.text: The Angel of the Lord told Zachariah that a son would be born to him and that the son would

make the disobedient repent of their sins

turn many of the sons and daughters of Israel to God

And he will go on before the Lord, in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the parents to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
Step 3: Match the Prophecy with the Given Options
Go before God in the spirit and power of Elijah: Correct. This is part of the prophecy regarding John the Baptist.
Make the disobedient repent of their sins: This is a part of the prophecy but not the specific statement given in the question.

Turn many of the sons and daughters of Israel to God: This is included in the prophecy but is not the specific answer required.
Answer: Go before God in the spirit and power of Elijah.

questions.text: What did King Josiah do the idolatrous priests of Judah?

Step 1: Understand the Context

2 Kings 23:5 (NIV): “He did away with the idolatrous priests appointed by the kings of Judah to burn incense on the high places of the towns of Judah and on those around Jerusalem—those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the constellations and to all the starry hosts.”
Step 3: Analyze Each Option
He killed all of them: Although Josiah took severe measures, he did not kill all the idolatrous priests. The text does not specify mass executions.
He sent all of them on exile: There is no mention of Josiah sending the priests into exile.
He deposed all of them: This is correct. Josiah deposed the idolatrous priests, removing them from their positions of authority.
He demoted all of them: Demotion is not mentioned; instead, Josiah removed them from their positions.
Answer: He deposed all of them.

questions.text: When Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem, He
options: contended with the Scribes and the Pharisees
read from the book of Isaiah
beat everyone that sold and bought
drove out all who sold and bought
questions.explanation:
The correct answer to this question can be found in the accounts of Jesus' actions in the temple as recorded in the Gospels.
Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passages
The relevant passages are found in Matthew 21:12-13, Mark 11:15-17, Luke 19:45-46, and John 2:13-16.
Step 2: Understand the Context
Situation: When Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem, He was angered by the commercial activities taking place in the temple courts, which were supposed to be a place of prayer.
Step 3: Examine Jesus' Actions in the Temple
Matthew 21:12-13: "And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, 'It is written, My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers.'"
Mark 11:15-17, Luke 19:45-46, and John 2:13-16 provide similar accounts where Jesus drives out those who were selling and buying in the temple.
In all these accounts, Jesus' primary action was driving out those who were engaged in buying and selling within the temple, as well as overturning the tables of the money changers.
Step 4: Compare and Eliminate Incorrect Options
Contended with the Scribes and the Pharisees: While Jesus often debated with the Scribes and Pharisees, this is not what He did when He first entered the temple.
Read from the book of Isaiah: Jesus did read from the book of Isaiah in a synagogue (Luke 4:16-21), but this is not what He did when He entered the temple in Jerusalem.
Beat everyone that sold and bought: Although Jesus did drive out those who were selling and buying, the accounts emphasize that He drove them out and overturned the tables, not that He beat them.
Drove out all who sold and bought: Correct. This aligns with the accounts in the Gospels, which state that Jesus drove out those who were selling and buying in the temple.
Answer: Drove out all who sold and bought.

questions.text: "...But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing..." From your assessment of Jesus teaching about giving, what do you think is a violation of the statement__________
options: One give only what one has
One does not give from freewill
One gives only what is requested
questions.explanation:
To determine which option is a violation of Jesus' teaching about giving, let's first analyze the context of the statement and the principles that Jesus emphasizes.
Step 1: Understand the context
The statement "do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing" comes from Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, specifically in Matthew 6:3-4. In this teaching, Jesus is instructing His followers on how to give alms (charitable giving) in a way that is humble and not done for public recognition.
Step 2: Identify the key teaching
The key principle Jesus emphasizes is that giving should be done quietly, without seeking attention, praise, or recognition from others. The focus is on sincerity and humility, rather than on showing off or being self-righteous.
Step 3: Analyze the options
One gives only what one has: This is not a violation because giving within one's means is appropriate and realistic.
One does not give from freewill: This could be problematic, but it does not directly address the issue of seeking recognition, which is the focus of the statement.
One is judgmental in giving: Being judgmental can be contrary to the spirit of giving, but it is not directly related to the public display or secrecy emphasized in the teaching.
One gives only what is requested: This option does not involve seeking attention, so it does not violate the principle.
Step 4: Select the correct answer
The teaching is violated when a person gives in a way that seeks public recognition or when they are judgmental in their giving. However, the most direct violation of Jesus' teaching about giving secretly is related to seeking recognition, which being judgmental can imply, as it involves giving with a self-righteous attitude rather than quietly and sincerely.
Answer: One does not give from freewill.
One is judgmental in giving
Being judgmental in giving reflects a self-righteous attitude, which contradicts Jesus' teaching about giving with humility and without seeking recognition.

questions.text: The presiding judge at the Jerusalem Council was
questions.explanation:
Answer: James.
The Jerusalem Council, which is described in Acts 15, was convened to address the issue of whether Gentile converts to Christianity needed to follow the Mosaic Law, specifically the practice of circumcision. During this council, various leaders, including Peter and Paul, spoke about their experiences with Gentile converts. However, it was James, the brother of Jesus and a prominent leader in the Jerusalem church, who presided over the council and gave the final judgment.
Context of the Jerusalem Council
The council was called because of a disagreement within the early church about whether Gentile converts should be required to follow Jewish customs, such as circumcision.
Key Figures at the Council
Peter spoke at the council, recounting how God had shown him that Gentiles could receive the Holy Spirit without following the Jewish law (Acts 15:7-11).
Paul and Barnabas also shared their experiences of how God was working among the Gentiles (Acts 15:12).
James gave the concluding judgment after listening to the testimonies and discussion. He referenced Scripture to support the decision that Gentile converts should not be burdened with following the Mosaic Law, except for a few necessary things (Acts 15:13-21).
Analyze the Options
Peter: While Peter played a significant role in the discussion, he was not the presiding judge.
James: This is the correct answer. James, who was a leading figure in the Jerusalem church, presided over the council and gave the final decision.
Barnabas: Barnabas was present and supported Paul, but he did not preside over the council.
Paul: Paul was a key participant but not the presiding judge.
Conclusion
The presiding judge at the Jerusalem Council was James.

questions.text: When David's son died, his servants refused to tell him because they feared that he might

questions.text: When Paul and his companions were shipwrecked, the soldiers planned to kill the prisoner but the centurion prevented them because
options: they would have to account for them
it was not lawful to kill
questions.explanation:
To determine why the centurion prevented the soldiers from killing the prisoners when Paul and his companions were shipwrecked,
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Event
The event is recorded in Acts 27. Paul, along with other prisoners, was being transported by ship to Rome under the custody of Roman soldiers. During the journey, the ship encountered a severe storm, which ultimately led to a shipwreck.
Step 2: Understand the Soldiers' Plan
Acts 27:42: "The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping."
The soldiers were concerned that if any of the prisoners escaped during the chaos of the shipwreck, they would be held responsible. Under Roman law, soldiers could be executed if prisoners under their watch escaped, which is why they considered killing the prisoners.
Step 3: Analyze the Centurion’s Motivation
Acts 27:43: "But the centurion, wanting to save Paul’s life, kept them from carrying out their plan."
The centurion, Julius, who had previously shown kindness to Paul (Acts 27:3), valued Paul’s life. He was aware of Paul’s significance and influence and wanted to ensure his safety. Thus, he intervened to prevent the soldiers from executing their plan.
Step 4: Evaluate the Options
They were Roman citizens: This is incorrect. The passage does not indicate that all the prisoners were Roman citizens, nor does it suggest that their citizenship status was the reason for the centurion’s intervention.
They would have to account for them: While this is a valid concern for the soldiers, the text specifically highlights that the centurion’s primary motivation was to save Paul, not merely to account for the prisoners.
He wanted to save Paul’s life: This is the correct answer. The centurion’s primary motivation for preventing the soldiers from killing the prisoners was his desire to protect Paul.
It was not lawful to kill: This is incorrect. The soldiers' plan was not based on concerns about legality but rather on their fear of punishment if any prisoners escaped.
Answer: It was not lawful to kill.
The correct answer is he wanted to save Paul’s life. The centurion intervened and prevented the soldiers from killing the prisoners because he was determined to protect Paul.

questions.text: The exiles returned to Jerusalem in the reign of________
questions.explanation:
To answer this question,
Step 1: Understand the Context
The return of the Jewish exiles to Jerusalem occurred after the Babylonian captivity. The captivity began under King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and took many Jews into exile. However, the return from exile was initiated by a later king.
Step 2: Identify the Key Figure
The key figure who allowed the exiles to return to Jerusalem was King Cyrus of Persia. After conquering Babylon, Cyrus issued a decree that allowed the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. This is recorded in Ezra 1:1-4, where it is stated that in the first year of King Cyrus, he made a proclamation allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem.
Step 3: Analyze the Options
Nebuchadnezzar: Nebuchadnezzar was the Babylonian king who initially took the Jews into exile, not the one who allowed them to return.
Cyrus: This is the correct answer. King Cyrus of Persia issued the decree that allowed the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple.
Zerubbabel: Zerubbabel was the leader of the first group of returning exiles and oversaw the rebuilding of the temple, but he was not the king who allowed the return.
Huldah: Huldah was a prophetess in the time of King Josiah, long before the exile. She is not related to the return from exile.
Answer: Cyrus.
The exiles returned to Jerusalem during the reign of Cyrus.

questions.text: "To you I will give all this authority and their glory; for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will..." This statement was made during the
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Context of the Statement
The statement, "To you I will give all this authority and their glory; for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will," reflects a temptation involving authority and glory.
Step 2: Review the Events
Ascension of Jesus: During the ascension (Acts 1:9-11), Jesus returns to heaven, but this statement is not part of that event.
Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem: This event (Matthew 21:1-11, Mark 11:1-11, Luke 19:28-44, John 12:12-19) involves Jesus entering Jerusalem, but it does not include this statement.
Sermon on the Mount: This teaching (Matthew 5-7) includes various teachings of Jesus but does not include this statement about authority.
Temptation of Jesus: During the temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11, Luke 4:1-13), Satan offers Jesus authority and glory over all the kingdoms of the world, which is the context for this statement.
Step 3: Match the Statement with the Given Options
Ascension of Jesus: Incorrect.
Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem: Incorrect.
Sermon on the Mount: Incorrect.
Temptation of Jesus: Correct. This statement is part of the temptation where Satan offers Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if He will worship him.
Answer: Temptation of Jesus.
This statement reflects the offer made by Satan to Jesus during His temptation in the wilderness.

questions.text: Jesus charged His followers to walk in the light while they had the light so that they may

Understand the Context
Jesus' instruction to walk in the light is found in John 12:35-36. He emphasizes the importance of using the opportunity to follow Him while He is present, which is metaphorically referred to as walking in the light.
Analyze Each Option
Option 1: Have eternal life:
While walking in the light is associated with following Jesus, the specific focus in this context is on having the light of life rather than directly obtaining eternal life.
Option 2: Become Sons of it:
This option does not align with the context. Jesus does not specifically refer to becoming "Sons of the light" in this passage.
Option 3: Have the light of life:
This option is correct. Jesus refers to Himself as the light of the world (John 8:12) and instructs His followers to walk in the light to have the light of life, which represents living in His truth and guidance.
Option 4: Become custodians of it:
Although being custodians of the light might be a metaphorical interpretation, the specific purpose Jesus mentions is having the light of life rather than taking on the role of custodian.
Select the Correct Answer
Jesus instructed His followers to walk in the light to ensure they have the light of life, which represents living in His truth and guidance. Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3: have the light of life.
Answer: Have the light of life.
Jesus charged His followers to walk in the light while they had it so that they may have the light of life, which means living in His truth and guidance.

questions.text: God decided not to bring evil in Ahab's days but in the days of his son because Ahab

Step 1: Identify the Biblical Passage
The relevant passage is found in 1 Kings 21. This chapter describes the events surrounding Ahab's acquisition of Naboth's vineyard and God's subsequent judgment.

Location in the Bible: 1 Kings 21:27-29.
Situation: After Ahab and Jezebel conspired to have Naboth killed so that Ahab could take possession of Naboth's vineyard, God sent the prophet Elijah to pronounce judgment on Ahab and his house. However, Ahab's response to this judgment led to a delay in the full execution of God's wrath.

1 Kings 21:27: "When Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and fasted. He lay in sackcloth and went about meekly."
1 Kings 21:28-29: Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite: "Have you noticed how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself, I will not bring this disaster in his day, but I will bring it on his house in the days of his son."
This passage makes it clear that because Ahab humbled himself before God, the full punishment was delayed until the days of his son.
Step 4: Compare the Answer Choices
Fasted for forty days: Although Ahab fasted, the text does not specify that it was for forty days, and the emphasis is on his humility rather than the duration of the fast.
Returned Naboth's vineyard: There is no indication in the text that Ahab returned Naboth's vineyard.
Humbled himself before God: This directly matches what is stated in 1 Kings 21:29.
Asked God for mercy: While Ahab's actions can be seen as seeking mercy, the text specifically mentions his humility as the reason for the delayed judgment.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Humbled himself before God.
The text in 1 Kings 21:27-29 confirms that God's decision to delay the disaster was due to Ahab's act of humbling himself before the Lord.

questions.text: According to Matthew, the disciples of Jesus fell on their faces during the Transfiguration when
options: they heared a voice from the cloud
Jesus face shone like the sun
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The Transfiguration of Jesus is a significant event described in the Gospels, where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, and there He is transfigured before them. This event is recounted in Matthew 17:1-9.
"Jesus' garment became white": Explanation: During the Transfiguration, it is mentioned that Jesus' clothes became dazzling white, as noted in Matthew 17:2. However, this event alone did not cause the disciples to fall on their faces.
"They heard a voice from the cloud"
Explanation: This is the key moment. According to Matthew 17:5-6, while Jesus was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my Son, whom I love; with him, I am well pleased. Listen to him!" When the disciples heard this, they were terrified and fell facedown to the ground. This indicates that it was hearing the voice of God from the cloud that caused them to fall on their faces.
"Jesus' face shone like the sun": Explanation: Matthew 17:2 describes how Jesus' face shone like the sun during the Transfiguration. This was a remarkable and awe-inspiring event, but the disciples did not fall on their faces at this point.
"They saw Moses and Elijah": Explanation: Moses and Elijah did appear with Jesus during the Transfiguration, as noted in Matthew 17:3. However, the appearance of these figures did not cause the disciples to fall on their faces. Their reaction was prompted specifically by hearing the voice from the cloud.
Answer: They heared a voice from the cloud.
The disciples of Jesus fell on their faces during the Transfiguration when they heard a voice from the cloud. This voice was understood to be the voice of God, which filled the disciples with awe and fear, leading them to fall facedown.
"They heard a voice from the cloud"
This answer is consistent with the account in Matthew 17:5-6, where the disciples' reaction of falling facedown is directly linked to hearing the divine voice from the cloud.

questions.text: David did not allow Abishai to destroy Saul because he
options: wanted to disarm Saul before killing him
believed in the judgement of God
wanted to see if Saul would repent evetually
wanted to avoid being guity before the LORD
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is that David did not allow Abishai to destroy Saul because he wanted to avoid being guilty before the LORD.
Step 1: Understand the Context
This event occurs in 1 Samuel 26. Saul was pursuing David to kill him, but David had the opportunity to take Saul's life when Saul was sleeping in his camp. Abishai, one of David's men, offered to kill Saul, but David refused.
Step 2: Analyze David's Reasoning
1 Samuel 26:9-11 provides David's reasoning: "But David said to Abishai, 'Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the Lord's anointed and be guiltless?' And David said, 'As the Lord lives, the Lord will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish. The Lord forbid that I should put out my hand against the Lord's anointed.'"
Step 3: Compare with the Answer Choices
Wanted to disarm Saul before killing him: This is not the reason David gave.
Believed in the judgment of God: While David did believe that God would judge Saul, this was not his primary reason for sparing Saul's life in this particular moment.
Wanted to see if Saul would repent eventually: This isn't mentioned as the reason David refrained from killing Saul.
Wanted to avoid being guilty before the LORD: This matches David's concern about not being guilty of shedding the blood of the Lord's anointed.
Answer: Wanted to avoid being guity before the LORD.
Wanted to avoid being guilty before the LORD
David did not allow Abishai to destroy Saul because he wanted to avoid being guilty before the LORD, respecting Saul as the Lord's anointed.

questions.text: "... Let all the house of Israel therefore know assuredly that God had made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.." As a reaction to this declaration, the Jews
options: decided to kill Peter and the apostles
went back to their houses in anger
were deeply troubled and asked what they should do

This statement is part of Peter's sermon on the day of Pentecost, as recorded in Acts 2:36. Peter was addressing the crowd in Jerusalem after the Holy Spirit had descended on the apostles, enabling them to speak in different languages.
Step 2: Analyze the Reaction of the Jews
Acts 2:37: "Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, 'Brothers, what shall we do?'"
This passage shows that the Jews who heard Peter's message were deeply convicted ("cut to the heart") and asked what they should do in response to the message.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Decided to kill Peter and the apostles: This is incorrect. There is no indication in this passage that the crowd reacted with violence or a desire to kill Peter and the apostles.
Went back to their houses in anger: This is incorrect. The crowd did not leave in anger; instead, they were deeply moved by Peter's message.
Were deeply troubled and asked what they should do: This is correct. The crowd was deeply troubled by Peter's words and asked what they should do to respond.
Ridiculed Peter and the apostles: This is incorrect. There is no mention of ridicule in response to Peter’s sermon in this passage.
Answer: Were deeply troubled and asked what they should do.
After Peter's declaration, the Jews were convicted by his words and asked what steps they needed to take in response to the message.

questions.text: According to Jeremiah, the new covenant is based on
questions.explanation:
Answer: Righteousness.
The concept of the new covenant is discussed in Jeremiah 31:31-34. In this passage, God speaks through the prophet Jeremiah about a new covenant that will be different from the old covenant made with the ancestors of Israel.
Jeremiah 31:33-34 (KJV) states:
> "But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall teach no more every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them, saith the Lord: for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
This new covenant emphasizes a personal, internal relationship with God based on His laws being written on the hearts of the people, leading to righteousness.
Circumcision (Circumcision was a sign of the old covenant, not the new one).
Providence (This is not the specific basis of the new covenant).
Righteousness: (This aligns with the new covenant, as it is based on God's law being internalized and leading to a righteous relationship with Him).
Restoration (While restoration is a theme in Jeremiah, the new covenant specifically emphasizes righteousness).
According to Jeremiah, the new covenant is based on righteousness, with God's law written on the hearts of the people, leading to a personal and internal relationship with God.

questions.text: Pilate delivered Jesus to be crucified because he
options: was afraid of the chief priest
questions.explanation:
To determine why Pilate delivered Jesus to be crucified,
Step 1: Identify the Context
The events leading to the crucifixion of Jesus are recorded in all four Gospels. Pilate, the Roman governor, found himself under pressure from multiple sources regarding the fate of Jesus.
Step 2: Analyze the Relevant Biblical Passages
Mark 15:15: "So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them. And after having Jesus scourged, he delivered Him to be crucified."
Matthew 27:24: "When Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, ‘I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves.’"
In these passages, it is clear that Pilate did not believe Jesus was guilty of a crime deserving death, but he was under immense pressure from the crowd and the Jewish leaders. Ultimately, he decided to crucify Jesus to avoid a riot and to placate the crowd.
Step 3: Evaluate the Options
Wished to satisfy the crowd: This is correct. Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified primarily to appease the crowd and prevent unrest.
Feared Caesar: While Pilate was concerned about his position and how a riot might be reported to Caesar, the immediate reason for his decision was to satisfy the crowd.
Found Him guilty: This is incorrect. Pilate repeatedly stated that he found no fault in Jesus and did not believe He was guilty.
Was afraid of the chief priest: While the chief priests pressured Pilate, his primary concern was the reaction of the crowd.
Answer: Wished to satisfy the crowd.

questions.text: When prophet Isaiah saw the Lord of hosts in the Temple he______________
options: was ashamed of himself and his people
questions.explanation:
To answer this question, we need to examine the specific event being referred to, which is found in the book of Isaiah, chapter 6 in the Old Testament.
Step 1: Understand the Context
The question refers to the vision of Prophet Isaiah as described in Isaiah 6:1-8. In this vision, Isaiah sees the Lord sitting on a high and exalted throne, with the train of His robe filling the temple. Seraphim (heavenly beings) are in attendance, praising God's holiness, saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory."
Step 2: Analyze Isaiah’s Reaction
When Isaiah saw the vision of the Lord, his immediate reaction was a profound sense of unworthiness and sinfulness. Specifically, in Isaiah 6:5, he says:
"Woe is me! For I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts."
This statement shows that Isaiah was deeply aware of his own sinfulness and the sinfulness of his people. He was overwhelmed by the holiness of God and felt condemned.
Step 3: Analyze the Options
Condemned himself and his people: This aligns with the passage where Isaiah declares "Woe is me" and recognizes both his own sinfulness and that of his people.
Was ashamed of himself and his people: While Isaiah felt unworthy, the specific term used in the scripture is "Woe is me," which expresses a sense of doom or condemnation rather than shame alone.
Praised His glory: Although the seraphim were praising God's glory, Isaiah’s first reaction was not praise but a feeling of being overwhelmed by his unworthiness.
Prayed fervently: Isaiah’s initial response was not a prayer but an expression of his unworthiness.
Answer: Condemned himself and his people.
The correct interpretation of Isaiah's reaction is that he condemned himself and his people due to their uncleanliness in the presence of the holy God.

questions.text: The two sons of Samuel that became Judges in Israel were
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understand the Context
Biblical Background: Samuel was a prominent prophet and judge in Israel. He had two sons who were appointed as judges in Israel. This is mentioned in the Bible, specifically in 1 Samuel 8:1-3.
Step 2: Analyze Each Option
Joel and Abijah: According to 1 Samuel 8:2, Samuel's sons were Joel and Abijah. They were appointed as judges but did not follow Samuel’s example, leading to dissatisfaction among the Israelites.
Abimelech and Abijah: Abimelech was a different figure. He was one of Gideon’s sons who declared himself king for a time, but he was not a son of Samuel.
Hophni and Phinehas: These were the sons of Eli, not Samuel. They were priests, but their corruption was a major issue, as noted in 1 Samuel 2:12-17.

questions.text: When Paul and Barnabas healed a cripple at Lystra, the people named them
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer to the question about what names the people of Lystra gave to Paul and Barnabas after they healed a crippled man,
Step 1: Identify the Source of the Information
This event is recorded in the Book of Acts, Chapter 14. In this chapter, Paul and Barnabas perform a miracle by healing a man who had been crippled from birth.
Step 2: Understanding the Context
In Acts 14:11-12, it is written:
"When the crowd saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the Lycaonian language, 'The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!' Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker."
Step 3: Evaluating the Options
Zeus and Hermes: This is the correct answer. The people of Lystra identified Barnabas as Zeus (the chief of the Greek gods) and Paul as Hermes (the messenger god), because Paul was the main speaker.
Zeus and Apollo: This pair is incorrect. Apollo is another Greek god, often associated with the sun, music, and prophecy, but he is not mentioned in this passage.
Jupiter and Mercury: These are the Roman equivalents of Zeus (Jupiter) and Hermes (Mercury). While the Roman names are sometimes used in translations, the specific Greek names Zeus and Hermes are used in the original context of this passage.
Zeus and Mars: This pair is incorrect. Mars is the Roman god of war and does not correspond to the role of Hermes or Paul in this passage.
Answer: Zeus and Hermes.
The people of Lystra called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes after they healed the crippled man, believing that the gods had come down to them in human form.

questions.text: After the healing of the demaniac in the country of the Gerasenes, the people begged Jesus to
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Understanding the Context
This question refers to the event described in the Gospels, particularly in Mark 5:1-20 and Luke 8:26-39. In this account, Jesus heals a man possessed by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes (or Gadarenes). The demons are cast into a herd of pigs, which then rush down a steep bank and drown in the sea.
Step 2: Analyzing the Options
Stay with them: This option suggests that the people asked Jesus to stay in their region. However, this is not what is recorded in the Gospel accounts.
Visit them always: This option implies that the people wanted Jesus to visit them regularly, but this is not the response given by the people of the Gerasenes after the miracle.
Go away from them: This option is consistent with the biblical account. After the dramatic event of the demons entering the pigs and the subsequent loss of the herd, the people of the Gerasenes were frightened and asked Jesus to leave their region. In Luke 8:37, it states, "Then all the people of the region of the Gerasenes asked Jesus to leave them, because they were overcome with fear."
Heal their sick: While Jesus was known for healing the sick, the specific response of the Gerasenes after the healing of the demoniac was not a request for further healings.
Answer: Go away from them.
This aligns with the biblical narrative, where the people of the Gerasenes, overwhelmed by fear after witnessing the miracle, begged Jesus to leave their region.

questions.text: How did Joshua react to the defeat of the Israelites by the men of Ai?
questions.explanation:
Answer: He rent his clothes.
"
The event occurs in Joshua 7. After the Israelites were defeated by the men of Ai, Joshua, their leader, reacted with deep distress and sought God's guidance.
Joshua 7:6 states:
"Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the Lord until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads."
Tearing one's clothes was a traditional sign of mourning, distress, or repentance in ancient Israel.
He prayed to God: Joshua did pray to God, but his immediate reaction included tearing his clothes.
He rent his clothes: This is the correct answer, as it was his immediate physical reaction to the defeat.
He consulted the priest: There is no mention of him consulting the priest at this moment.
He fasted all day: The text does not specifically mention fasting as part of Joshua's reaction.
Joshua reacted to the defeat of the Israelites by the men of Ai by tearing his clothes, which was a traditional expression of grief and distress.

questions.text: The disciples became terrified when they saw Jesus walking on the sea because
options: they thought He was a ghost
questions.explanation:
Answer: They thought He was a ghost.
The disciples were terrified when they saw Jesus walking on the sea because they initially did not recognize Him and thought they were seeing a ghost. This event is recorded in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and John.
Context of the Event
The event where Jesus walks on water is described in Matthew 14:22-33, Mark 6:45-52, and John 6:16-21. The disciples were in a boat on the Sea of Galilee, and a strong wind was blowing against them. In the early hours of the morning, Jesus approached them, walking on the water.
Key Verse
In Matthew 14:26, it says: "But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, 'It is a ghost!' And they cried out in fear."
Analyze the Options
They thought He would drown: This option is incorrect because the disciples were not worried about Jesus drowning; they were terrified because they thought they were seeing a ghost.
They thought He was a ghost: This is the correct answer. The disciples were frightened because they thought Jesus was a ghost.
They lacked faith in Him: While their faith was tested, their immediate reaction of fear was due to thinking they saw a ghost, not specifically because of a lack of faith.
There was a great storm: Although there was strong wind, their fear at this moment was specifically because they thought Jesus was a ghost.
Conclusion
The disciples became terrified when they saw Jesus walking on the sea because they thought He was a ghost.

questions.text: Obadiah showed his great reverence for the LORD by
options: handing over five hundred Baal prophets for slaughter
falling on his face before Elijah
hiding Elijah in a cave for two years
feeding the prophets of the LORD with bread and water
questions.explanation:
To answer the question about how Obadiah showed his great reverence for the LORD,
Step 1: Understand the Context
Obadiah was a devout believer in the LORD who served in the court of King Ahab, a king of Israel who, along with his wife Jezebel, promoted the worship of Baal. During a time when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah took significant risks to protect them.
Step 2: Identify the Relevant Passage
The relevant passage is found in 1 Kings 18:3-4. This passage describes what Obadiah did during the time Jezebel was persecuting the prophets of the LORD.
Step 3: Analyze the Passage
1 Kings 18:3-4 states:
"Ahab had summoned Obadiah, his palace administrator. (Obadiah was a devout believer in the LORD.) While Jezebel was killing off the LORD's prophets, Obadiah had taken a hundred prophets and hidden them in two caves, fifty in each, and had supplied them with food and water."
This passage highlights Obadiah's reverence and devotion to God, demonstrated by his courageous act of hiding and providing for the prophets of the LORD.
Step 4: Match the Answer Choices
Handing over five hundred Baal prophets for slaughter: There is no biblical record of Obadiah doing this.
Falling on his face before Elijah: Although Obadiah showed respect to Elijah, this is not the act that demonstrates his great reverence for the LORD.
Hiding Elijah in a cave for two years: The Bible does not mention Obadiah hiding Elijah for two years.
Feeding the prophets of the LORD with bread and water: This directly matches what Obadiah did, as described in 1 Kings 18:4, where he hid the prophets of the LORD and provided them with food and water.
Step 5: Select the Correct Answer
Answer: Feeding the prophets of the LORD with bread and water.
Obadiah showed his great reverence for the LORD by feeding the prophets of the LORD with bread and water while hiding them from Jezebel’s persecution. Therefore, the correct answer to the question is "Feeding the prophets of the LORD with bread and water."

Their women were becoming barren: The text does not mention barrenness among the women.

The hand of God was heavy upon them: This directly matches the explanation in 1 Samuel 5, where the Philistines experienced severe plagues and afflictions, leading them to conclude that God's hand was heavy upon them.

The text in 1 Samuel 5:6-11 confirms that the Philistines wanted to get rid of the Ark because they were suffering under the heavy hand of God.

questions.text: How did David know that Saul had come against him in the wilderness of Ziph?
options: it was revealed to Prophet Nathan
it was revealed to him in a dream
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Context
The wilderness of Ziph is the location where David was hiding from King Saul, who was seeking to kill him. This story is recorded in 1 Samuel 23. During this time, Saul was actively pursuing David, and there were several incidents where David became aware of Saul's movements.
"It was revealed to Prophet Nathan": Explanation: Prophet Nathan was indeed a prophet during the reign of King David, but he is not mentioned in the narrative of David’s flight from Saul in the wilderness of Ziph. There is no biblical record that Nathan was involved in informing David about Saul’s actions at this particular time.
"A Ziphite informed him": Explanation: The people of Ziph were the ones who betrayed David's location to Saul. According to 1 Samuel 23:19, the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and informed him that David was hiding in their territory. However, the question is about how David knew Saul was coming against him, not how Saul knew David’s location. The Ziphites informed Saul, not David, so this is not the correct answer.
"His spies informed him": Explanation: This option aligns with what is recorded in the Bible. In 1 Samuel 23:24-25, we see that David had his own network of informants or spies. It was through this network that David learned about Saul’s plans and movements. His spies were actively gathering intelligence, which allowed David to evade Saul’s attempts to capture him.
"It was revealed to him in a dream": Explanation: There is no biblical record of David receiving information about Saul’s pursuit through a dream during this event. While dreams were sometimes used by God to communicate with people in the Bible, this was not the method by which David learned about Saul’s approach in this situation.
Answer: His spies informed him.
The correct answer is that David knew about Saul's approach because his spies informed him. This aligns with the biblical narrative in 1 Samuel 23, where David was consistently aware of Saul’s movements through the information provided by his network of spies.
This answer is supported by the specific details in the biblical account, making it the most accurate choice among the options provided.

questions.text: The man who first saw Absalom hanging did not kill him because he was
options: not armed enough to do so
met by the Commander-in-Chief of David's army
aware that David did not want Absalom killed
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct answer
Step 1: Review the Context
Absalom, the son of King David, had rebelled against his father and was eventually defeated in battle. As Absalom was fleeing on his mule, his hair got caught in the branches of a tree, leaving him hanging there. One of David's men saw Absalom in this vulnerable position but did not kill him.
Step 2: Analyze the Options Based on the Biblical Text
Not armed enough to do so: Explanation: The man did not cite being unarmed or lacking the weapons necessary to kill Absalom as his reason for not doing so.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Afraid of Absalom's army: Explanation: There is no indication in the text that the man refrained from killing Absalom because he feared Absalom’s army.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Met by the Commander-in-Chief of David's army: Explanation: The man did later encounter Joab, the Commander-in-Chief of David's army, but this was after he had already chosen not to kill Absalom. This encounter was not the reason he didn’t kill Absalom.
Alignment: Incorrect.
Aware that David did not want Absalom killed: Explanation: The correct answer is found in 2 Samuel 18:12. The man who saw Absalom hanging in the tree explicitly said to Joab, "Even if I had the weight of a thousand shekels of silver in my hand, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son. For in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake, protect the young man Absalom.'" The man was aware that King David had commanded his commanders to deal gently with Absalom, and he feared the repercussions of disobeying the king's orders.
Alignment: Correct.
Answer: Aware that David did not want Absalom killed.
The man refrained from killing Absalom because he knew King David had specifically commanded that Absalom's life be spared, despite Absalom's rebellion.

questions.text: What did Ahab do to Prophet Micaiah for speaking the truth about the war between Israel and Syria
questions.explanation:
To solve this question, we need to refer to the story of King Ahab and the prophet Micaiah as recorded in the Old Testament, specifically in the Book of 1 Kings.
Step 1: Identify the Relevant Scripture
The story is found in 1 Kings 22. In this chapter, King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah were deciding whether to go to war against Syria at Ramoth Gilead. The prophet Micaiah was summoned to give a prophecy about the outcome of the battle.
1 Kings 22:17 (NIV) says: "Then Micaiah answered, 'I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd, and the LORD said, ‘These people have no master. Let each one go home in peace.’"
After Micaiah prophesied the truth that Ahab would be defeated, Ahab reacted negatively.
1 Kings 22:26-27 (NIV) says: "The king of Israel then ordered, 'Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon the ruler of the city and to Joash the king’s son and say, ‘This is what the king says: Put this fellow in prison and give him nothing but bread and water until I return safely.’"
Step 2: Understand Ahab's Reaction
King Ahab was angered by Micaiah's prophecy because it predicted his defeat and death in the battle. As a result, Ahab ordered Micaiah to be imprisoned and given only bread and water until Ahab's return.
Step 3: Match Ahab's Action with the Answer Choices
He promoted him: - This is incorrect; Ahab did not promote Micaiah.
He gave him a gift: - This is incorrect; Ahab did not give Micaiah any gift.
He denied him any food: - This is partially correct, but specifically, he ordered that Micaiah be given only bread and water, not that he be completely denied food.
He imprisoned him: - This is correct, as Ahab ordered that Micaiah be imprisoned.
Answer: He imprisoned him.
"

questions.text: The signs that God showed to Moses at his call were meant to
options: convice Pharaoh that he was the prophet of God
portray him as superior to the Egyptian magicians
enable him to perform miracles before Pharaoh
convince the people that he has been sent by God
questions.explanation:
Answer: Convince the people that he has been sent by God.
"
When God called Moses at the burning bush and sent him to deliver the Israelites from Egypt, Moses expressed concern that the Israelites would not believe that God had sent him.
Exodus 4:1-5 states:
"Then Moses answered, 'But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, "The Lord did not appear to you."' The Lord said to him, 'What is that in your hand?' He said, 'A staff.' And he said, 'Throw it on the ground.' So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it. But the Lord said to Moses, 'Put out your hand and catch it by the tail'—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand—'that they may believe that the Lord, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.'"
God provided Moses with signs, such as turning his staff into a serpent, to convince the Israelites that he was indeed sent by God.
Convince Pharaoh that he was the prophet of God: The signs were not primarily intended to convince Pharaoh, but rather the Israelites.
Portray him as superior to the Egyptian magicians: Although Moses did perform miracles that surpassed those of the Egyptian magicians, the primary purpose of the signs was to convince the Israelites.
Enable him to perform miracles before Pharaoh: While the signs could be used before Pharaoh, the immediate purpose was to convince the Israelites.
Convince the people that he has been sent by God: This is the correct answer, as the signs were specifically meant to convince the Israelites that Moses was sent by God.
The signs that God showed to Moses at his call were meant to convince the people of Israel that he had been sent by God.
